noticias.titulo: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
noticias.resumen: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
noticias.texto:
Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
- Published
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (Â£3,058).
The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
Its new owner has not been named.
Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.
Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.
McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".
Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.
Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.
Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.
"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.
As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.
In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

noticias.titulo: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
noticias.resumen: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
noticias.texto:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.
Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.
Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.
But tech stocks more broadly also fell.
Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

noticias.titulo: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
noticias.resumen: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
noticias.texto:
Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
- Published
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
- Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back 
  - Published2 days ago
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

noticias.titulo: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
noticias.resumen: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
noticias.texto:
Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
- Published
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.
Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.
US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.
Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.
He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".
India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.
At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.
"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.
Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.
The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.
Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."
- Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader 
  - Published14 February
- Who was Canadian Sikh leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar? 
  - Published2 October 2023
- Why are some Sikhs calling for a separate state? 
  - Published1 December 2023
- Canada accuses India of role in Sikh leader's murder 
  - Published19 September 2023
India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun said the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.
"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.
In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

noticias.titulo: Cost of living protests sweep across Europe
noticias.resumen: Thousands marched across European cities on Friday to protest against the cost of living and other issues.
noticias.texto:
Cost of living protests sweep across Europe
Protests took place across European cities on Friday as marches were held over the cost of living and other issues, including housing shortages and underfunding in education.
Demonstrations took place in Germany, France, Croatia, Italy, the United Kingdom and elsewhere, attracting a lot of young adults.
The BBC's Europe correspondent, Nick Beake, has been reporting from Rome, where thousands of people took part in a march organised by Italy's main trade union.

noticias.titulo: What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine
noticias.resumen: Russia struck bridges and railway stations in the capital Kyiv in a major attack.
noticias.texto:
What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The BBC's Sarah Rainsford is in Kyiv after the night of strikes.

noticias.titulo: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
noticias.resumen: When 16-year-old Landon Tresp met a teenage girl in an online game, it led to him and his mother helping the FBI rescue her from kidnapping.
noticias.texto:
How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
- Published
Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.
She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.
He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.
Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.
That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.
"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.
The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.
Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.
"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".
"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.
But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.
They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".
After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.
Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.
Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.
During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".
Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".
The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.
"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.
Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.
The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.
Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.
"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.
"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.
When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.
He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.
After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.
The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.
He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.
As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.
While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.
She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.
Law enforcement was "phenomenalâ¦giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.
Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.
But she kept any of those fears from Jenny.
"I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can â¦ Grab that basement door.
"I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front doorâ¦ do not stop.'"
The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.
Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.
He remains behind bars awaiting trial.
A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her.
"Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner â¦it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away."
"She's doing great for what she's gone through."
They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen.
"I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

noticias.titulo: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
noticias.resumen: Fewer young people have registered to vote in next year's election than in 2023 - are young people losing faith in democracy?
noticias.texto:
Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
- Published
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.
"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.
But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.
Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.
His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.
Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).
Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.
The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.
In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".
His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.
But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.
"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.
The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.
Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.
But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.
Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.
But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.
Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.
"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.
The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.
Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.
Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.
Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.
This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.
But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.
Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.
"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.
Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.
For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.
Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.
The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.
Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (Â£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.
The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.
The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; Â£56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.
Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.
These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.
Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.
The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.
Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.
"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.
"Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she says, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.
But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.
"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he says.
"The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the big positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal."
Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally important.
"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she says.
"Old men are still holding on to the system."
Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.
"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.
He said the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.
He called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?
"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

noticias.resumen: Bahrain has condemned Iran's strikes on US military assets in the Gulf country, as Houthis keep Saudi Arabia on edge.

noticias.titulo: Lebanese president demands Israel withdrawal, decries Iran’s interference
noticias.resumen: Joseph Aoun says 'two fundamental obstacles, inseparably linked' mean Lebanon cannot fully celebrate its independence.
noticias.texto:
Lebanese president demands Israel withdrawal, decries Iran’s interference
Joseph Aoun says ‘two fundamental obstacles, inseparably linked’ mean Lebanon cannot fully celebrate its independence.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has decried Iran’s meddling in Lebanon’s affairs and demanded Israel’s withdrawal from his country’s south.
In a speech on Saturday, on the eve of Lebanon’s 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun said Lebanon faces two interconnected fateful tests: the “Israeli occupation of parts of our land” and “foreign interference” from “some influential parties in the Iranian regime” through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state.
These “two fundamental obstacles, inseparably linked” mean that Lebanon cannot fully celebrate its independence, he added.
“Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks. And return our captives,” Aoun demanded of Israel.
Dozens of Lebanese citizens are believed to be held in Israeli detention centres, including civilians as well as members of the Hezbollah armed group captured during fighting in southern Lebanon.
The president also pledged to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control, declaring that there would be “no weapons outside the state that take orders from, or serve the interests of foreign powers.”
“You must hand over your weapons,” Aoun said.
Lebanon’s government has promised to disarm Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese group whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and that has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel.
Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement in June, following US-mediated talks, which included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanese territories and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
But implementation has stalled, with Hezbollah refusing to surrender its weapons and Israel continuing to strike Lebanon.
Israeli strikes
On Saturday, Israeli strikes hit the districts of Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun in southern Lebanon.
Al Jazeera correspondents reported that one of the air strikes hit the outskirts of Baraachit, a town in Bint Jbeil.
They said Baraachit came under Israeli gunfire at dawn and reported the movement of Israeli military vehicles on the outskirts of the town.
Israeli warplanes launched a second missile attack on the town of Kfar Tebnit in Nabatieh, after the first failed to detonate, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA).
The NNA reported that Israeli forces carried out three explosions in Wadi al-Khiam in the Marjayoun district, but gave no further details.
Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon have killed at least 4,386 people and wounded 12,407 others since March 2, when the latest Hezbollah-Israel war started.
Lebanon’s Ministry of Health said that since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, Israeli strikes in Lebanon have killed 8,953 people and injured 30,643 others.

noticias.titulo: Bahrain says Iranian attack causes fire at industrial facility
noticias.resumen: Bahrain reports no injuries, as Iran's IRGC says it targeted US military positions at two bases in al-Riffa and Awali.
noticias.texto:
Bahrain says Iranian attack causes fire at industrial facility
Bahrain reports no injuries, as Iran’s IRGC says it targeted US military positions at two bases in al-Riffa and Awali.
Bahrain says an Iranian attack has struck a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire, in the latest escalation of the war in the Middle East.
Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks late on Saturday.
In a post on X, Bahrain’s Ministry of Interior said the attack was part of “Iranian aggression”.
It said preliminary reports pointed to material damage but no injuries, and that civil defence teams were working to bring the fire under control.
The Interior Ministry did not name the facility or say where it was. Earlier, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain, and the ministry urged residents to move to the nearest safe place without saying what the threat was.
In a statement after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting United States military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain.
The IRGC claimed it destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
The attack was “in response to continued aggression and violations of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran”, the statement said.
“After two US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones violated Iranian airspace, US military positions at the aforementioned bases were targeted in an operation by the IRGC Aerospace Force,” it added.
Earlier, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported that the IRGC had attacked two military bases used by US forces at Sheikh Isa and Juffair.
The IRGC said that operation, as well as being in response to continued violations of Iranian airspace, came following a US attack on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island.
Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain had also crashed on Sitra Island and started a large fire. It cited an outlet called Bahrain News, which blamed a recurring malfunction in the Patriot air defence system.
Bahrain hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. It has been attacked repeatedly since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February, including three drone attacks in recent days after a lull of several weeks.
Other Gulf states have also come under repeated fire from Tehran since the US-Israel war began.
Reactions to latest Iranian strikes
In a statement on X, Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry called on the United Nations Security Council to take “firm measures to compel Iran” to implement Resolution 2817.
The resolution, adopted on March 11, condemns Iranian attacks against Gulf states and Jordan, and demands an immediate halt to hostilities and maritime interference.
The head of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) expressed his “full solidarity” with Bahrain following Iran’s attack on the industrial facility.
Jassim Mohamed AlBudaiwi, GCC secretary-general, said Bahrain’s security, territorial integrity, facilities, citizens and residents are an integral part of the security of the GCC states, and that the council stands united in confronting threats to their security and stability.
The GCC backs “all measures” Bahrain takes to deal with the attack, he added.

noticias.titulo: Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
noticias.resumen: The former president, serving a sentence for plotting a coup, is stable and breathing on his own, the hospital says.
noticias.texto:
Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
The former president, serving a sentence for plotting a coup, is stable and breathing on his own, the hospital says.
Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro is in intensive care after being diagnosed with an acute bowel obstruction, according to the DF Star hospital where he is being treated.
Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted on Friday with abdominal pain. In a bulletin on Saturday, the hospital said doctors have started giving him fluids and nutritional support, and inserted a tube into his stomach.
It said the former president is clinically stable and conscious, although they said there was no projected date for his discharge.
“There is hope that his condition will improve,” his son, Senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro, wrote on X on Saturday afternoon. “He is being closely monitored and is fighting to get his bowels working again, with his usual grit and focus.”
In the early hours of Saturday morning, he described his father’s difficult night of treatment, where food residue was removed from his stomach using a tube inserted into his nose, and bouts of nausea.
“I’m not a doctor, but I’ve never seen him like this,” he wrote, suggesting that his father might need another surgery, which would be his 10th in less than eight years.
“All this is happening to a man sentenced to 27 years in prison without having committed any crime, while criminals do whatever they want with what’s left of this country,” the younger Bolsonaro continued.
Bolsonaro has been serving a 27-year sentence since last year for an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro has denied the charges.
He has been hospitalised repeatedly and has had to undergo surgeries after being stabbed in 2018 during a campaign event.
He was transferred in March to house arrest after spending several months in jail because of his health issues.
Next month, Brazil’s Supreme Court is set to consider the constitutionality of a law that changes how sentences are calculated, which could shorten his sentence and those of others convicted in the 2022 coup plot.

noticias.titulo: Iran says held talks with Qatari mediators, urges US to accept conditions
noticias.resumen: Iran's foreign minister says reopening the strait is 'not difficult' if the US accepts reasonable conditions.
noticias.texto:
Iran says held talks with Qatari mediators, urges US to accept conditions
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says reopening the strait is ‘not difficult’ if the US accepts reasonable conditions.
Iran says Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran as the country’s foreign minister urges the United States to accept Iranian conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
News of the talks came as the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) toured an underground missile facility on Saturday and the country’s president said Iran is facing a “silent economic war”.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night and held two hours of talks with Iranian officials, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said, according to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy,” he said on Saturday.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. The conflict has drawn in countries across the region, disrupted shipping and pushed up global energy prices.
Gharibabadi said the talks have not yet become formal negotiations. If they do, the technical details of Iran’s nuclear programme would be discussed, he added, but Iran’s position is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country.
He also said Iran regards the US economic blockade as an act of war and will “take any action necessary” to break it.
For his part, US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a “permanent” deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are “very, very difficult”.
“We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he added.
Reopening Hormuz ‘not difficult’
The ongoing talks in the region “must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, according to state television.
“Our position is clear: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” he said.
“At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves.”
Iran’s conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Araghchi also said reopening the strait is “not difficult”, and requires the US only to “accept reasonable conditions that are in accordance with international law”, Tasnim reported.
The minister said there is “no solution” unless Washington acknowledges its mistakes and fulfils its previous commitments.
Iran has restricted shipping through the strait, which normally carried about a fifth of the world’s oil, since the war began. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports in response.
‘Silent economic war’
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that his country is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles”, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian told a meeting of investors and producers that “a group of bullies, oppressors, and coercers sought to bring down our country”, but that Iranian businesses had managed market conditions well.
He said the government was working to avoid power cuts over the winter.
Meanwhile, IRGC commander Major-General Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility, accompanied by Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, who heads the IRGC Aerospace Force, Tasnim reported.
Vahidi was briefed on the force’s readiness and recent developments in its missile programme.
The visit follows the Aerospace Force’s unveiling of a new underground facility earlier this month, where it displayed ballistic and cruise missiles and their launchers, Tasnim said.

noticias.titulo: Thousands protest across Europe over living costs and housing
noticias.resumen: Demonstrations in France and Portugal follow youth-led protests over education and economic hardship across Europe.
noticias.texto:
Thousands protest across Europe over living costs and housing
Demonstrations in France and Portugal follow youth-led protests over education and economic hardship across Europe.
Thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe to protest against rising living costs, unaffordable housing and cuts to public services, as students and workers demand action from their governments.
Demonstrators marched across France and Portugal on Saturday, following youth-led protests in several European countries on Friday.
The gatherings reflect overlapping concerns about economic insecurity, education and future opportunities, although their demands and scale differ considerably between countries.
In France, the Ministry of Interior said 82,500 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Saturday, including 21,500 in Paris, down from 106,000 the previous weekend. Organisers estimated a higher turnout of 150,000.
The protests, now in their sixth consecutive weekend, began in September with students demanding better schools before expanding to include trade unions and the Yellow Vests, a movement that emerged in 2018 over rising fuel prices and living costs.
Demonstrators have also criticised police violence and a new law strengthening protections for officers who use firearms.
Portugal protests
In Portugal, thousands marched through Lisbon despite heavy rain, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and relief from rising prices.
The demonstration was organised by CGTP, the country’s largest trade union federation, which also demanded higher pensions and cheaper essential goods.
Portugal’s housing pressures have intensified as property prices have more than doubled since 2017.
Average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 percent below the European Union average, according to the EU’s statistics agency, Eurostat.
The weekend’s demonstrations followed Friday’s youth protests in Germany and Sweden.
About 4,000 people gathered in Berlin, while police reported roughly 200 participants at a Saturday march in Helsinki organised by left-wing and student groups.
Organisers of an international youth strike said demonstrations were planned in at least 25 countries, with demands ranging from greater education funding and climate action to opposition to compulsory military service.
In Germany, the youth campaign Gen Z regelt, meaning “Generation Z takes charge”, announced demonstrations in 73 locations.
In Italy, a nationwide strike organised by the CGIL, one of the country’s main trade union confederations, disrupted transport, schools and some healthcare services on Friday.
Demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities, with union leader Maurizio Landini claiming more than one million participants nationwide.
While some protests were linked through the international youth initiative, others grew out of established national campaigns, bringing different groups onto the streets over concerns about living standards and government spending.
Separately, thousands protested in the Croatian capital, Zagreb, on Saturday over the death of a man at a psychiatric hospital.
Four medical technicians are under investigation on suspicion of aggravated murder.

noticias.titulo: Why is the US Army detonating lead-rich explosives in Iowa?
noticias.resumen: The delayed blasts have stoked environmental fears and concerns about health effects in the state.
noticias.texto:
Why is the US Army detonating lead-rich explosives in Iowa?
The delayed blasts have stoked environmental fears and concerns about health effects in the state.
The United States Army is slated to conduct two controlled detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the Midwestern state of Iowa, aiming to destroy 68 drums of degraded lead azide — a highly volatile, lead-based explosive used to trigger the main charges in some conventional munitions.
Announced just five days before an original Friday, November 20, detonation date, the Army’s decision was authorised by an emergency permit issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
Residents, environmental health experts, and Iowa elected officials have decried the detonation of lead-rich explosive material, citing scant public notice and potential environmental and health harms.
In a statement posted on X on Thursday, Iowa Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek stressed the need for greater transparency.
“Iowans deserve to know that every safety precaution has been taken and exactly what the associated health risks are. Until those questions are answered, the detonation should not proceed,” he wrote.
Mounting public pressure has prompted the military to push the controlled blasts back to Monday, November 23.
But a late-stage legal challenge has cast doubt on whether the army will be able to proceed at all.
On the eve of the originally scheduled operation, two Iowa environmental advocacy groups — the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter — petitioned a federal appeals court to overturn the EPA emergency permit, arguing that the agency had not given the public meaningful advance notice, failed to require adequate safeguards to protect human health and the environment, and sanctioned the operation without sufficient consideration of safer disposal alternatives.
Here’s what we know so far:
What is happening at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant?
In a November 15 advisory, the US Army warned residents of Middletown, a southeastern Iowa city of about 360 people, that the emergency blasts would loft a dust plume containing “some lead”, accompanied by loud explosions and ground vibrations.
The army’s containment strategy centres on thoroughly drenching the soil above the existing igloo-like, earth-covered concrete magazines — where the chemicals have been stored — with water before and during the detonations to help suppress airborne dust and particles.
The magazines are ringed by sand-filled barriers rising roughly two storeys high, designed to eject the force of the blast vertically into the sky, rather than laterally across the surrounding landscape.
“These measures should reduce the amount of lead that migrates from the detonation through the air off the installation,” the advisory reads.
According to the military’s modelling predictions, the blasts will deliver elevated airborne lead levels, but will remain “below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken”.
That’s reassurance with a blind spot, experts say.
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, an environmental health professor at the University of Iowa, who will be monitoring the environmental fallout from the detonations, says that for all the assumed precision of the army’s modelling, its most consequential variable remains undisclosed to the public: precisely how much lead each explosion will propel into the air.
It is the very quantity that will shape the scale of the downwind exposure.
“The unprecedented aspect of it is that normally in the world of air pollution, we have some estimation of what’s called the emission factor, the emission strength. We know how many pounds per second will be distributed out into the air from a smokestack,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera, “but in this case, we have no idea.”
The longer-term, more invisible peril, O’Shaughnessy said, is lead settling on playground equipment, getting into crops, landing in back yards and on other play surfaces where people could be exposed.
Why is the US Army detonating the explosives?
During a safety review in March, technicians discovered a stockpile of deteriorating lead azide that had languished in storage bunkers for 20 years at its Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a sprawling 19,000-acre installation in Des Moines County, about 16 kilometres (10 miles) west of the Mississippi River, which separates Iowa and the state of Illinois.
Since then, the Army says it has engaged with the local community, including at an open house at the Army Reserve Center in mid-October for residents within a 50-mile (80km) radius of the facility, where it outlined its developing plans to eliminate the explosive hazard.
The stockpile includes roughly 9,700 pounds (just under five tonnes) of the explosives across 68 barrels, set to be detonated in place — material that contains roughly 6,900 pounds (about 3.5 tonnes) of lead by chemical mass.
During long-term storage, liquid in the drums evaporated and caused the lead azide to recrystallise.
According to the environmental assessment for Lead Azide Risk Mitigation, prepared by the Army, the recrystallisation had heightened the material’s sensitivity to shock and friction.
“Due to its chemical degradation, the material’s legal status transitioned from a viable production component to an unserviceable hazardous waste,” the report states.
Army Sustainment Command spokesperson Justine Barati said the Army faced a narrowing window to destroy the chemical material before colder weather or disturbances increased the risk of spontaneous detonation, which would pose an unacceptable risk of killing technicians on-site.
“We’re trying to do a controlled detonation to minimise the impact to the community and the environment. This is not something that we take lightly. We know that this is a disruption to people and that is not our intent, but we’re trying to do this in the safest manner possible,” Barati told a local television news station earlier this week.
What is lead azide, and why is it dangerous?
Lead azide is an inorganic chemical compound made of lead and nitrogen, with lead accounting for about 71 percent of its mass.
Elemental lead cannot be destroyed by heat. It decomposes, melts, vaporises or fragments into fine particulate dust.
“Everyone should be shocked to learn this problem has been left long enough to warrant the potential catastrophic fallout from this situation,” said Dr Aaron Specht, an associate professor at Purdue University’s School of Health Sciences.
A fact sheet issued by the Army in advance of the scheduled disposal asserts that the heat generated by a proper detonation “incinerates” the lead azide.
Bruce Lanphear, a paediatric epidemiologist and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University, disputed the chemistry explanation.
“When lead azide detonates, it decomposes primarily into nitrogen gas and lead,” he told Al Jazeera, “the lead may be released as fine particles of metallic lead, lead oxides, and other lead compounds. The explosion doesn’t destroy the lead. It redistributes it.”
The risks of lead exposure are particularly pronounced for fetuses exposed in utero through the mother’s bloodstream, as well as the pregnant women themselves. Young children, whose developing nervous systems are acutely susceptible to lead, are also at risk. Because of their smaller body mass, comparatively little lead is required to reach biologically significant doses in children.
What are the health risks associated with exposure to lead dust?
Lead can cause serious harm even below regulatory limits.
There is no blood level of lead in a child that is deemed safe, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Lanphear has spent four decades studying how even low-level lead exposure can severely blunt children’s cognitive function.
“The danger of lead exposure as a distinct threat has been known for over a hundred years,” said Lanphear, “the neurotoxin causes permanent neuropsychological and developmental injuries … lower IQ, less tolerance for frustration, ADHD, and weak executive control functions.”
At high doses, lead poisoning can precipitate encephalopathy, a severe disturbance of brain function, or induce premature death.
Lead also figures prominently in cardiovascular mortality, said Lanphear, who co-authored a 2018 study estimating that long-term lead exposure was linked to 412,000 deaths annually across the US, including 256,000 deaths from cardiovascular disease.
The uncertain fate of Monday’s blasts
While the original detonation was scheduled for Friday, Army acting Secretary Adam R Telle announced on social media Thursday night that the operation would be postponed until Monday, which he described as “the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material”.
The Army did not announce a time for the deferred blasts.
Later on Thursday, in response to the Iowa groups’ lawsuit, the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted an interim stay of the EPA’s emergency authorisation, temporarily blocking the military from proceeding while the court weighed the groups’ request for a longer-term injunction.
It is an interim measure, not a final ruling on the legality of the permit.
The Army cannot technically detonate the chemicals under its EPA permit while the suspension remains in force, but the court may lift the pause beforehand.
While the court has put the brakes on the planned detonation for now, Justice Department lawyers, on Friday, pointed to separate emergency powers that the federal government could still invoke to bypass the permit requirement and press ahead with the blasts.

noticias.titulo: Noni Madueke salvages draw for Arsenal at Newcastle United as Raya injured
noticias.resumen: League leaders Arsenal miss the chance to go eight points clear of second placed Brighton, who play on Sunday.
noticias.texto:
Noni Madueke salvages draw for Arsenal at Newcastle United as Raya injured
League leaders Arsenal miss the chance to go eight points clear of second placed Brighton, who play on Sunday.
Arsenal missed the chance to open up an eight-point lead at the top of the Premier League after a stirring second-half fightback from Newcastle held the defending champions to a 2-2 draw.
The Gunners led on Saturday through Eberechi Eze’s strike after a dominant first 45 minutes.
But Mikel Arteta’s men were suddenly headed for defeat when goals from Harvey Barnes and Malick Thiaw provided a much-needed boost for under-fire Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle.
Noni Madueke salvaged a point for Arsenal and stretched their lead at the top over surprise package Brighton to six points.
However, the loss of influential goalkeeper David Raya to injury could provide a twist in the title race that many believed Arsenal would cruise.
Newcastle remain in the bottom half of the table with just one win in six games in all competitions.
Yet, Jaissle can point to his side’s second-half performance as a potential turning point after a difficult start to his reign at St James’ Park.
Arsenal move back six points clear of third-placed Manchester City, but missed the chance to put their foot down in the defence of their title.
Madueke continued his impressive form in the injury absence of Bukayo Saka and hit the post early on.
Former Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes was roundly booed on his first return to Tyneside since making a 75 million pound ($98m) move to the Emirates Stadium in August.
The Brazilian nearly silenced his former faithful when he prodded just wide from a Madueke cross as Arsenal pressed for the opener.
It duly arrived 10 minutes before the break when Kai Havertz pounced on a poor touch by Lewis Hall and brilliantly played in Eze to blast high past Lukas Hornicek.
Jaissle got the response he needed from his half-time team talk as Newcastle came out a completely different proposition after the break.
Arsenal also played a part in letting the home side back into the game and lifting the 50,000 crowd in doing so.
Martin Odegaard shanked his attempt at a long ball forward to allow William Osula to play in Barnes to level.
Suddenly, an Arsenal side that had kept seven clean sheets in their opening 10 league games was on the rocks.
Thiaw bundled home a second for Newcastle just 13 minutes later after Dan Burn was left completely unmarked from a corner and his header was only parried by Raya.
That proved to be one of Raya’s final interventions as the Spaniard had to be replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
Raya would be a massive miss if the Spaniard is sidelined for a significant spell.
But Arsenal regained their composure in time to salvage a point that keeps them well in the driving seat to retain the title.
Odegaard made amends for his earlier error by freeing Madueke down the righ,t and he cut inside before his tame deflected shot found a way past Hornicek.
Madueke told Sky Sports that he thought 2-2 was a “fair” result.
“Game of two halves is fair. First half we were outstanding. Should have got three goals, to be honest. Missed a couple of chances myself. Everything else was there,” he said.
“The second half, the first 20 minutes, was not good by our standard. When you give this team and crowd belief at home, it is difficult. We showed character to get back in the game, but 2-2 is a fair result.”
