noticias.titulo: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
noticias.resumen: The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma – a blood cancer linked to the herbicide.
noticias.texto:
Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.
On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.
The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.
Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.
In a statement, the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.
The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."
Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.
Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.
The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."
The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.
More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.
But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.
The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.
Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.
However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.
Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

noticias.titulo: The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals
noticias.resumen: We take stock of who’s up and who’s down after London and Brussels sign three new deals.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — U.K. and EU leaders on Friday hailed a “win-win” as they announced long-awaited deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth visas scheme. The reality is more complicated. A summit press conference failed to resolve questions over whether the much-lauded deals are contingent on a tuition fees agreement set to be negotiated over the next six months. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted that the deals are “done” and tuition fees are still to be negotiated — despite EU claims to the contrary earlier on Friday. If all the agreements take effect, there will be winners and losers on both sides of the English Channel and beyond. We take stock of who’s up and who’s down. Winners Students British and EU students are among the biggest winners from today’s announcements, benefiting from both a youth experience scheme and the planned tuition fee deal. Under the new scheme, 100,000 young people will be able to spend up to three years working or studying in Britain or the EU respectively — a significant improvement on current visa requirements. Under a deal yet to be thrashed out, students could also benefit from lower tuition fees when studying abroad. Two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to discuss the plans, said London had so far offered fees of £12,000. The EU would lower its fees too. If agreed, this would be a significant win for Brussels, with EU students currently subject to international student rates of up to £38,000 per year in the U.K. British supermarkets U.K. supermarkets — many of whom import from and export to the EU — were among the first to praise the agrifood deal, with major brands like Tesco and M&S saying the deal would make it easier and cheaper to trade with Europe. The deal will see Britain align with EU food and agriculture rules by 2028, removing the need for costly certification requirements and checks in a move the U.K. government claims could add up to £5.1 billion a year to the British economy. “Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow,” said M&S managing director Alex Freudmann. “When this deal comes into force, it will remove this bureaucracy.” That said, there are questions over whether retailers will be in a position to pass on any savings to the customer amid spiraling energy costs. Renewables providers British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive. Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers. “That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,” RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.” EU renewables groups have made the same point. The tech industry The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel. The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit. The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID. Of the more political parts of the agreement, the youth visas scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene. The City While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry. The City has been shut out of EU markets since Brexit, with only London’s clearinghouses, a key part of the plumbing of the financial system, maintaining the ability to directly serve European clients. Brussels for years refused to even talk to Britain about financial services until issues on the Northern Ireland border were resolved. Now, as Burnham pushes for better, financial services could yet benefit. While the City is in no great rush to give up the new U.K. regulatory regime developed since Brexit, there is hope of more collaboration in areas like investment, particularly for defense and start-ups, where both sides face a lack of cash and fears over economic resilience Losers British universities With so much potentially hinging on a tuition fee deal, the U.K. government is under increasing pressure to get this agreement over the line. But it’s also under a lot of domestic pressure from universities, which have warned the move could cost them £500 million a year — money that they say would otherwise be used to help fund research, teaching and jobs. Currently, tuition fees for EU nationals studying in the U.K. can reach up to £38,000 per year, in line with other international students, while British students pay a maximum of £9,790 a year in England. Hollie Chandler, director of strategic policy at the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said any reduction in EU student fees would “put pressure on U.K. student places and take more money out of U.K. higher education, without necessarily achieving the ambition of growing opportunities for EU students to study in the U.K.” Chinese carmakers It could have been worse for Chinese carmakers, but they aren’t in the clear just yet. The EU wanted the U.K. to agree to a commitment binding it to the EU’s tariff regime on Chinese cars and other imports. The U.K. successfully pushed back, instead saying it would “ensure outcomes consistent with the relevant EU measures in order to ensure that the supply chain in question is protected in a consistent way” across the two markets and “guard against potential risks of circumvention.” But as talks over British access to the EU’s Made in Europe industrial scheme continue over the coming months, that phrasing leaves the door open to raising tariffs in the future. China experts Gregor Williams and Noah Barkin had previously warned that “acting before the terms of Made in Europe access are settled would weaken London’s negotiating leverage.” “The UK has an incentive to signal a willingness to align with the EU while stopping short of imposing immediate restrictions on Chinese imports, not least given Beijing’s threats of retaliation,” Williams and Barkin added. They expect “some form of UK trade action on Chinese vehicles will come in the next 12 months.” Food manufacturers A major selling point of the SPS deal is the idea that it will bring down food prices for British consumers — one that government ministers have pounced on during the cost-of-living crisis fueled by the Iran war. But U.K. food firms have taken issue with this framing , pointing out that alignment with EU rules will mean costly changes for manufacturers as they align with EU requirements on issues like food safety, packaging, labeling and pesticides. In guidance published alongside the summit statement, the U.K. government sets out a series of transitional arrangements aimed at helping firms adapt to the new changes. While she welcomed the prospect of closer trade ties with the EU in the longterm, Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation, warned that “the timing remains tight.” She urged the U.K. government to pass the relevant legislation and publish detailed business guidance “as quickly as possible” to give firms time to make necessary changes. British steelmakers The deal might be a win for steelmakers in the long-run, but the sector will have to wait some time to feel the benefits. While the emissions trading scheme deal will ultimately spare Britain’s steel producers from the EU’s carbon border tax regime, it won’t take effect until 2028, leaving British producers exposed for at least another year. Brussels and London are also still in talks to forge a steel alliance that would see the two sides harmonize new quota and tariff regimes imposed in July after they slashed market access for each other. But they couldn’t get things wrapped up in time for the summit and talks are proving challenging. Defense firms Although the two sides committed to immediately setting up a new Dialogue on Economic Security to tackle shared economic dependencies, they said little about defense sector collaboration. Reviving talks for Britain to get access to the EU’s €150 billion SAFE fund for joint defense procurement loans “isn’t part of the summit negotiation,” Britain’s Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said Friday. But if the EU “wanted to return to it, I’d certainly suggest we’d be willing to do so,” he told Sky News. Potentially significant language in the joint statement includes plans to “enhance exchanges on defence industrial issues,” including the prospect of British involvement in the EU’s “Capability Coalitions” — groups of member states which pool resources and coordinate investment in making new defense capabilities.

noticias.titulo: Andy Burnham discovers nothing in Brussels is ever easy
noticias.resumen: Britain’s prime minister is banking on a ‘brainstorm’ to decide Britain’s future with the EU. He just has to get through the spin wars first.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Hours before Andy Burnham arrived at a long-planned U.K.-EU summit Friday, it seemed like it’d be a humdrum victory lap. Talks ran late Thursday but that always happens; Britain seemed to believe everything was wrapping up as planned; Burnham even brought a super-delegation of seven Cabinet colleagues. “Deal done,” texted one U.K. official at 14 minutes to midnight. The spin war only came Friday morning — and not for the first time in Britain’s long Brexit saga, it arrived in a dry technical briefing in the European Council’s Europa building HQ. A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.” This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling. Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa. They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme. David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what. Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.” “The U.K. wanted to get something on Made in Europe, so that meant tuition fees being delayed as well. Somehow this has turned into a great defeat for the U.K. government because everything would be at the mercy of tuition fees,” he said. “That was what the U.K. government actually wanted.” Opposition politicians seized on the row, with Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage calling Burnham “naive.” Oliver Lewis, the former Conservative Brexit aide who has founded a new anti-EU campaign called Stay Out, said he had “been played like a fiddle by Brussels.” Brussels waffle If intended to seize the narrative, the statement worked. Other EU officials tried to downplay its significance as the morning unfolded — the key phrase “equal treatment” was, in fact, not in the final summit text — but the issue still dominated questions at a joint press conference by Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. U.K. officials sprang up an unplanned briefing to counter-spin while Downing Street aides texted journalists with lines from a government spokesperson saying the deal was done. Burnham himself told the press conference: “I don’t think there’s any confusion at all. The deal is done. It’s there in black and white.” A senior U.K. official insisted to POLITICO that the three deals on food standards, emissions and youth experience were not contingent on a pact on tuition fees. Yet EU diplomats continued to suggest they were part of a “package,” a concept neither Costa nor von der Leyen tried very hard to shoot down. (Von der Leyen told journalists merely that the tuition fees deal was “on a different sheet of paper,” before Burnham was treated to a battered fish lunch with a dessert of fruit with actual Brussels waffle.) Later Friday, Britain’s European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told POLITICO he was “confident” that a tuition fees deal would be reached over the next six months. But the risk is not negligible. The six-month deadline to ink an agreement includes a French presidential election; if the far-right politician Marine Le Pen wins it could have unpredictable results for the EU’s legislative agenda, including Made in Europe. And negotiations on the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (the legislation behind Made in Europe) are behind schedule, with talks between the Council and European Parliament yet to begin and disagreements over the automotive package adding to the complexity. Lower tuition fees, please The Commission and Council statement Friday morning seized the headlines for two reasons. The first was that it indicated the three deals tied up on Thursday night would not go ahead if Britain broke its promise to cut tuition fees. EU officials insisted they were not holding Britain “hostage,” but it was difficult to interpret the statement otherwise. The second was the phrase “equal treatment” — which appeared to suggest the whole deal was contingent on something Britain was not even willing to offer. Britain has signaled it will cut the international fees charged by U.K. universities — often well over £30,000 per year — to a lower level for students coming from the EU. But crucially, the U.K. has resisted European demands to match EU students’ fees with the £9,790-a-year “home fees” paid by U.K. students. Instead both sides have talked about a figure somewhere in the middle; negotiators have discussed a possible figure of £12,000 in private, according to two people with knowledge of the talks, who like others cited in this story were granted anonymity to share candid details. This is a deeply personal issue for many European politicians and diplomats, who either spent their youths at Britain’s famed elite universities — think Oxford, Cambridge or the London School of Economics — or now have children attending them, or hoping to, at least. There were immediate suspicions on the U.K. side that the EU’s statement was a piece of spin in the midst of a negotiation. The U.K. is holding its cards close on tuition fees to keep leverage over Made in Europe. A resolution on both issues was delayed because Made in Europe, designed to protect the bloc’s industries from a flood of cheap imports, remains in its early stages. The summit text agreed by the U.K. and EU contained no direct reference to the scheme, merely a pledge to “limit negative effects on one another in their measures impacting specific supply chains.” Despite this, there was a view in the British contingent that the U.K. pushed the EU successfully for assurances on Made in Europe — meaning the EU had to flex its muscles somewhere else. “It was a pretty complicated discussion, and the British took a very hard line,” said one EU diplomat. This person added: “The discussion on tuition fees fell out because of the issue related to equal treatment… Ultimately, it’s not the statement we would have wanted, but with a partner like this, it’s important to maintain dialogue.” ‘Dear Andy’ Both sides put on smiles at the press conference, with Burnham calling the deals a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe.” Von der Leyen heaped praise on the man she referred to from the podium as “dear Andy.” Ultimately, the most important question about Friday’s row will be whether the deals Burnham announced are at any genuine risk of falling apart. “Six months seems a bit short to me” to sort out the tuition fees issue, said the EU diplomat quoted earlier in this story. British officials insist there is no issue. To make matters more complicated, Brussels is also pressing London to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, potentially tying this to Made in Europe provisions. The U.K. has yet to decide, though there is a widespread expectation among Labour MPs and some ministers that Britain will end up raising tariffs on Chinese EVs. If Friday’s deals do go ahead, the spin battle will be filed alongside countless other technocratic spats of the Brexit wars that fade into background noise. But even so, the deals are not expected to see the light of day until at least 2028 — undercutting Burnham’s pitch to the British public that they will cut food costs and ease business red tape. (The prime minister highlighted Treasury analysis that showed Friday’s deals could add 0.5% or £17 billion to U.K. GDP.) Implementation of the agrifood deal is not planned until March 2028, while a deal to link the U.K. and EU Emissions Trading Systems is only expected in the same year — meaning British firms will see no immediate relief from EU carbon border taxes, a further blow to the struggling steel industry. With the youth experience scheme not expected to be up and running until 2030, there are also questions over whether the program will survive the next election, which must happen before August 2029. There will be other challenges in selling the deal too. The U.K. claimed a late breakthrough on Thursday night in securing a role in shaping EU food standards rules — but hours later, Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds suggested Britain’s role would be limited. “We’d have experts in the room. We’d have the ability to put our point of view into that process. We’re not getting a vote because we’re not a member of the EU,” Reynolds told the BBC. Farage seized on this Friday, saying Britain would be forced to follow European rules on agricultural technology and pesticides rather than forging its own path. ‘Informal brainstorm’ Perhaps most importantly, Friday’s spin war is a reminder that nothing in Brussels is ever easy. It is a collision between Burnham’s big-picture way of doing politics and the EU’s hard, rules-based world. This will matter for a prime minister who plans to stake much of his campaign at the next election on a battle for hearts and minds over Europe. That ballot isn’t due until July 2029, but Farage predicted on Friday that the election would come as soon as May 2027, about a year after Burnham’s ascent from the Greater Manchester mayoralty to Westminster. As POLITICO reported this week , the personally pro-rejoin Burnham has not decided exactly what to promise the British public — and is caught between his aspirational rhetoric and the reality of a divided Cabinet. Now he can throw in the difficulty of dealing with the EU too. Costa reflected this neatly in the press conference, telling Burnham he was “always welcome in the EU” — but almost in the next breath, reminding him that the EU’s principles, including the “indivisibility” of free movement from access to the single market, would “guide our engagement with the United Kingdom.” Burnham plans to set out the options he believes are available for the future relationship next month, tied in with his promised “10-year plan” for Britain. It will kick-start a conversation that will likely culminate in a Europe-shaped offer to the public in Labour’s election manifesto. But he also indicated Friday that he would not seek more policy-by-policy deals with the EU ahead of the next election, instead favoring a broader conversation. Even Starmer promised “iterative” deals once per year. The U.K. prime minister also continued to be vague about how that process would unfold. He spoke of “informal brainstorming” with the EU ahead of another summit next year. “We are open for brainstorming,” Von der Leyen replied. Sebastian Starcevic, Sam Francis and Sam Blewett contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: France and Germany complete political deal for ECB leadership
noticias.resumen: Paris’ new market-operations portfolio at the European Central Bank could become pivotal in a French debt crisis.
noticias.texto: FRANKFURT — France and Germany on Friday submitted their candidates to fill two looming vacancies on the European Central Bank’s Executive Board, completing a political package that’ll decide the institution’s leadership for years to come. Berlin presented Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, as the ECB’s next chief economist, after the Irish incumbent Philip Lane concludes his eight-year term on May 31. Paris put forward Laurence Boone — a former minister of Europe and political ally of President Emmanuel Macron — who is now head of corporate and investment banking at Santander, to take over the ECB’s markets portfolio. That post will become available on Jan. 4, when Isabel Schnabel leaves the ECB for a job at the International Monetary Fund. The new set-up paves the way for Spain’s former central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to become ECB President once Christine Lagarde steps down on Feb. 7. The Netherlands had hoped to secure the top job. But having Dutch and German monetary hawks in what are typically the ECB’s two most influential posts would have been unacceptable to the dovish south, analysts said. If approved, Boone will step into a pivotal position at the Bank if strains in French and other European debt markets continue to worsen — a clear risk in the European Commission’s new forecasts that show many eurozone members’ budget deficits widening next year. In an October interview with POLITICO, former ECB Chief Economist Peter Praet said the markets role matters most when market tensions increase pressure on the ECB to intervene in bond markets. “I think this would be a very strong board, combining deep economic expertise, extensive policymaking experience and strong international networks,” EFG Chief Economist Stefan Gerlach said. “These are all important qualities, particularly at a time when the ECB faces considerable economic and political uncertainty.” Fewer politicians A board stacked with economic expertise would mark a break from the previous lineup, when former politicians, Lagarde and Luis de Guindos, held both the presidency and vice-presidency. De Cos and Vice-President Boris Vujčić are seasoned central bankers, as is Piero Cipollone, who heads the payments department. Before becoming a politician, Boone had been chief economist at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. While the reshuffle will leave the six-strong board looking more apolitical, the game of ECB musical chairs has been anything but, according to ING’s head of macro, Carsten Brzeski. “It looks like another masterpiece of French diplomacy and strategic personnel policy,” he said. “With the move to opt for the markets operation, France gave the impression of passing the more important job of chief economist to Germany.” “However, with a Spanish president and France holding the markets operation, the risk of a more dovish ECB has clearly increased,” Brzeski said.

noticias.titulo: Latvian leader calls for closure of EU borders to all Russians
noticias.resumen: Andris Kulbergs warned that Europe cannot screen hundreds of thousands of Russian tourists as Moscow escalates its hybrid attacks.
noticias.texto: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs called for the EU to close its borders to all Russian citizens, warning that the bloc cannot vet the hundreds of thousands of Russian tourists it still lets in. “Letting so many people into the EU is currently too dangerous. We must not give in to Russia, we must not show weakness,” Kulbergs told WELT , which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. “Nobody can screen that many people.” He also ruled out a return to normal ties with Moscow after any ceasefire in Ukraine. “Some believe that after a ceasefire there can be a return to normal relations with Russia. There cannot. It is a new era,” he said. Latvia was among the 11 countries that signed a Swedish-led letter in June urging Brussels to restrict visas for Russians. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner suggested to POLITICO in October that the European Commission could present a proposal next year. Kulbergs warned that Russia’s hybrid attacks on NATO’s eastern flank were intensifying. “The situation is escalating,” he said, adding that Latvian and Estonian special forces had arrested eight people on Estonian soil last weekend who had “concrete instructions to attack a production facility in Estonia that supports Ukraine.” Russia, he said, “is behind this.” He called the coming months “a winter of truth,” arguing that Russia was striking Ukraine’s water, heating and power supplies because it was making little progress at the front, while also trying to sway public opinion in Germany and elsewhere. “Putin wants the Germans to be frightened and to demand that their government stop supporting Ukraine,” he said. Kulbergs dismissed fears that Thursday’s summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen amounted to a new Yalta as “an exaggeration,” arguing that the Russian leader had been humiliated. The Yalta summit in February 1945, where U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin shaped Europe’s postwar order, is widely seen as having left much of Central and Eastern Europe under Soviet domination. Kulbergs urged larger countries, especially Germany, not to give in to war fatigue. “It is entirely possible to be pro-European, to support Ukraine vigorously, to stand up to the aggressor — and still win an election by a large margin,” he said. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

For Indonesia, easier exports of palm oil, textiles and footwear, and it arrives just before its current EU trade preferences end on the 1st of January. To discuss the deal Airlangga Hartarto, Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs in Indonesia joined us on the programme.

noticias.titulo: Rwanda return hubs may violate EU human rights law, MEPs warn ahead of 2027 deportations
noticias.resumen: EU member states are aiming to deport rejected asylum seekers as early as 2027. But many MEPs believe that sending them to Rwanda is illegal as well as wrong.
noticias.texto: Plans by five member states and Rwanda to establish a migrant return hub, as confirmed on Monday (16 November), could be in violation of EU human rights obligations – and liberal and leftwing MEPs are asking the European commission to review its legality. On Monday (23 November), at least 40 MEPs from the Greens/EFA, the Left, Socialists and Democrats, and liberal Renew, will write to the EU Commission to express concerns Rwanda may be unable to fulfil key conditions under Europe’s return regulation. They are worried about international human rights standards being applied toward any people who might end up being hosted in Rwandan return hubs. In 2023, the UK’s Supreme Court blocked migrant transfers to the east African nation on the basis of human rights concerns and the principle of non-refoulement. Despite no agreement having yet being signed with Kigali, leaders and ministers from Denmark, Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands announced in Vienna last Monday that a “partnership” had been agreed. Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, joined them in Austria to say human rights concerns were founded on “cliches.” Read more Five EU countries tout Rwanda deportation partnership, but no formal deal as key details remain secret The group met amid outstanding technical issues, with deportations to mainland Africa’s most densely populated country expected to start in 2027. Migrants from as far afield as Afghanistan could end up in Rwanda, a country most of them would have no connection to, if their asylum applications were rejected in the EU and they do not voluntarily comply with a return order. Right-wing and far-right groups in the European Parliament rammed through the return regulation, which broadly mandates deportations, in June. A letter by 22 EU leaders in August also urged the acceleration of the process after the mass arrival of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in north Africa in July. Guardian of the treaties Inscribed as a political footnote, the caveat on human rights monitoring in the return regulation is still to be seen working in practice, but MEPs still aim to hold the commission to its obligations as guardian of European treaties, in which it monitors the implementation of EU laws. noticias.titulo: ‘Fight for our future, not their wars’: youth protests sweep across Europe
noticias.resumen: Youth movements took to the streets of Europe's cities on Friday. Organised across the continent, they demand more government spending on education, welfare and action in curbing high housing costs.
noticias.texto: Europe’s young people from more than 20 countries across the continent took to the streets on Friday (20 November), joining forces in an International Youth Strike demanding a future built around education, housing and welfare rather than militarisation and war. Under the slogan “ Fight for our future, not their wars “ , more than 50 separate youth organisations joined the initiative, creating the biggest coordinated European youth protest in recent years. “We need a better education, we need housing, we need measures to deal with the rising cost of living,” Alessandro Di Miceli, an Italian organiser, told EUobserver. The movement demands that money currently being spent on militarisation and rearmament be redirected towards education and welfare. The strike is the result of months of organising. According to Di Miceli, organisations from around ten countries began coordinating in June, before the recent wave of youth demonstrations and labour unrest across Europe that spread across the continent over the summer. Read more Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down The forms of protest on Friday differ across countries, with some organising demonstrations and marches, while others will hold actual strikes. “The different modalities are due also to the fact that country by country, the political context is different. Also, mobilisation tactics that are used are also historically different,” said Di Miceli. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: Russian cruise missiles land in Poland, drones explode over EU diplomats in Kyiv (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,730)
noticias.resumen: With bridges shattered, power cut and ships burning off EU coasts, this latest Russian barrage also turns Ukraine’s struggle into a direct test of safety for millions of Europeans and the trade routes they rely on.
noticias.texto: Russian aggression has once again crossed Nato’s borders. Russian missiles damaged three Kyiv bridges, power outages hit several areas, people died at a railway station in Lviv, and a drone exploded above the Slovak EU ambassador to Ukraine. There is nowhere to hide, the Russians are attacking everywhere, a Slovak diplomat wrote from Lviv. Russians are sinking ships off the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts. The railway section of the Crimean Bridge was hit where the arch joins the pier. Ukrainian pressure towards Velyka Novosilka continues. The Ukrainian army has halted the formation of new brigades. Maps of the day — Velyka Novosilka Videos of the day — Russian weapons in Poland; a Russian drone over central Kyiv; the Russian air force receives another Su-57, while a Ukrainian pilot suggests it is not a new aircraft; HIMARS in action; a Ka-52 helicopter repelling an attack on the Crimean Bridge. Russian aggression has once again crossed Nato’s borders. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk convened a state security council after Russian weapons entered Polish territory during a massive Russian air raid on western Ukraine. According to the latest information, these were two Kh-101 cruise missiles and one drone. “We know for certain that we are dealing with Russian devices. It appears to be a deliberate provocation,” Tusk said . “It is difficult to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincided with an exercise by the coalition of the willing in Nowa Dęba,” deputy prime minister and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote . “This is a dangerous incident — it is a consequence of Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine,” Nato secretary general Mark Rutte added . The drones landed in the east of the country, in Molodych and Rudnik nad Sanem in the Podkarpackie region, as well as in Nowy Lipowiec in the Lublin voivodeship. This was not a minor airspace violation that could simply be brushed aside. Rudnik nad Sanem is 80 km from the Ukrainian border as the crow flies. noticias.titulo: Burnham hails UK-EU reset on food, carbon markets and youth mobility, after Brexit ‘decade of drift’
noticias.resumen: There was plenty of warmth on display at an EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday. The agreements on carbon emissions, food and youth mobility could form the foundation for a decade of closer EU-UK integration.
noticias.texto: The ‘reset’ deal between the EU and UK ends “a decade of drift and division”, UK prime minister Andy Burnham told reporters on Friday (20 November), after concluding a series of pacts with the EU at a summit in Brussels. “It is in tune with public opinion,” said Burnham, referencing recent opinion polls suggesting that 75 percent of Britons favour closer ties with the EU and “want a better deal than the hard Brexit they were given.” At the heart of the new agreements are food, youth mobility and carbon markets. The Youth Experience Scheme (YES) will allow 100,000 young people from the EU to live in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa. This comes in addition to the UK’s participation in Erasmus+ from 2027, agreed at the first Brexit reset summit in May 2025. “Brexit did take opportunity away from young people,” said Burnham, noting that they had been the biggest single losers from the UK’s EU exit. “We missed [British Erasmus students in the EU] so much,” said EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen. “The spirit of our cooperation is win-win”. Agreements on carbon emissions trading and food and agriculture, meanwhile, align EU and UK laws. Harmonising rules on emissions trading will also give the EU and UK mutual exemptions from their carbon border taxes. noticias.titulo: Estonia’s border closure makes Russia pay a price for alleged arson, as sabotage attacks spread across the EU
noticias.resumen: After eight Latvians were caught allegedly trying to burn down an Estonian drone maker, Tallinn’s swiftly decided to close its border with Russia.
noticias.texto: Estonia decided on Friday (20 November) to close all land border crossings with Russia from 1 December, in response to ongoing acts of sabotage across Europe. “Russia’s hostile actions have consequences. This is not a response to a single incident, but to Russia’s continued aggression, sabotage and hybrid operations targeting Estonia and Europe,” said the foreign affairs minister Margus Tsahkna. “We are protecting not only Estonia’s security, but also that of the European Union and the Schengen area,” he added. The move was announced earlier this month, following an attempted arson attack on a drone manufacturing plant on 14 November. Prime minister Kristen Michal said that the recent break-in at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia’s “wider hybrid war against Europe”. According to Estonia’s security service, Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, ordered the attack. On Monday, Moscow described the accusation as “unsubstantiated” and accused the Estonian government of “building a wall” between neighbouring countries. This was the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence company in the space of several months that Estonia has attributed to Russia. What happened over the weekend, and why is Estonia responding to Russian attacks differently from most European countries? A coordinated operation Early last Saturday, several people smashed windows at the premises of Threod Systems, a company in the town of Viimsi that manufactures long-range strike and reconnaissance drones. Its website lists Ukraine and Nato member states among its customers. The attackers then poured flammable liquids into the building. However, a security guard spotted them and immediately called the police. As the investigation is being conducted in secrecy, little is yet known about the planned attack. Estonian media reported that this was not a chance discovery but a coordinated operation by Latvian and Estonian security services. Agents from Latvia’s State Security Service (VDD) had obtained advance information about the planned sabotage and passed it to Estonia’s internal security service, KAPO. Thanks to cooperation between the two services, Estonian police detained all eight suspects that same night. All are Latvian nationals. Margo Palloson, head of Estonia’s internal security service, said that Russia was behind the attempted attack and that Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, had coordinated the entire operation. “This was another attempt by Russia to carry out sabotage in Estonia,” he added, saying that had it gone exactly as the attackers planned, it “would have caused the company very serious damage”. Palloson also said that no one was injured in the incident, the company was not damaged in any way, and its production and supply capacities were not disrupted. Although police detained eight people, only five were remanded in custody. “Estonia has long sought to be as transparent as possible in informing the public about Russia’s hostile activities,” Estonian security expert Henrik Praks of the International Centre for Defence and Security (CDS) in Tallinn told Euobserver. According to him, this includes prosecuting people who cooperate with Russian intelligence services, as well as publicly attributing specific attacks to Russia where there is sufficient evidence. Although the attack took place on Saturday morning, Estonian authorities and politicians attributed it to Russia as early as the following day. “This approach is based on the belief that decisive action against such activities and publicly exposing them can help deter further aggressive acts. Estonia proceeds from the assumption that Russia sees restraint and leniency as a sign of weakness that it can exploit to exert further pressure,” Praks explained. Estonia’s response will be exactly the opposite Responding to the attempted sabotage, Michal announced that the country would close all its land border crossings with Russia. He said the move was necessary to reduce the risk of further attacks and to send a “clear signal that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities are unacceptable”. noticias.titulo: ‘He who pays the piper calls the tune’: Czech media-freedom attack is part of wider EU malaise, ex-commissioner Věra Jourová says
noticias.resumen: Věra Jourová, former values commissioner and vice-president of the EU Commission, warns of the consequences of abolishing licence fees in the Czech Republic, while warning of numerous attacks on media freedom across Europe.
noticias.texto:
November has come around again, and at least in Czech Republic, it comes in a particularly turbulent year.
Those who can think as far back as 1989 may recall the wonderful and hopeful atmosphere of the Velvet Revolution. And if you smell a euphoric nostalgia in that sentence, your nose is working well.
I vividly remember people in the streets, united by the common enemy of Bolsheviks and the Communist party’s idiotic administration. Czechs revolted against a regime kept alive by most of its people surviving with bent backs.
And this year’s protests in my country took place under the slogan: “Don’t touch our fees”.
But most of us know that thinking of the controversial media bill merely as a “fees” issue is diversionary and dangerous.
Of course, it is possible to fund public service media from the state budget; many EU member states do just that.
But in the Czech context, the step is clearly an effort by politicians in government to take control of public TV and radio.
Some lawmakers do not even bother to hide their mentality of “He who pays the piper calls the tune.”

noticias.titulo: Listen: Europe relaxes methane rules while pledging to cut emissions at COP31
noticias.resumen: Negotiators from the European Parliament and the 27 EU member states agreed yesterday to postpone some of the rules aimed at cutting methane emissions. This happened while COP31 was still underway, with the EU pledging to reduce emissions globally. Can the EU be trusted to tackle greenhouse gas emissions?
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : Negotiators from the European Parliament and the 27 EU member states agreed yesterday to postpone some of the rules aimed at cutting methane emissions. This happened while COP31 was still underway, with the EU pledging to reduce emissions globally. Can the EU be trusted to tackle greenhouse gas emissions? In 2024, the EU adopted its methane regulation. So, what does it actually say? It requires companies in the energy sector to monitor and measure methane emissions from their operations, for example, during gas production. It also restricts venting and flaring. These are two ways of releasing excess gas into the atmosphere: either by releasing it directly or by burning it. Both contribute to global warming. Companies are also required to detect and repair methane leaks from their infrastructure. The regulation was also supposed to impose new requirements on imports of gas, coal and oil starting next year. But that will no longer be the case. In record time, the EU’s co-legislators have agreed to postpone some of these requirements by two years. Read more EU gives oil and gas importers until 2029 on methane checks, rules out more delay Importers will not have to demonstrate that methane emissions from the production of the gas, oil and coal they buy are properly monitored and verified until 2029. As a reminder, methane is responsible for roughly one third of global warming. In the end, the requirement to comply with maximum methane-intensity limits will only come into force in 2031. Why did the EU agree to this legislative rollback? The EU argues that the postponement is necessary in the context of the crisis in the Middle East. This, even though the commission has repeatedly said that there is no risk to gas supplies for the coming winter. Earlier this year, the US ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, criticised the methane regulation, arguing that it would severely discourage exporters from selling to the EU, including American companies. More than twenty organisations representing the fossil fuel industry in Europe and the US also called on the commission to postpone the implementation of the rules applying to fossil fuel imports. Read more ‘Made in Europe’ and low-carbon rules up for debate as EU eyes industrial law deal Two organisations representing the oil and gas industry commissioned a study from Wood Mackenzie, with the following findings: If the methane regulation were implemented as planned, up to 43 percent of EU gas imports could be jeopardised after 2027. This helped convince a majority of EU countries to call for a postponement. Environmental NGOs, however, dispute the industry’s figures. They commissioned a study of their own, which found no risk to gas supplies after 2027. This is the result of an intense lobbying campaign by fossil fuel companies and the Trump administration, said Jutta Paulus, German MEP from the Greens group. Following the agreement, her fellow MEP Dimitris Tsiodras, a Greek from the EPP, defended the decision, saying it provided realistic deadlines and the legal certainty that energy suppliers and operators needed, while maintaining ambition on methane emissions. But here’s the thing: in the end, the actual means to cut methane emissions in imports are just nonexistent: The new limits on methane intensity will not come into force until 2031.

noticias.titulo: [Interview] Scottish priority is to rejoin the EU after Brexit ‘badly damaged’ UK, Scotland’s Europe minister says
noticias.resumen: Scotland, which wants to rejoin the EU and leave the United Kingdom, has pushed for more free movement and less red tape for food and drink exports ahead of a UK-EU summit. Brexit left the UK "badly damaged", Stephen Gethins said.
noticias.texto: Scotland, which wants to rejoin the EU and leave the United Kingdom, has pushed for more free movement and less red tape for food and drink exports ahead of a meeting between the leaders of Britain and EU. Brexit has left the UK “badly damaged”, Scotland’s Europe minister Stephen Gethin said in an interview with EUobserver. He discussed Scottish interests, as Britain and the EU seek tighter relations. What are Scotland’s priorities at the EU-UK summit in Brussels? Stephen Gethins : I think it’s very important to be straightforward and tell you the context in which we’re having this conversation. Scotland voted to remain in the EU twice [In 1975, the UK voted to remain in the European Community and in 2016 most Scottish voters cast their ballots against Brexit]. Opinion polls tell us that three‑quarters of the population would vote to rejoin. Bluntly, our priority is to rejoin the EU. And we feel that anything that brings us closer in line with the rest of Europe helps. Leaving the EU is costing Scotland £9m (€10.7m) per day in terms of lost tax revenues. And that’s before you’ve even considered business being harder and fewer rights for UK citizens, who now have less rights than citizens in any other Western European democratic country. Read more UK-EU summit to see mutual love-bombing, but British must decide what to do next Leaving the EU was catastrophic, which is why I refused to vote to trigger Article 50 , and I stand by that decision. We obviously want to see alignment on food and drink, since it has become harder to import into the EU. We want to see further opportunities for young people, ideally a return to freedom of movement – anything that helps to unpick the damage of being outside the EU. But we have to be mindful of unintended consequences, and we must respect devolution , because we don’t obviously have the treaties in place that the European states do when they interact with each other. We lost the helpful umbrella of the EU that respects decentralisation, unlike the UK. Read more ‘Emperor’s New Clothes’: Burnham breaks 10-year taboo on Brexit The Scottish National Party has campaigned to break away from the United Kingdom, with EU membership lauded as a potential benefit. But under prime minister Andy Burnham, Britain is cosying up to the union anyway. So would you prefer EU accession via a newly independent Scotland or as part of the UK?
