noticias.titulo: Eleven killed in burst of violence during Mexican cartel leader’s capture
noticias.resumen: Seven alleged cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed in operation to arrest cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
noticias.texto:
Eleven killed in burst of violence during Mexican cartel leader’s capture
Seven alleged cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed in the operation to arrest Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
The operation to capture Mexican cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores in the country’s Sinaloa state has left at least 11 people dead.
Mexico’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed in the overnight operation.
Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was captured on Friday and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after hours-long violence involving a firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight, roadblocks and burning trucks in the city of Guasave.
Two other men were also captured and flown to Mexico City. The ministry identified them as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, an alleged financial operator of the cartel. Both were also flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, climbed the ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the boss of his own group, the Meza-Flores transnational criminal organisation.
He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos”, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which the United States designated as a “foreign terrorist organization” last year.
The US wanted Meza Flores for trafficking drugs to the country and offered a $5m reward for information leading to his arrest.
Residents terrified
The firefight in Guasave broke out about 7pm on Friday (02:00 GMT on Saturday), according to residents. Military helicopters and drones were soon flying overhead, with helicopters opening fire on key locations across the city.
Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below.
Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4am (11:00 GMT) on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to discuss the case.
While a tense calm has settled over Guasave since the operation, experts warned that picking off cartel bosses could set off more waves of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring factions.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on cartels and has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors. Homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration commended Mexican authorities, as did Washington’s ambassador to Mexico.
“Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” US Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post.

noticias.titulo: Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least 24 in Nigeria
noticias.resumen: Police say the boat driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
noticias.texto:
Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least 24 in Nigeria
Police say the boat driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
A boat believed to be carrying hundreds of attendees to a funeral has overturned in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, according to authorities.
The overcrowded vessel capsized on Friday in Bayelsa State after a mechanical failure while travelling from the communities of Ayama to Ukubie, according to police.
“So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing,” Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency, said on Saturday.
Rescue and search operations were continuing, he added.
Two children were among the four bodies initially recovered from the water on Friday, police said at the time, adding that 24 people were rescued, with 19 treated at a local clinic and five taken to hospital in the state capital.
Police did not say how many people were on board, but some residents told the Reuters news agency there were at least 300.
Police said the driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
According to a statement from the Bayelsa State Police Command, the accident occurred at the river junction between the Oweikorogha and Otuan communities, in the state’s Southern Ijaw district.
The boat that capsized was travelling “for a burial ceremony”, the statement also said, adding that police are “coordinating efforts with local divers and other responders”.
Such boat accidents are common on Nigeria’s busy rivers and waterways, often caused by overloaded vessels, poor maintenance, or failure to comply with safety regulations.
A similar incident occurred in August, when at least 51 people died after a boat sank in northwest Nigeria’s Sokoto State. In another incident, in January, at least 26 people drowned after a boat ferrying people from Jigawa to Yobe State capsized.

noticias.titulo: Displaced Palestinians protest as Israeli air strikes continue in Gaza
noticias.resumen: Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings as part of a 'gradual displacement' policy, a Gaza mayor says.
noticias.texto:
Displaced Palestinians protest as Israeli air strikes continue in Gaza
Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings as part of a ‘gradual displacement’ policy, a Gaza mayor says.
Hundreds of displaced Palestinians have protested as Israeli forces continue to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire.
Al Jazeera journalist Moath al-Kahlout, reporting from Gaza’s Deir el-Balah, said displaced Palestinians who live in the area near the “Yellow Line” gathered on Saturday to demonstrate against Israel’s intensifying air strikes.
The “Yellow Line” separates Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas in Gaza since the “ceasefire” signed in October 2025.
“More than 500 housing units have been destroyed in less than a month,” said Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir-el Balah’s Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera.
“This is part of what appears to be a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement aimed at forcing residents out of their camp and destroying as many homes as possible,” Musleh said.
Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing says 350,000 families are homeless after Israeli attacks destroyed 80 percent of the enclave’s homes.
Meanwhile, flooding in recent weeks devastated temporary tent housing, the ministry said.
The original “Yellow Line”, established under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, marked the area to which Israeli forces initially withdrew. They were expected to make further withdrawals gradually, but instead seized more territory.
“If we go back to October 2025, when the ceasefire was signed, the ‘Yellow Line’ was much further east,” al-Kahlout said.
Now, nearly two-thirds of Gaza is under Israeli army control or subject to access restrictions.
Rising death toll
Israeli attacks killed at least four Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday, including three who died when an Israeli drone struck a van delivering food aid to displaced people in Gaza City.
In the past 48 hours, Israeli strikes killed at least nine people, taking the death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,661, according to the latest report from Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
The ministry said 55 Palestinians were wounded in the past 48 hours, putting the total number of the wounded since October 2025 at 6,062.
More than 100 remains recovered
Gaza’s Civil Defence said on Saturday that its crew members recovered the bodies and remains of 129 people from 39 homes and other Israeli-destroyed buildings in the Nuseirat refugee camp, az-Zawayda and Deir el-Balah in central Gaza.
Rami al-Aidi, Civil Defence director in central Gaza, said 233 people had been reported missing beneath the rubble of those buildings.
The 53-day operation marked the conclusion of the second phase of a recovery project in central Gaza funded by the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Gaza’s Civil Defence said in October that about 8,000 bodies remained under the rubble across the enclave, including about 4,000 in Israeli-controlled areas. The agency warned that recovery could take eight to 10 years with the equipment available.

noticias.titulo: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba
noticias.resumen: New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people • Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research. Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian
noticias.texto:
British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.
Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.
In the 1840s, Cuba was the most important foreign source of copper ore for the UK. Copper was critical to Manchester’s cotton industry, railways and telegraphy.
Previous research has revealed that dozens of financiers involved in the founding in 1694 of the Bank of England invested in enslavement.
Now, Evans’s research reveals that ties between key figures in the UK’s financial system and enslavement of African peoples continued even after the government outlawed it.
Britain abolished its trade in enslaved people in 1807 and passed legislation abolishing slavery in most of its empire in 1833.
However, as Britain’s Slavery Abolition Act was coming into force, “City of London figures” were developing mining of El Cobre’s copper ore deposits, an operation which depended on enslavement in Spanish-controlled Cuba.
Key players in the highly lucrative operation included the Bank of England directors Charles Pascoe Grenfell (1790-1867) and William Thompson (1792-1854), acting in a private capacity.
Enslaved copper miners at El Cobre were likely to have been trafficked to Cuba by illegal voyages from the Bight of Biafra, in modern-day Nigeria, as Evans details in his book, Slavery’s Long Goodbye – Capitalism, Nationalism and Christianity in the Age of British Emancipation.
The death rate at El Cobre means it is likely that thousands of Africans were exploited there. Their life stories remain largely undocumented. At the time, slavery was legal in Cuba but the importation of enslaved people was not.
As a partner in the Cobre mining and export company, Grenfell was a driving force in enslaved miners’ exploitation.
Cobre was “likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere” by the 1840s, Evans said. Investors who held Cobre shares from the outset received £102 in dividends for every £40 share between 1836 and 1865.
Grenfell was also a partner in a Swansea-based smelter Pascoe, Grenfell & Sons, which bought imports from the mine, in an era when the Welsh port was the centre of the global copper trade.
Meanwhile, Thompson, a former lord mayor of London, exploited enslaved miners through the ore export firm he directed, the Royal Santiago Company.
The UK is facing increased pressure to make a formal apology to Caribbean and African nations for Britain’s centuries-long perpetuation of transatlantic chattel slavery. Commonwealth leaders say “structured dialogue” with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, will begin in the next year.
While the Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has claimed Britain has nothing to apologise for, scholarship – dating back to the Trinidadian statesman Eric Williams’s 1944 book, Capitalism and Slavery – reveals the global impact of the colonialism and chattel enslavement that was integral to British capitalism’s success.
Evans, a former professor at the University of South Wales, said: “As Britain ostentatiously winds down its own slave system in the 1830s, British capital is boosting slavery elsewhere in the western hemisphere.
“The illegal trade, involving French and Spanish merchants, was flourishing and substantial. There were British (anti-slavery) patrols off the coast of Cuba, but they’re relatively few in number and intercept only a very small proportion of slave ships.”
Conditions at El Cobre were “extremely brutal”, with daily violence and torture. “Slave catchers” were employed to snatch miners who tried to escape to the mountains.
In 1817, under British pressure, Spanish authorities signed a treaty that banned trafficking enslaved Africans to Cuba. But as Cuba’s sugar and coffee plantations relied on enslaved African workers, local colonial authorities ignored it, with 25,000 captives arriving in 1859 alone.
In 1843, pressure from the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society prompted legislation intended to prohibit British subjects from owning enslaved people in other jurisdictions, after undercover investigations exposed British mining companies’ activities in Brazil and Cuba, including at El Cobre.
But after lobbying by mining interests, parliament diluted the legislation, allowing companies to retain enslaved workers as their “property” and hire others. The concessions prompted abolitionists to withdraw their support for the law, which failed to end the exploitation.
Neither Grenfell nor Thompson appears to have faced legal penalties for their involvement. Grenfell became the Liberal MP for Preston in the late 1840s, later boasting that his father had been an abolitionist. Grenfell remained a B of E director until 1864.
Enslavement at El Cobre finally ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. The rebel commander proclaimed the miners’ emancipation on New Year’s Eve, and formerly enslaved workers later joined Cuba’s liberation army.
Evans’s book explores Britain’s overlapping histories of slavery, capitalism and missionary Christianity through the lives of Grenfell and two of his cousins.
Evans added: “The British in the early 19th century had started to understand slavery as a national sin.
“In the classical age of abolition, you could do things like abstain from eating sugar from the West Indies.
“But with copper, you can’t do that because it’s embodied in the industrial world, and, in the age of joint-stock capitalism, you have many British people who invest in mining companies who genuinely didn’t know these companies were using enslaved workers.
“Slavery was rendered invisible by the complexity of industrial society. But British engagement with slavery continued long after Emancipation. It involved the mercantile-financial elite of London as well as hundreds, possibly thousands, of rank-and-file investors from the Victorian middle class.”
A Bank of England spokesperson said: “We have previously acknowledged the role of former governors and directors in the slave trade.”

noticias.titulo: Fire at confectionery factory in Indonesia leaves at least three dead and dozens missing
noticias.resumen: Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says. Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.
Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.
Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.
The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.
“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.
Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.
Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.
“When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.
The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.
Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.
In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

noticias.titulo: South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
noticias.resumen: Choi Kyo-jin said he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams. The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam k
noticias.texto:
South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.
The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.
The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the entrance exams last week, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.
But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.
The annual eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.
“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.
President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.
Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old Choi replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew public backlash.
Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.
South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.
In the aftermath of the cheating scandal earlier this month, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.
With Agence France-Presse

noticias.titulo: Police say man whose body lay undiscovered in Sydney bushland for 12 days was killed in suspected hit-and-run
noticias.resumen: Joshua Howard, 31, is believed to have been struck by a car and thrown over the guardrail as he was walking home from a party in Rouse Hill Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The twin brother of a man whose body lay undiscovered for 12 days after he was killed in a suspected hit and run in Sydney says it has left him feeling like half a person. Joshua Howard was last seen at a bus interchange in Parramatta, in western Sydney, about 10pm on 7 November. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The twin brother of a man whose body lay undiscovered for 12 days after he was killed in a suspected hit and run in Sydney says it has left him feeling like half a person.
Joshua Howard was last seen at a bus interchange in Parramatta, in western Sydney, about 10pm on 7 November.
The 31-year-old was reported missing the following day and detectives later established he had been walking along Garfield Street East in Rouse Hill, in the city’s north-west, about 12.45 that morning.
An extensive search for began in the Rouse Hill area on Thursday with help from Blue Mountains Rescue, the New South Wales State Emergency Service and the Rural Fire Service.
His body was found by police in a bushland gully near Windsor Road in Rouse Hill about 2.45pm on Friday.
Superintendent Jason Joyce said police believe Howard was hit by a car as he was making his way home from a friend’s Diwali party.
“We believe he’s been walking along the side of the road and then been struck, and that’s propelled him over the guardrail into the bushland,” Joyce told reporters on Sunday.
“Based on his injuries … we believe there was some level of force of him being struck by the vehicle.”
It took police 11 days to start the land search because they were initially trying to track Howard’s movements through CCTV footage and doorknocking houses in the area, Joyce said.
Howard’s parents, Peter and Sue, described him as a loving son and sibling to his twin David and older brother Matthew.
He was a talented artist who graduated from the National Art School and always carried a sketchbook and pen with him, they said.
“When he was missing, David went through his room to see whether all those books were gone,” Sue Howard told reporters.
“But they were all there, indicating he was coming home that night.”
She said her family was heartbroken to learn they had likely driven past him the day after he was killed, without knowing his body was there.
“Our poor boy was there for 12 days,” she said.
She said David was particularly devastated, telling her: “I feel as if I’m half a person now.”
Peter Howard pleaded for anyone with information about the suspected hit and run to contact police.
“We don’t want Joshua’s passing to be wasted,” he said.
“We want drivers to know the impact of speeding or whatever happened.
“Think of others. Stop. Ring triple zero and take responsibility for [your] own actions.”

noticias.titulo: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
noticias.resumen: Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products. The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.
The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.
The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.
However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.
“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.
Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.
The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.
Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.
While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.
“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.
Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.
“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”
The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.
Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.
British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.
The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.
Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.
The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.
Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.
Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.
“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.
However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.
The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.
Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.
“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.
“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex

noticias.texto:
With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.
On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.
Those who flocked to the venue – which hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and is part of the same complex as the techno club Tresor – had come for the launch of Clarity, an AI targeting system developed by the German arms startup Helsing.
Kraftwerk Berlin this week apologised for a “serious error of judgment” and vowed to revise its commercial rental department’s booking policy, after outrage over the event rippled through Berlin’s music scene. The row has raised uncomfortable questions about the commercialisation of the German capital’s famed nightlife, and the culture sector’s traditional pacifism at a time of growing security threats.
The Munich-based Helsing was founded in 2021 and counts the Swedish tech entrepreneur and Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek among its investors and board co-chairs. On its website, it describes Clarity as an agentic intelligence platform designed to use drone, satellite and sensor data to lock on to targets.
It claims that human operators remain responsible for approving any strikes.
Helsing says Clarity is “developed and built in Europe under European control”. The market leader for battlefield software is Palantir’s Maven, the system that has powered US military strikes on Iran this year. European governments have been scrambling for alternatives to US-developed systems. France’s domestic intelligence service has already announced it is dropping Palantir for a homegrown rival.
But European governments’ boosting of their arms industries is also clashing with an anti-militaristic cultural consensus – nowhere more so than in the former cold war pressure cooker of Berlin, where nightclubs became spaces to dance away the anxieties of the arms race.
“The fact there is a war in Europe and that Ukraine needs German support should not mean that we switch off all our critical faculties,” said Michail Stangl, a Berlin-based music curator and DJ. “We are already seeing how AI-driven targeting systems are being used in Gaza, and it’s hard to imagine that once a company like Helsing develops a successful arms system, it would not sell it on to authoritarian regimes, domestic police, or organisations like Frontex to be used against migrants.”
Speaking to the German broadcaster RBB at its launch event, a Helsing spokesperson said none of its military systems were designed to identify persons, and that Clarity was built to seek out objects such as radar systems, launch pads and ships.
It also said Clarity’s agents specialised in “looking for patterns of behaviour”, which could be interpreted as relating to human activity. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment.
The Clarity launch event was condemned in the strongest terms by Tresor, a nightclub and record label that acted as a bridge between post-Wall Berlin and Detroit’s electronic music scene in the 1990s. “It has no place in the spaces our community has built,” it said in a statement.
Tresor’s founder, the Berlin nightlife entrepreneur Dietmar-Maria “Dimitri” Hegemann, is also the managing director of Kraftwerk Berlin. Hegemann has called the booking “unacceptable”, saying it was done by “a staff member at the company responsible for Kraftwerk’s commercial rental business”, without him being consulted. Given his central role at the arts complex, and the level of planning usually required for such a high-security event, this has surprised some Berlin clubland insiders.
That Berlin’s former underground music venues are rented out for commercial purposes is no longer a deviation from the norm. As recently as 19 October, Kraftwerk Berlin hosted an investment summit organised by the German government and featuring a podium discussion between the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and the chip manufacturer Nvidia’s then chief executive, Jensen Huang.
In a Q&A released after the Clarity row, Kraftwerk Berlin said it had declined a proposed Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams.
Defenders of such commercial usages point out that many of Berlin’s nightclubs are struggling with rising rents and plummeting bar revenues. Kraftwerk Berlin may not be one of them, however. The total assets of its operating company, Schaltraum Berlin, were reported in June as having a value of €4.3m (£3.6m).

noticias.titulo: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
noticias.resumen: As nationalist, Eurosceptic parties surge in four of the bloc’s biggest member states, the coming year’s polls could test its resilience like never before In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them. Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. noticias.texto:
In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.
Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.
Not quite three decades later, the continent’s politics once again seem to be tilting in a single direction – except this time, the momentum belongs to the nationalist far right, and the outcome could be a significant unpicking of the postwar European consensus that built the EU.
Between the end of this month and the end of next year, an extraordinary electoral sequence will sweep the bloc. Voters in four of the EU’s five biggest member states, by population and economy, head to the polls, with parliamentary elections also due in Estonia, Finland, Greece and Slovakia, and regional ballots in Germany.
Spain kicks off the cycle with a snap general election on 29 November, with prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s socialist coalition facing probable defeat to rightwing parties in the shape of the conservative People’s party (PP) and far-right Vox, which already govern together in some Spanish regions.
Next come presidential and parliamentary elections in France in the spring. The clear frontrunner in the presidential race is Marine Le Pen of far-right the National Rally (RN), well ahead of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and a hopelessly divided mainstream opposition.
When Poland votes later next year, nationalist parties that between them command nearly half the national vote could well unseat the liberal coalition of prime minister, Donald Tusk, despite recent splits. And in Italy, Giorgia Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party has far-right roots, hopes to secure a second term in elections due before the end of 2027 – while facing pressure on her right flank from the upstart National Future party.
Paradoxically, this nationalist surge arrives amid strong public support for the EU. Shocked by the chaos of Brexit and seeking reassurance in an increasingly alarming world, a record 74% of Europeans say their country benefits from membership, and very few Eurosceptic parties now advocate leaving outright.
The Eurosceptics and nationalists do, however, still view the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty, and aim to transform it into an altogether looser association of sovereign nation-states. In the words of the Italian political scientist Natalie Tocci, that means this coming electoral supercycle could “dramatically change the face of Europe” – triggering not simply “a slow erosion of the European project but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion”.
All elections differ and national specifics loom large. But analysts agree the underlying forces at work here are connected: sluggish growth, ageing populations, strained public finances and a spiralling cost of living have chipped away at support for Europe’s traditional catch-all centre-left and centre-right parties. The wave of youth-led protests sweeping Europe is only the most visible sign of deep voter discontent.
Meanwhile, nationalist parties have become increasingly adept at conjuring and exploiting an ever-evolving list of supposed threats and crises, from migration and vaccines to the green transition, support for Ukraine, globalisation, international elites and supranational institutions – narratives bolstered by Russian disinformation and overt backing for “patriotic” parties from Donald Trump’s White House. As a result, politics has fragmented, and polarised: nearly one in four voters now backs far-right parties – a share that has grown almost fivefold since the mid-1990s.
The rise has not been linear: over the past year or so, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland scored a historic regional election victory in eastern Germany, in the Netherlands Geert Wilders’s Freedom party lost nearly a third of its seats, Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz was soundly beaten in Hungary and the far-right Sweden Democrats shed support for the first time in 16 years.
But the underlying upward trend appears clear – fuelled above all, political scientists argue, by the normalisation and mainstreaming of far-right ideas, most notably on immigration. Centre-right parties are gradually dismantling “firewalls” that once barred cooperation with the radical right. At the European level, the centre-right European People’s party has increasingly turned to farther-right groups to roll back parts of the European green deal and tighten migration rules.
For the EU, the biggest impact of this election supercycle could be in the European Council of national leaders, which now features just three centre-left heads of government out of 27. If Eurosceptic leaders in France, Spain and Poland join those of Czechia, Italy, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia by the end of 2027, they would not have the numbers to rewrite EU law – but they would constitute a formidable blocking minority.
EU budget negotiations, future enlargement, aid to Ukraine and deeper integration in essential fields such as defence, energy, finance and technology could all face paralysis, analysts warn.
Safety in numbers, notes Tocci, could change current leaders’ behaviour in the council. Meloni’s relative restraint has been dictated, in part, by her relative isolation among mainstream peers such as Tusk, Sánchez and France’s Emmanuel Macron (alongside Rome’s reliance on €200bn in EU recovery funds).
If she were instead sitting down with the likes of Le Pen, Poland’s far-right Law and Justice (PiS) leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, and a Vox-backed Spanish government, with National Future’s hardline Roberto Vannacci breathing down her neck at home and those EU funds winding down, she might have less incentive to play pro-EU ball.
Analysts agree, though, that the decisive battleground is France. Le Pen’s election platform sets her on a collision course with Brussels: she aims to cut €11bn from France’s EU budget contribution, hold a constitutional referendum to proclaim the supremacy of French over European law, and breach various single-market rules.
And France “carries very significant influence over the EU”, said Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group consultancy. Compared with Orbán, he notes, a president Le Pen would have “far more leverage to carry out the far-right playbook of subverting the EU’s law-based, supranational architecture”.
Until now, Brussels has contained disruptors such as Orbán largely because there were rarely more than two or three round the table. A cohesive Eurosceptic bloc would leave the EU unable to enforce rule-of-law standards, further integrate economic and security policies or, indeed, agree on anything much at all. The first victim would very probably be Ukraine, with Le Pen leading a blocking caucus against further aid.
Three decades on from 1998, Europe’s coming elections, concluded Stefan Lehne of the Carnegie Europe thinktank, could well turn into “key tests of the EU’s resilience”. The threat to the bloc might not be immediate or existential, he said, but the medium-term risks were significant.
“A stronger role for the radical right may be unlikely to dismantle the EU as it exists today,” Lehne said, but could “prevent it from becoming what it needs to be to deal with the challenges of the future”. And gradually but inevitably, prolonged failure to act collectively as and where needed would lead a “loss of relevance”.

noticias.titulo: Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes
noticias.resumen: Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices. In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ accounts, a day after clashing with police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.
In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.
The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.
Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down on government orders, he added.
India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.
Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Meta has said it restricts content in India to comply with local laws.
Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing accounts.
A video from Friday’s demonstration showed protesters spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office and clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.
In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, online posts showed.
An opposition politician from Telangana state criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.
Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, also criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.
“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.
Reporters Without Borders has said the removal of journalistic content from social media has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media companies hardly any time to review and decide on takedown requests.
In February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.
Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4m posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.
“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.

noticias.titulo: Burnham should ‘move on’ from Brexit, says Theresa May, as critics hit out over closer EU ties – UK politics live

noticias.texto:
Welcome: Burnham should 'move on' over Brexit, says May
Good morning and welcome to our UK politics blog.
Brexit – or reversing it, 10 years after the event – is the topic dominating the Sunday politics shows this morning after major deals were struck with the EU on Friday on trade, travel, emissions and visas for young people.
Andy Burnham says these are the first steps towards rebuilding “the bridges broken all of those years ago” with “our nearest neighbours and our largest market”.
While he’s voiced support for re-joining the bloc, he’s also stressed that all options are on the table and there’s a long road ahead in convincing the British public and securing the unanimous assent needed from the 27-nation bloc.
Critics have piled in this morning, warning how tricky of an endeavour this could be. Ex-PM Theresa May, whose government was brought down by Brexit in 2019, has told the BBC that the divorce “is done” and he should “move on”.
That interview’s coming up on Laura Kuenssberg’s show later this morning. Meanwhile over on Sky, Brexiteer Michael Gove is hosting Reform and Tory naysayers as well as the European relations minister. I’ll recap their comments.
UK politicians uniformly condemn Trump's post calling Putin 'my friend'
European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer on Sky this morning criticised the post from earlier this week, where the US president shared a picture of him embracing Putin under the caption “My Friend”.
Falconer said Putin was a “butcher” and “not a friend of the UK”.
One area where the UK is absolutely and completely united across the whole political spectrum is standing with Ukraine against Russia’s barbaric, illegal war.
So would Vladimir Putin be my friend? No. And he’s not a friend of the UK either.”
He said Andy Burnham had also made the UK’s position clear to Trump.
The Prime Minister speaks to the president regularly, and is in absolutely no way pulling his punches about the strength of feeling that the UK has as a whole about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Tory deputy leader Burghart and Reform’s deputy Tice also condemned Trump’s post.
Burghart said:
“I’m sad and I’m depressed because you know the world that I grew up in was one in which the United States was a defender of freedom, and I worry that we might be moving into a world where that isn’t the case.
Tice said Trump’s post was “wrong at every level”.
It’s a grave mistake. He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator and no-one is in any doubt about that.
Govt can tackle Neets while also offering young people opportunity, says Miliband
Critics of the youth mobility deal have mainly focused on the idea of an “influx” of European youth competing with Brits for jobs when there’s this ongoing Neets crisis.
Roughly one million 16-24 year-olds in the UK aren’t in education, employment or training (Neet).
Miliband on the BBC, points out that the UK already has such youth mobility deals with several countries, and the offer goes both ways.
There’ll be young people from Britain going to work in Europe, and study, and live, and there’ll be young people from Europe coming to our country as well.
I absolutely believe we can both address the issue of Neets, which I think Alan Milburn did excellently this week, and we can address the issue of young people having the freedom to go and work and live in Europe.
I think young people have got a really raw deal over the last decade, and it starts to put it right.
Miliband says current food exports red tape 'worst of both worlds'
The Tories and Reform have made the argument this morning that the new food deal is “bad” for British farmers, because they will be subject to EU rules and standards.
They say more than 90% of British farmers currently don’t export to the EU- so why should Britain have to cede that control over standards?
The government’s response to this is that well, at the moment, farmers who sell into the EU already have to comply by the rules and also fill out loads of forms to prove they’re matching the standards.
“This is why it’s the worst of both worlds. We have to abide by the rules and fill in all the forms. What is the point of that?” says Ed Miliband on the BBC.
What we’re saying is that actually, yes, we should integrate into the market where for the first time, we’ll be able to shape decisions agreed to in the EU.
Reform UK’s deputy leader Richard Tice has also slammed the new EU agreements as “a really bad deal”.
He says “it’s not a reset, it’s a reverse” and claims that it won’t add to GDP but actually reduce GDP. The government says it could lead to a 0.5% bump.
Tice doesn’t elaborate on details here, or where that cost will come from but it appears his argument is: “The extra burdens of EU regulations that will be forced through dynamic alignment across all UK businesses is way more than that small net benefit.”
“Yes, a few exporting food businesses may benefit. But what about all the bakers in Boston and Skegness and elsewhere in the country who don’t export to the EU who will then have to suffer dynamic alignment amongst hundreds of thousands of other UK businesses that don’t export.”
Tories would repeal new EU deals on food, trade, youth visas
A chief concern for the Europeans as to the idea of the UK rejoining the bloc is frankly, the lack of British political stability this past decade, and the fear that a change in government down the line would lead to another backflip.
Burghart this morning went as far as saying that a future Tory government would reverse the deals secured on Friday.
Foreign secretary Ed Miliband on the BBC was also pressed on the business argument that cutting EU red tape on food and agricultural trade will make a grocery shop cheaper.
Kuennsberg raises the statement from the British Retail Consortium which says that the deals to cut red tape on food and agricultural products will “reduce pressure on trading costs” but are “unlikely to have any impact on prices in the near future” as “most of our food already comes from the United Kingdom.”
Miliband refers to the statements from the big supermarkets.
“If you look at what Morrisons, the Co-op, Marks, and Spencer’s, all of the food rate retailers have all welcomed this. And they’ve also said, it would apply downwards pressure on prices.”
He says the government won’t provide a number, or specify a certain item that will become cheaper but points out since Brexit, food exports have fallen 20% “because of the massive Brexit red tape that we have put on us”.
And this deal will make a positive impact on both exports and imports, and crucially- this is the point that I noticed the retailers were making - it will reduce the costs that the retailers face, all of that Brexit red tape, millions of forms that they were having to fill in, frankly, pointlessly, as a result of the bad deals that we had.
If people think the status quo is really good on Brexit and that that’s been great for Britain, well, they won’t like this deal. I think most people think the status quo has been actually pretty rubbish. And we need to make it better and that is what this deal does.”
Tory deputy head Alex Burghart has been arguing against the deals on Sky and the BBC this morning.
He argues the removal of red tape on food and agricultural products is “really bad for business” as British farmers now will have to follow EU regulations when some don’t even trade with the bloc.
He says this is a “a huge deadweight cost for them”, and that that the EU has added even more regulations in recent years.
He also says that linking the emissions schemes means that “forces the UK to adopt the higher price of carbon that EU puts on businesses”, and he argues that the 100,000 places youth mobility scheme will take jobs away from young Brits.
Gove puts to him that “business is pretty clear, that it’s a good deal” and “almost every supermarket CEO says it will be good for consumers.”
“So you’re setting yourselves against businesses, and cheaper prices.”
Theresa May spent three years as prime minister (2016-2019) trying to negotiate the Brexit deal, before resigning.
She has told the BBC this morning she is “aghast” at the idea of Burnham resurrecting the issue, warning him of the enormous effort ahead:
What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it’s across the whole of government. It’s not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers’ time, officials’ time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you’re getting out what you want.
And that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU.
And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit. When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote.
So I’m afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.
A summit in Brussels this week produced agreements which will:
Allow 100,000 young adults from each side to live and work in the other’s countries for up to three years
Scrap border checks on plant and animal products, which Burnham says will lower the cost of food
Link emissions trading schemes, lowering carbon taxes on some exports
The PM says these first package of deals will create opportunities for young people and keep supermarket prices down. Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Co-op, has been among the supermarket giants welcoming the move for customers.
At Brussels, there were also commitments to keep negotiating other areas. One key subject to be sorted out in the next six months is university fees for European students in the UK and vice versa.
An EU official briefing media said negotiations hadn’t been easy but there had been good will to find solutions.

noticias.titulo: Exquisitely decorated home of Victorian workman David Parr wins blue plaque
noticias.resumen: Working-class man who covered mansions with William Morris’s patterns spent his nights filling his Cambridge terrace house with his own designs As a Victorian working-class labourer, David Parr was paid to spend his days decorating the interiors of private mansions and Cambridge colleges with William Morris’s magnificent designs. But as an artist, Parr chose to spend his nights filling his modest two-bed terrace house with the most resplendent decor and exquisite craftsmanship he could create. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
As a Victorian working-class labourer, David Parr was paid to spend his days decorating the interiors of private mansions and Cambridge colleges with William Morris’s magnificent designs.
But as an artist, Parr chose to spend his nights filling his modest terrace house with the most resplendent decor and exquisite craftsmanship he could create.
Often working by candlelight, he spent 40 years covering his walls and ceilings with his own designs, inspired by the Morris patterns his elite clients coveted for their far grander homes and dining halls.
Yet while Morris and his wallpaper became legendary, Parr’s contributions to the Arts and Crafts movement – like those of the other skilled “art-workmen” who painted Morris’s designs – went unnoticed and overlooked.
His extraordinary home on Gwydir Street in Cambridge, which was preserved by his granddaughter Elsie throughout her lifetime, lay hidden behind an ordinary front door for more than 80 years after his death in 1927.
Now, Parr is to be honoured with a blue plaque, thought to be the first ever dedicated to a working-class Victorian art-workman.
“The Victorians used the term ‘art-workman’ for the skilled painters, carvers and craftsmen who turned designers’ ideas into finished work, usually as employees of a decorating firm,” said Annabelle Campbell, the director of the David Parr House & Gallery charity. “Their work demanded great accuracy and artistry, yet they sat at the bottom of a hierarchy of client, designer and firm, and were rarely named.”
The plaque will be unveiled on 8 February 2027, the anniversary of the day in 1886 that Parr signed the mortgage on his home, which was acquired by the charity after Elsie’s death and opened to the public in 2019.
The David Parr House, as it is now known, was discovered by accident in 2009. Tamsin Wimhurst, a social historian, knocked on 93-year-old Elsie’s door and found herself standing inside the astonishing living room of the small Victorian worker’s cottage, staring at the century-old hand-painted walls in disbelief.
“David Parr’s life was transformed by his apprenticeship and the varied and significant opportunities it opened up,” said Campbell. “As a highly skilled art-workman employed by FR Leach & Sons [a Cambridge-based decorative arts company], he was one of a class of unnamed workers who brought to reality the designs and schemes of the great figures of the Arts and Crafts movement, most notably William Morris and George Bodley.”
Yet in the records of his working life, his name appeared only as initials in a wage list, if at all, she said.
“The plaque recognises the importance of the art-workman within the successful Victorian decorative arts economy. It also recognises the vision and aspiration of a working-class family man.”
Parr spent all his free time decorating his home with designs he came up with himself, while engrossed in the work of Morris and Bodley. “He was inspired to create a house for his own family that was just as beautiful, on a smaller scale, as those he was painting.”
Many of Cambridge’s existing blue plaques honour elite academics such as Bertrand Russell and John Maynard Keynes. Campbell is proud that the new plaque will highlight the working-class heritage of the Mill Road area of the city and its important contribution to the nation’s cultural history. “Lots of these houses were occupied by highly skilled working-class Victorian artisans,” she said. “Who is commemorated with a blue plaque is changing.”
The charity is in the process of crowdfunding £6,000 to pay for a ceramic plaque to be made by a local artist, David Stonehouse, along with a short film that documents its making and an exhibition. “We don’t want to just badge the house, but to add a new layer to its history,” Campbell said. “At David Parr House, the maker, the making and the made are of equal importance and value.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Intimidating’ vigilantes posing as far-right security on the rise, UK experts say
noticias.resumen: Volunteers in black uniforms and body armour increasingly seen with figures such as Tommy Robinson There is a worrying rise in “reckless and intimidating” vigilantes posing as security guards around far-right figures, security experts have said. In recent months, uniformed figures wearing all black and body armour have been seen in the entourages of far-right figures including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who goes by the name Tommy Robinson, and Paul Golding, the leader of the far-right political party Britain First. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
There is a worrying rise in “reckless and intimidating” vigilantes posing as security guards around far-right figures, security experts have said.
In recent months, uniformed figures wearing all black and body armour have been seen in the entourages of far-right figures including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who goes by the name Tommy Robinson, and Paul Golding, the leader of the far-right political party Britain First.
This group of “security volunteers” has also been seen at far-right protests, most recently this week in London and in Oxford, where the controversial “race philosopher” Nathan Cofnas was due to speak. They were seen scuffling with anti-racism protesters. They have also provided security for the rightwing provocateur Katie Hopkins.
The ensemble calls itself British Security UK (BSUK), and says it is a volunteer-led security group. Those who join it are given all-black uniforms featuring black and white union flags, and they are not required to have any security qualifications or training.
Usually security guards are asked to have a Security Industry Authority (SIA) qualification, meaning they know how to de-escalate situations, only use proportionate force and are trained in keeping members of the public safe.
The website for the “security service” carries the disclaimer: “BSUK is not the police. Wearing BSUK uniform does not confer police powers. Any security services requiring an SIA licence must be carried out by appropriately licensed personnel. For emergencies, call 999.”
The registered director of BSUK is Anthony Roberts, 53, who has volunteered as a security guard for Yaxley-Lennon and Golding. He wears combat trousers, a union jack-emblazoned body armour kit, and has facial tattoos.
Posting on social media, he said “the police never handle the left properly … [they] let them run riot” because of “DEI training”. He said his organisation was “there to observe the police do their job, hold them accountable to the very laws we live under, and showcase the two-tier society we all live under”.
He appears to share political views with those his group “protects”. He has posted on social media in favour of “remigration” and described the UK as a “playground for savages” as a result of immigration. Roberts also appears to be a supporter of the hard-right political party Restore UK and has posed for photographs with its leader, Rupert Lowe.
Daniel Garnham, the general secretary of the Security Industry Federation and a police officer for 20 years, said he was concerned by the rise of “street vigilantes” disguised as legitimate security officers.
“It is definitely on the rise, I put it in the category of vigilantism and people who are based in rightwing politics that want to make a point and a protest. I don’t see it as legitimate security,” he told the Guardian. “They have security in their name but it is a vigilante group.”
Garnham said no one should be acting as a security officer without an SIA licence: “My concern is the people who sign up for this in a voluntary role, they aren’t covered, they aren’t trained and they do not have insurance or trade union support. These people are not trained in personal force.”
Roberts has said that his group does not need to be trained or licensed, explaining: “Under UK law (Private Security Industry Act 2001), SIA licences are only required for paid/contracted security work. Genuine unpaid volunteers with an agreement of no payment or reward do not need licences.”
Garnham disagreed. He argued: “It gives off the wrong message. They call themselves British Security, members of the public could be fooled into thinking they are actual security when they aren’t.”
He said he thought the mass of people dressed in black and body armour could intimidate members of the public, adding: “I think the uniform they wear is intimidating, it’s all black, with masks. This organisation shouldn’t be advertising themselves as security and shouldn’t be turning up en masse at these events. It is irresponsible and absolutely reckless.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “No one is ever entitled to intimidate or incite disorder. Anyone who breaks the law will rightly face the full force of the law.”
Rightwing figures have made increasing use of private security in recent years. There is no suggestion any of these security guards do not have the appropriate qualifications and training.
One of Nigel Farage’s security team who accompanied him on the local election campaign trail this year was facing a rape charge and was later jailed for eight years, which raised questions around vetting within Reform UK.
Roberts did not respond to a request for comment, but posted on social media after being approached: “Under the Private Security Industry Act 2001 and current SIA guidance, genuinely unpaid volunteers do not need an SIA licence, provided they have a written or spoken agreement that they will receive no payment or reward for the work.
“It has come to our attention that sections of the mainstream media are preparing critical coverage of myself and my team. We are accustomed to this. Those of us who seek to contribute positively to our communities and country are frequently subjected to scrutiny that appears more interested in fitting a preferred narrative than in examining the facts.”

noticias.titulo: Labour MPs sign up for leadership course to counter rightwing populism
noticias.resumen: Course run by former No 10 advisers is funded by Gary Lubner, who has given more than £11m to Labour More than 20 Labour MPs have signed up to a year-long leadership course helping them to counter rightwing populism and deal with hostility, run by two former No 10 advisers and ultimately funded by multimillionaire donor Gary Lubner. The training courses worth about £9,600 are being led by Ruth Turner, who was Tony Blair’s director of government relations, and Peter Hyman, who has worked for Blair, Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham’s governments. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
More than 20 Labour MPs have signed up to a year-long leadership course helping them to counter rightwing populism and deal with hostility, run by two former No 10 advisers and ultimately funded by multimillionaire donor Gary Lubner.
The training courses worth about £9,600 are being led by Ruth Turner, who was Tony Blair’s director of government relations, and Peter Hyman, who has worked for Blair, Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham’s governments.
About 18 MPs including former ministers Dawn Butler, Rachel Blake and Fleur Anderson declared their attendance at a three-day residential training course from a company called August Ltd, which is owned by Turner. Several more have been trained by the programme without attending the awaydays.
The programme on the “craft of leadership” and the “unique demands” facing MPs is ultimately being funded by a grant from Lubner, who made his fortune running the car repair company Autoglass.
He has given more than £11m to Labour and the thinktank Labour Together, now known as ThinkLabour. Under the terms of the grant, Lubner does not have any influence over or input into the leadership course.
Three themes of the sessions are resilience, agency and teamwork, with MPs also learning about countering far-right populism, including how algorithms can radicalise people and allow their grievances to be exploited.
Turner said she and Hyman came up with the idea for better training for MPs on leadership after seeing how many are thrown into the deep end on entering the House of Commons.
She said from her time at No 10 it struck her “that we were getting very senior people to make consequential decisions and largely keeping them quite isolated and unsupported”. She said ministers now get training from the Institute for Government and other places but “backbenchers are a much more neglected bunch”.
Turner said the MPs had helped to “co-design” the programme based on what they need as they learn how to navigate an “age of upheaval”.
She said that one of the learning areas was about “individual resilience” and the “sense of threat that MPs have – not just the physical threat, but also just the hostility that they face”.
She added: “I’m not sure people perform at their best when they’re feeling constantly under threat.”
Turner said teamwork was a “really underbaked quality in a sector that can be hyper-individualised, and hyper-competitive” but it was important for MPs to work together and with people leading society and business leaders in their constituencies .
She said another one of the aims was for the current MPs on the leadership course “to help shift the culture a little bit to make [it] much more normal” to undergo training.
When entering the Commons, MPs do not get mandatory training on how to do their jobs or hold leadership roles, which span from attending to parliamentary business to dealing with the concerns of constituents.
They are not employed by the House of Commons, and operate as effectively self-employed people, making them responsible for their own training and development as well as that of their staff.

noticias.titulo: Conservative media weighs its future as cracks emerge in Trump’s movement
noticias.resumen: Two weeks after Democrats flipped Congress, conservative outlets are having conversations on whether to distance themselves from Trump or double down on Maga As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy. “In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year
noticias.texto:
As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy.
“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as the president’s director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.
But two weeks on, Trump’s electoral wipeout is facilitating difficult conversations about the future of the conservative media ecosystem – and whether outlets that target a Republican-voting audience need to create some distance from an unpopular president. Some other outlets, like the Maga-aligned Real America’s Voice News network, are planning to go the other direction and double down on Trump.
“The whole landscape can now be reordered, and I think it will be,” said Steve Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump during his first administration who now hosts a show for Real America’s Voice.
Several conservative media personalities pinned the blame on Fox News for leading the party – and Trump – astray, with former host Tucker Carlson saying that the results signaled the end of “the Fox News era”. (Carlson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.)
Bannon, who contends that Rupert Murdoch has long “hated Trump”, predicted that the network will utilize the party’s recent “rejection” at the polls to move away from Trump and embrace more traditional, George W Bush-era Republican priorities.
“They’re going to try to kick Trump into the dustbin,” he said. “They clearly have moved beyond Trump and they want to move beyond Trumpism … What they’re going to do is, with a thousand cuts, convince their ageing audience that Maga and what Maga stands for is too extreme.”
In contrast, Bannon said he expects Real America’s Voice and other outlets to “triple down” on the Maga movement and “populist nationalism.”
Bannon is not alone in his criticism of Murdoch’s media empire. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter said that she views the channel and its sister outlet, the New York Post, as “90% responsible for the GOP wipeout in the midterm elections”, blaming voices in the Murdoch media empire for encouraging Trump to launch – and sustain – an unpopular war against Iran.
Atlanta-based conservative radio host Erick Erickson said a realignment away from Trump will probably start in his medium before it carries over to conservative television – though he said it will take time, and will depend on how important access is for certain personalities.
“The more often you spend time at Mar-a-Lago, the less likely you are to distance yourself from Trump, because you still want in,” said Erickson, who vocally opposed Trump in 2016 before coming around ahead of his 2020 re-election bid.
Charlie Sykes, a former conservative radio host who also opposed Trump from the beginning, said the election has shown “cracks in that alternative reality silo” on Trump-aligned channels and platforms.
“In general, I think the scope of the blowout was just so great that even deep in the rightwing media ecosystem, they had to feel the tremors of it,” said Sykes, a former MS Now commentator who now writes on Substack. “And so that has been kind of interesting, this sense of like, ‘OK, we need to really come to grips with this and maybe figure out a way to move on.’”
Trump’s decision to attack Iran in February fomented division within the conservative media ecosystem, with many commentators viewing it as an abdication of his promise to abstain from foreign wars and focus on the US.
“I think those divisions are just going to widen,” Sykes said.
The Daily Caller, which was co-founded by Carlson in 2010 as something of a conservative alternative to the New York Times, made waves ahead of the midterms for calling out Trump’s war against Iran – and the high prices that have come out of it. “The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post-Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intraparty media battle,” the digital publication Semafor wrote on 1 November.
In an interview, Daily Caller editor-in-chief Amber Duke said the publication is more focused on reflecting the mood of the American people – particularly younger people affected by a challenging economy – than boosting Trump and the Maga movement.
“I think what we are doing is so unique that we are really setting ourselves apart,” she said. “We view ourselves as a principled, America-first outlet. I think there’s a difference between Maga and America-first.”
Duke also acknowledged the economic opportunities that drive support for the president. “Trump is a content goldmine. He drives a lot of traffic, a lot of clicks,” she said. “That content mine is eventually going to dry up. I would definitely be concerned if I had my entire business model tied around this uniquely celebrity-oriented newsmaker. How am I going to continue to stay in business after that? For us, it’s: Let’s just tell the truth to the American people, and that truth is not going to be dependent on any one person or political party.”
Some conservative outlets that are closely tied to Trump, however, don’t see any reason to do anything differently.
“Nothing changes with us,” Newsmax chief executive Christopher Ruddy said. “We’re going to continue reporting on the administration and we will continue to cover the Congress. We make a very concerted effort to always get both sides on our reports and in our TV opinion segments.”
Charles Herring, president of the far-right One America News Network, echoed that sentiment: “Our reporting doesn’t change based on the political pendulum or who resides in the White House. We are working hard every day to further enhance our coverage for our viewers.”
