Still, there are limits to how far some conservative media organizations can stray from the president, considering the economic imperative to retain a pro-Trump audience. “The thing to understand about conservative media is that it’s not necessarily always top down,” Sykes said. “It’s often: What will the audience tolerate? … Nobody wants to get too crosswise with their audience.”
But the vast majority of conservative news sites have already seen declines in online traffic in recent months, according to industry tracker Howard Polskin, an early warning sign for the party’s midterm chances. “Audiences are not buying what Maga media is selling anymore,” he said.
“My prediction would be that in the next two years, rightwing media will become fractured with more infighting, breaking into two camps: pro-Maga/Trump and anti-Maga/Trump,” Polskin added. “Traffic to rightwing websites will continue to nose dive, much more so than mainstream media.”
Several conservative media veterans who spoke with the Guardian said the selection of a 2028 Republican presidential nominee will probably be a defining moment for the sector, and one that could split conservative media into different camps.
On the notion that vice-president JD Vance will be Trump’s heir apparent, Erickson said: “I actually am kind of encouraged by the level of pushback after the election that maybe this isn’t a good idea.” Brian Kilmeade, the co-host of the influential Fox News morning show Fox & Friends, has been particularly critical of Vance for seeming to distance himself from Trump’s decision-making on Iran. On his radio show this past week, Kilmeade said that Vance “never should have been vice-president” and that he’s “amazed that President Trump puts up with it”.
Over the next two years, conservative media personalities will have to put their chips down on a candidate. The challenge, Sykes said, is “figuring out where the audience is going, and getting there first”. He also expects conservative media outlets to prioritize attacking Democrats and undermining their control of Congress.
“It’s no longer about defense of Trump,” he added. “It’s like: What’s next? And everybody’s got to make that pivot.”

noticias.titulo: Arizona grandfather hailed as a hero after finding missing toddler in desert
noticias.resumen: Jay Stewart joined search party after two-year-old Vella Campillo wandered off into desert from front yard of home An Arizona granddad has been formally recognized as a hero after recently volunteering to help search for a toddler who wandered off alone into the desert while wearing only a diaper – and finding her safely within several hours curled up under a bush, leading to her rescue. “I’ll never forget it as long as I live,” Jay Stewart said of recovering Vella Campillo, two, while recalling the moment at a news conference held later. “I’ve never wanted to find something so bad in my life
noticias.texto:
An Arizona granddad has been formally recognized as a hero after recently volunteering to help search for a toddler who wandered off alone into the desert while wearing only a diaper – and finding her safely within several hours curled up under a bush, leading to her rescue.
“I’ll never forget it as long as I live,” Jay Stewart said of recovering Vella Campillo, two, while recalling the moment at a news conference held later. “I’ve never wanted to find something so bad in my life – or somebody to find her, anybody to find her.”
Stewart’s emotional comments came at the end of an ordeal for Vella that began with her toddling off by herself from the front yard of her family home in the desert community of Eloy, Arizona, wearing only a diaper, at about 5pm on 17 November, authorities reported to local media. Vella’s parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, later told news station KSAZ that Vella was playing with her siblings and being cared for by another family member when she ran off.
An intense search effort ensued, drawing in dozens of law enforcement officers and community members volunteering to help comb the remote surrounding desert.
Stewart, described as both a father and grandfather, was among the volunteers. And at about 12.15am on 18 November, with temperatures cold at about 50F (10C), Stewart was shining a flashlight through the darkness along a particular ditch lined with bushes.
Vella suddenly “popped out” of one of the bushes, Stewart would later tell reporters. The girl was shivering, about two miles (3.2km) away from her home. Stewart said Vella came up to him and jumped into his arms, and he called first responders to alert them of his discovery.
A deputy with the local Pinal county sheriff’s office soon came up on Stewart and Vella, with his body-worn camera recording video of the scene. “That’s where she was at, right in that spot – I was just walking the ditch,” a visibly relieved Stewart told the deputy, pointing to a nearby bush with a shirtless Vella in his arms.
“Are you OK? Are you so cold?” the deputy could be heard saying on the video as he covered her in a blanket and Vella babbled excitedly.
Stewart tried to hand Vella over to the deputy, saying, “She’s got a hold of me.” He managed to do so after the deputy gently asked Vella, “Can you let go? We’re going to move you over here and sit you in [a] chair.”
“I’ll go with you,” Stewart reassured her.
Paramedics subsequently brought Vella to the hospital for a medical evaluation, and soon she was back with her family.
At a news conference later that day, the Pinal county sheriff, Ross Teeple, explained that the timeliness of Stewart’s intervention was vital for Vella. Prolonged exposure to the temperatures Vella experienced wearing only a diaper during her night alone in the desert could lead to hypothermia, which is life-threatening.
“Very remote areas like this can get extremely cold very fast,” Teeple remarked. “And she’s a small body producing very little heat.”
Teeple’s office later published a video on social media showing the sheriff presenting Stewart with a plaque recognizing him as an outstanding citizen. He also gave Stewart a badge distinguishing him as an honorary member of the office’s search and rescue posse.
As the sheriff put it in the video, Teeple had heard Stewart express discomfort with being labeled a hero. Yet “I’m here to tell you that when you watch the body camera footage, it’s obvious you’re that little girl’s hero”, Teeple said. “And today you’re Pinal county’s hero.”
Fritz, Vella’s mother, told KSAZ that Vella’s disappearance marked “the worst day of our entire lives”.
“We’re beyond blessed for the man [who] found her,” Fritz said to the outlet, while also thanking everyone else involved in the search for Vella.
In the video with Teeple, Stewart said he would treasure the tokens of appreciation that the sheriff presented him. He also said at the news conference that it was not necessary for Vella’s parents to thank him, declaring: “It’s what we do.”
“The scariest thing for parents is to lose a child,” Stewart said. “I can’t imagine what they were going through.”
He added that everyone searching for Vella was “doing it for the same reason”.
“We loved her and wanted her back – she may not be our child, but she could be,” Stewart said.

noticias.titulo: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments
noticias.resumen: Officials have publicly questioned whether Musiala will ever fully recover from a debilitating neurological condition and queried the validity of his contract, prompting criticism from fans, media and the FIFPRO union.
noticias.texto:
Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments
November 22, 2026
In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.
But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health issues – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.
What is wrong with Jamal Musiala?
Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.
Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.
Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.
The situation has now prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.
What have Bayern Munich officials said?
"It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.
"It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances."
Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable."
Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge said he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his new contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.
"I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem."
Rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma."
"He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," said Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money."
Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks."
FIFPRO: 'Bayern should know better'
The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.
The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better."
"Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."
Former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala."
The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.
One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and said that patients suffering from such conditions require "support."
He said Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.
Bayern president: 'Musiala will get time and support'
Bayern president Herbert Hainer, the club's most senior elected official, attempted to deescalate the situation, responding to Hoffmann by saying: "Health and difficult situations are fundamentally always taken into account at FC Bayern."
Indeed, Bayern have recently been praised for their considerate handling of captain Joshua Kimmich following the unexpected death of his father, and of head coach Kompany, who returned to the touchline against Cologne on Friday following a month-long absence after collapsing due to a particularly serious viral infection.
"When it comes to Jamal, we all want the old Jamal back as he was before his injury," said Hainer. "And he will receive all the support and time he needs from the club."
Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting, chief executive Dreesen also attempted to row back on his comments, insisting to reporters that he and his colleagues had not been trying to put Musiala under pressure.
"We all want Jamal to return to the old Jamal. He needs time. We've said that several times. And he must get that. And then we'll see how things look in the new year," he said, adding that there was no need "to talk about the contract."
President Hainer also dismissed questions from journalists as to whether Bayern felt they had been misled by Musiala's agents before offering him a new contract, inferring that the player's representatives may have known about his neurological condition.
"I absolutely do not think that anyone knew beforehand," Hainer insisted.
German media criticize Bayern
But the public criticism has continued. Leading German sports publication Kicker said it was understandable for the Bayern bosses to be frustrated but called their approach "irresponsible" and said their anger "harms the wrong person" in Musiala.
"He can't help his injuries or neurological condition," wrote editor-in-chief Matthias Dersch. "Musiala is only 23 … and is in the most difficult phase of his career. We cannot imagine how he must be feeling, his insecurities and perhaps also fears about his health and his future. And no: the amount of money he earns is no cure."
German football magazine 11Freunde said the Musiala case offered "a glimpse into the abyss of professional football … an unembellished look behind the scenes of a business which is generally portrayed only as glamorous and exciting … into a shadow world where human beings are damned to function … where the value of a person is measured only by their ability to perform over and over again … That's football: capitalism in its purest form."
Meanwhile, the business of football continues. Borussia Dortmund capitalized on Bayern's draw to go top of the Bundesliga with a 1-0 win away at Borussia Mönchengladbach, Harry Kane underwent an operation on a torn ankle ligament but will be out until the new year, meaning he will miss Bayern's trip to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.
And the young Jamal Musiala will continue to battle the effects of serious physical and neurological conditions.

noticias.titulo: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct
noticias.resumen: The Philippines wanted a South China Sea code of conduct in place by 2026. But persistent disagreements between China and ASEAN countries are slowing progress toward a deal.
noticias.texto:
China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct
November 22, 2026
It was supposed to be a breakthrough year. The Philippines had intended to set up a code of conduct with China for the South China Sea during its 2026 ASEAN presidency. However, at the summit in Manila in mid-November they had to abandon their goal. Some 80% of the text had been negotiated, declared Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, but the key areas of dispute had remained unsolved.
Much more than diplomatic wording is at stake. The South China Sea is one of the world's most important shipping routes, it is rich in fishing grounds and may harbor significant oil and gas reserves. Primarily, however, it's a region of strategic competition: With its so-called Nine-Dash Line (often drawn in red), China claims a large portion of the sea. Its claims overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.
A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating. However, opinions differ, particularly with regard to its binding nature and its geographic scope.
"The basic problem with establishing such a code of conduct is that China is supremely powerful and has no real interest in a legally binding agreement," said political scientist Andreas Ufen, Southeast Asia expert at the German Institute of Global and Area Studies (GIGA). Beijing had little incentive to impose restrictions on itself as long as it was able to pursue its interests in the region even without such an agreement, Ufen told DW.
Mere recommendations or legally binding set of rules?
The Paracel Islands serve as an example of just how difficult the unresolved issues are. In China, the group of islands is known as Xisha, in Vietnam as Hoang-Sa. Hanoi apparently wants to include them in the code's geographic scope, but China rejects this. An agreement within the ASEAN framework could indirectly affect the territorial claims of the parties involved.
"A fundamental problem is that so far there's no consensus on whether the code of conduct should be legally binding," said Felix Heiduk, head of research division Asia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). China and the ASEAN nations have been negotiating an agreement for 12 years without major progress so far.
There were reservations about such a treaty not only in China but also in other ASEAN countries. They would subsequently have to ratify a legally binding agreement under international law in their own countries. A non-binding code of conduct, by contrast, would be little more than a voluntary declaration of intent, Ufen told DW.
The definition of an "incident" is controversial as well. Are coast guard missions with use of water cannons included? Or blockades of supply vessels? Or is the code only applicable when military force is involved? This will determine which actions will be covered by the regulations in the future.
"These are by no means just technical details. Their clarification determines to a great extent whether the code of conduct will in fact be effective or will ultimately remain only a non-binding declaration of intent," Heiduk said. An agreement without valid commitments would bring about little change.
Diverging interests
Ufen views China's attitude as a strategic calculation. "I believe that China is interested in keeping the conflict simmering, so to speak, without having to commit itself to a truly binding legal regulation," he said. In this way, Beijing could strengthen its position in the South China Sea without limiting its room for maneuver.
At the same time there are also diverging interests within the ASEAN group. The 11 member states are by no means united. The Philippines and Vietnam are particularly vocal in their opposition to China. Malaysia and Indonesia pursue a more restrained approach. Cambodia and Laos have close economic ties with Beijing and don't have any territorial claims in the South China Sea.
"From the start of the negotiations, the lack of unity within ASEAN has been a problem. In a way, it's a permanent obstacle," Heiduk said. The group makes decisions based on the consensus principle, which basically means that every member state can block a unified position. Recurring confrontations between China and the Philippines exacerbated the problem by undermining trust and making it more difficult to reach compromises.
Ufen also believes that diverging interests are a key impediment. "Reconciling them is extremely difficult," he said. China could take advantage of the discord. Beijing preferred bilateral negotiations with individual countries rather than dealing with an entire, united group of nations.
Fundamental conflicts unresolved
A study published by the Singapore-based Yusof Ishak Institute (ISEAS)reaches similar conclusions. Not only China but internal divisions within ASEAN stalled negotiations. The authors warn against exclusively relying on a comprehensive, legally binding treaty. Initially, partial agreements — for example, on crisis communication, rescue operations at sea or maritime environment protection — could be a first step. Developing the 2002 agreement on a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea could also be an intermediate step.
Ufen doubts whether Beijing is interested in a binding result. "For this reason, I can't really imagine that China has a real interest in a code of conduct that includes legally binding regulations," he said.
Heiduk warns against overestimating the significance of a potential agreement. "Even if the code of conduct was signed at some point, in whichever shape, that would in no way solve the conflict in the South China Sea," he said. The code could regulate how to handle incidents, but it could not eliminate territorial disputes and competing claims to maritime areas.
Hopes for future negotiations
This constitutes the dilemma for ASEAN nations as well, whose foreign policy oscillates between China and US ties: An agreement that's as binding as possible could fail because China and individual member states have reservations. A weak, non-binding code, however, could give the impression everyone agreed but would hardly change conduct at sea.
The American Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) summed up the situationafter the summit in Manila: "Whatever progress was made this year, it is almost certain that the hardest sticking points remain unresolved."
Negotiations will be continued in 2027 under Singapore's chairmanship. Whether this will turn into more than just another diplomatic effort will depend on whether China is prepared to submit itself to regulations which limit its scope of action and whether ASEAN will be able to reach a consensus.
This article was originally published in German.

noticias.titulo: Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029
noticias.resumen: "The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the political landscape?
noticias.texto:
A leftist Berlin 'Super PAC' shakes up German politics
November 22, 2026
Red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.
The Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.
Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.
Content creation, sharing, networking, campaigning
Neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram, Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.
Users with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of New York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.
And there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.
The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.
Super PAC-style campaigning is new in Germany
The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.
For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting new type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.
But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.
Haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.
That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.
"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles."
Stemming the rise of far-right AfD with digital know-how
The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.
The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms.
Haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he said.
Agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer says that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.
Big-tent parties in Germany in decline for decades
Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.
"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open."
The center-left and center-right big-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.
Party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) showed that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low.
In the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.
The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures."

noticias.titulo: Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike
noticias.resumen: Germany's biggest single union, IG Metall, is calling on car and shipyard workers to strike amid a pay row. Meanwhile, Germany's president is setting off on an Africa trip. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike
Published November 21, 2026last updated November 22, 2026
What you need to know
- The IG Metall union is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues to escalate
- The water level in the Rhine River is rising again after a long period during which shipping was hindered
- German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is kicking off an Africa trip that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya
- Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig wants to tighten laws on femicide
This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:
Steinmeier kicks off Africa trip
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is setting off on a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.
Steinmeier will be accompanied by a business delegation and is expected to focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers during the trip.
On Monday, Steinmeier is to be received by Ivorian President Allassane Outtara in Abidjan, Ivory Coast's largest city and seat of government.
The next day, in the Ghanaian capital, Accra, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which, according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."
On Wednesday, he will be received by Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi.
In Kenya, Steinmeier will also visit the Crescent Island Game Sanctuary on Thursday, the last day of his trip.
Rhine rises again after months of low water
The Federal Institute for Hydrology (BfG) has said it expects water levels in large rivers in western Germany, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days amid sustained rainfall.
It said the water level at the key gauge in Kaub near Koblenz, located at an important bottleneck on the Middle Rhine, could reach some 3.3 meters (10.8 feet), more than 3 meters higher than the last recorded low-water readings.
The BfG said it also expected rising water levels in the Weser and Danube rivers, with smaller increases in the Elbe and Oder.
Shipping returning to normal
The rising water level in the Rhine, an important shipping route, means that conditions for water-borne cargo transport have improved, according to Germany's inland navigation association BDB.
"The more abundant rainfall in the past days has caused the water level in the Rhine to rise considerably, and they will keep rising a great deal in the next few days as well, meaning that each ship has much more transport capacity again," said Fabian Spiess, the deputy manager at BDB.
In the middle of the year, many ships were forced to drastically reduce the loads they carried, leading to economic losses that will not be recuperated any time soon, according to Spiess.
He cited the year 2018, in which shipping on the Rhine was also hindered by extremely low water levels, saying that the months of improved conditions at the end of that year had not been enough to make good the economic damage incurred.
The conservation NGO also said that the current rain provided temporary relief to the environment but could not compensate for the negative consequences of the long dry period.
It said species of animals, such as amphibians and water insects, that lived in small bodies of water and moist habitats had been particularly impacted.
Justice Minister Hubig wants harsher penalities for femicide
Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig says that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.
"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.
"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.
She said that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.
However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), said she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.
She said that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages."
The proposals are currently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.
They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.
IG Metall calls warning strike for Monday
The powerful IG Metall union said on Sunday it would call another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues.
Altogether, some 23,000 workers at 19 companies in northern Germany have been called upon to participate, including employees at automaker Mercedes-Benz, shipbuilding company Meyer Werft and wind energy company
Siemens Gamesa.
The union said that a strike on Friday saw some 12,300 workers walk out at 17 facilities.
It says that the strikes are meant to increase the pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% wage increase.
So far, employers have offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.
Welcome back to our coverage
The DW newsroom says "Willkommen!" once more to all its readers as we resume our reporting on all things German.
Some good news is on the agenda: The Rhine River, which we can see from the window of our Bonn office, has recovered after a long period with little rainfall, meaning that the barges plying the waterway can load up properly again.
In other stories, the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is setting off on a trip to Africa, during which he is set to visit three countries with a businesss delegation in tow.
And Germany's powerful IG Metall union has said it is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday amid an escalating pay dispute.
Read on to find out more about what is happening in Germany on Sunday, November 22.
We're pausing our coverage
We're pausing our Germany news blog for now. Come back for more on Sunday!
Nmecha shows off new goal celebration after controversy
A new goal celebration was devised by Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha after his previous one caused controversy due to its religious aspect.
After scoring the goal that secured Dortmund's 1-0 victory over Borussia Mönchengladbach (see entry below), Nmecha knelt on one knee and crossed his arms in front of his chest. He then spread his arms, appearing to pray with his eyes closed.
Nmecha told broadcaster Sky that he intends to continue expressing his faith during goal celebrations, adding that he had once again given glory to Jesus.
However, he did not perform the controversial part of his usual goal celebration. In it, he removes an imaginary crown from his head and places it on the pitch in front of him while kneeling.
This celebration has been heavily criticized, even by Dortmund's fan department.
Nmecha explained that the celebrations is about "putting down my 'crown' in front of the soon-to-come king and point out to Jesus, my hope and my strength."
The gesture is used by Ballers in God, a network of Christian football players that has been criticized for the homophobic and queerphobic statements made by its members.
Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke said he asked the player not to do the celebration again.
Dortmund overtakes Bayern in Bundesliga standings
Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha led his team to the top of the German Bundesliga table with a 1-0 victory over last-place Borussia Mönchengladbach.
Meanwhile, Bayern Munich was held to a 1-1 draw at home by Cologne on Friday, and striker Harry Kane suffered a serious ankle injury. The Ballon d'Or winner is set to miss several months after undergoing ankle surgery earlier on Saturday.
Now, Dortmund has 24 points after 10 games, putting them two points ahead of Bayern and third-place Freiburg, who defeated Elversberg 1-0.
Fourth-place RB Leipzig had five different players score in a 5-1 victory over Union Berlin, bringing them to 21 points. Bayer Leverkusen scored four unanswered goals against Paderborn to stay in fifth place.
WATCH: Can Germany boost growth with its €500 billion infrastructure plan
Germany is seeking to redress years of underinvestment by pouring billions into the modernization of public infrastructure and digital networks, and the transition to renewable energy sources.
But will the plan bring real change amid the labor shortages, burdensome bureaucracy and low productivity currently besetting Europe's largest economy?
DW takes a look at what is one of Germany's biggest public investment drives in decades in this video:
Bayern announce record revenue for 2025–26 financial year
Bundesliga powerhouse Bayern Munich concluded the 2025-26 financial year with record figures.
According to the financial report released Saturday at the club's annual general meeting, the club's total turnover was €988.2 million ($1.08 billion) — that is around €10 million more than the previous year.
Operating profit (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million. Pre-tax profit was €35.3 million, and net profit for the year was €22.8 million.
Bayern had a particularly strong year in terms of sponsorships. Turnover increased by nearly €30 million, reaching €268.4 million. The club also set a record in merchandise sales, earning €152.8 million.
"We have achieved another record year," CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen said. "This shows that our club has a strong foundation. And we continue to invest to ensure the best possible conditions for the sporting success of our teams."
Record membership figures
Moreover, Bayern achieved another milestone. They reached 500,000 members — more than any other club in the world.
Over the past 12 years, the German giants have doubled their membership, growing from 250,000 in 2014 to 500,000 this year.
"Record champions, record members, record member champions," president Herbert Hainer said.
Members hold a 70% stake in the club, which is well above the simple majority required by German rules.
The remaining 30% is owned by four German companies with roots in Bavaria: Adidas, Audi, Allianz, and Viessmann.
Bayern won the league and cup double in the 2025-26 season, losing only three of 53 games across all competitions. In Europe, the club made it to the Champions League semifinals.
Free Voters leader Aiwanger laid to rest in Bavaria
Two and a half weeks after his sudden death, Free Voters leader Hubert Aiwanger, who was Bavarian Minister of Economic Affairs and Deputy Minister-President, was laid to rest in his hometown of Inkofen in Lower Bavaria.
A memorial service was held at the Parish Church of the Presentation of the Lord and broadcast on a screen outside. According to the organizers, around 2,000 people attended the solemn service.
Aiwanger's funeral was open to the public. His longtime partner, Tanja Schweiger, the Regensburg district administrator (Free Voters), stated that Aiwanger had been "a man of the people."
For that reason, she said, everyone "who liked and appreciated him" was warmly welcome. The politician had already been honored with a state funeral in Munich a week earlier.
Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel on November 4 after canceling an appointment for health reasons. The 55-year-old died of natural causes.
Bayern's Kane vows 'I'll be back' after ankle surgery
Harry Kane, Bayern Munich's star striker, has pledged to return to the field for the important matches at the end of the current campaign after undergoing surgery for a torn ankle ligament.
"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season," he wrote on social media above a photo of himself on his hospital bed, also thanking fans for their messages of support.
Kane, 33, was injured around 20 minutes into Bayern's 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday.
Bayern issued a statement on Saturday saying that Kane had "successfully undergone surgery" on his left ankle but was expected to be out for three to four months.
England captain Kane, who finished the 2025–26 season with over 70 goals for club and country, was awarded the Ballon d'Or for his efforts.
Bavaria's late vice premier, Hubert Aiwanger, laid to rest
Hubert Aiwanger, the deputy premier and economy minister of the southern state of Bavaria, is being buried on Saturday in his native town of Inkofen.
Aiwanger, the federal leader of the Free Voters (FW) party, died suddenly two weeks ago of natural causes at the age of 55 in a hotel in Berlin.
The funeral service ahead of the burial was open to the public, with police saying they expected some 1,000 participants.
A memorial service was held in Munich a week ago to honor Aiwanger.
Germany drops funding for hub documenting right-wing violence
An online portal set up to collate records of right-wing violence in Germany since World War II is to lose its funding from the start of next year, a parliamentary inquiry has revealed.
In response to a question from Green politician Marlene Schönberger, the minister of state for culture, Wolfram Weimer, said that "[a]dditional funds for financing beyond the end of 2026 are not available" for the online hub, hosted on the "Archivportal-D" of the German Digital Library.
Schönberger, a member of the Bundestag's Committee on Internal Affairs, said she could not understand the decision by the government to cease funding for the portal.
"Not even eight months after the launch of the 'Right-Wing Violence' thematic portal, the federal government is now pulling the plug. That is completely incomprehensible," she said.
"The federal government must prevent right-wing violence, and where it fails to do so, it must at least acknowledge and document its continuity. It owes that to those affected," she said.
The hub was set up to bring together documents held in various archives in one online location.
US court approves Bayer Roundup cancer settlement
A judge in the US state of Missouri has approved a settlement under which Germany-based agrochemical company Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion (€6.6 billion) over the next two decades to resolve lawsuits from cancer sufferers who say they should have been warned that its weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma.
The settlement, which applies nationwide, means both Roundup users who are already ill with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who develop it in future could an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, with factors such as their use of the product, their age at the time of diagnosis and illness severity determining the exact sum.
The decision could be appealed.
For more on this story, head over to our report.

noticias.titulo: US: ICE arrests 2 at Seattle airport in 'chilling' scenes — governor
noticias.resumen: Washington's governor has denounced the arrests made by ICE officers at Seattle's airport, calling the incident "horrific."
noticias.texto:
US: ICE arrests 2 at Seattle airport in 'chilling' scenes — governor
November 22, 2026
Masked US immigration officers have detained two people on an airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers boarded a flight to Los Angeles, prompting criticism from Washington state Governor Bob Ferguson and concerns from Alaska Airlines.
The arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport around 8 a.m. local time (1600 UTC) on Saturday. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa.
Agents also arrested Sofia Hernandez Mejia, who they alleged threw hot coffee at the ICE officers during the confrontation. ICE said she had also overstayed her visa and would face a charge of assaulting a federal officer.
Videos of the incident circulated on social media, showing officers struggling with a person on the ground as passengers look on. One woman could be heard shouting that her daughter was being taken away and that she had a work permit.
Washington governor slams 'out of control' ICE
Governor Ferguson, a Democrat, described the footage as "horrific" and "chilling", accusing ICE of being "completely and totally out of control."
He urged Alaska Airlines to ask federal immigration authorities to leave the state's airports and said he would make the same appeal to other airlines operating at Seattle-Tacoma.
Alaska Airlines said it had received no advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working to understand the circumstances.
The airline also expressed concern over the incident, which it said had been distressing for passengers and employees.
The operation drew criticism from April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, who said it had caused fear and disruption during one of the busiest travel periods of the year.
The flight was delayed, with Alaska Airlines saying many passengers were transferred to other flights. The original service eventually departed at 11 a.m. local time.

noticias.titulo: India: Nepal PM Balendra Shah heads to Delhi for first bilateral visit
noticias.resumen: Nepal's rapper-turned-prime minister Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for his first foreign bilateral trip since taking office. He is expected to discuss flood recovery, trade and energy in his talks with Modi. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
India: Nepal PM Balendra Shah heads to Delhi for first bilateral visit
Published November 21, 2026last updated November 22, 2026
What you need to know
- Nepal's Balendra Shah is set to arrive in India for his first foreign bilateral visit since becoming prime minister earlier this year
- India's men post a record 720 runs at stumps on day 4 of test against New Zealand
- Indian man is sentenced to 19 years in prison over plot to assassinate Sikh separatist leader
- Over 200 people are hospitalized after consuming toxic liquor in Manipur state
Here is a roundup of the main headlines from India on Saturday, November 21 and Sunday, November 22:
India declare at record 720-9, New Zealand fights back in Wellington
India declared at 720-9, the highest Test total by any team in New Zealand, on day four of the first Test in Wellington.
The innings gave India a 352-run first-innings lead. India's previous best in New Zealand was 520 all out in Hamilton in 2009.
Rishabh Pant struck 128 from 153 balls, his ninth Test century and fourth since returning to Test cricket in 2024. Dhruv Jurel added 78, and the declaration came midway through the second session.
Pant's sixes took him to 108 in Tests, behind only England's Ben Stokes: "I just keep it simple most of the time. Whenever I see the ball, I try to hit it," he said.
New Zealand closed on 119-2, still 233 behind, with Devon Conway unbeaten on 59 and Rachin Ravindra on 27. Jasprit Bumrah dismissed captain Tom Latham for a duck early in the innings, and Henry Nicholls, who made 175 not out in the first innings, fell for 31 to a sharp catch by Jurel off Prasidh Krishna.
New Zealand now need to bat out most of the final day, and India have at least 90 overs to take eight wickets.
Nepal PM Balendra Shah set to arrive in Delhi
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is set to arrive in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip since taking office in March.
The 36-year-old former rapper will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday. He will also meet Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and briefly visit President Droupadi Murmu.
Reconstruction after August's devastating floods is expected to dominate the talks. The disaster left some 1,500 dead and more than 5,200 missing, with roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes destroyed.
Nepal estimates rebuilding will cost $4.78 billion.
Nepal is also pressing for an extra route for commercial flights to Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
"India is a major and important partner for Nepal," Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai told reporters, saying the leaders would discuss trade, transit, investment, energy, connectivity and infrastructure.
New Delhi said the visit "reflects the importance India attaches to its relations with Nepal," AFP reported. Local media reported that talks may also touch upon unresolved border disputes.
India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60% of its imports, worth $8.6 billion, versus China's 13%, according to World Bank figures. India and China regularly compete for influence in Nepal.
Shah will be accompanied by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal.
Welcome back to our coverage
Hello! We are back with the latest news from India this Sunday.
Nepal's rapper-turned-prime minister Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for his first bilateral foreign visit since taking office.
Meanwhile, India has posted a record total of 720-9 on the fourth day of the first cricket test against New Zealand.
For this and more, follow our blog.
We're pausing the blog
We're logging off today, but we will be back tomorrow with the latest from across India.
Stay tuned for more!
Youth Congress protests at Meta offices over restricted Instagram accounts
Workers of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC), the youth wing of the opposition Indian National Congress, protested at US tech giant Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram on Friday, demanding that the group's leaders' Instagram accounts be restored.
In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building, smashed plants and clashed with police, according to footage the IYC released. Meta declined to comment.
The IYC said Instagram withheld the accounts of its president and in-charge on November 19 "on BJP orders," referring to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and restored both shortly after the protests.
Manu Jain, who runs the group's social media, told Reuters thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.
BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said: "Congress is a party of goons! Goons of Indian Youth Congress are not only vandalized and destroyed Meta's office in Hyderabad, & also are flaunting it on social media!"
Meanwhile, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav warned foreign companies against getting involved in Indian politics.
The Indian government says it orders takedowns only for content that breaches local laws or threatens public safety or national security. In February, it cut the deadline for removing unlawful content from 36 hours to three.
Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the previous six months, saying most were cases where local law required it to restrict content proactively.
Earlier this month, Brazil’s top electoral court fined Meta's Facebook $1.3 million for failing to comply with judicial orders during the country's presidential election runoff campaign. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's team accused the company of political bias.
Rahul, Gill puts India 118 ahead of New Zealand on day three in Wellington
India closed day three of the first Test against New Zealand on 486-4, a lead of 118 runs. KL Rahul made 136, Shubman Gill 98 and Rishabh Pant was unbeaten on 55 as every one of India's top five passed 50.
Rahul reached his 13th Test hundred off 207 balls, batting for more than eight hours and sharing stands of 165 with Devdutt Padikkal (80) and 91 with Gill. It completed a set of Test centuries in every major Test-playing nation outside the subcontinent for the Indian wicketkeeper-batsman.
"It feels really awesome, actually, to be able to achieve something like that," Rahul said.
He survived an LBW appeal on 5 that was given not out and New Zealand chose not to review. "Those 15 seconds were probably the slowest 15 seconds of my life," he said of the review process.
Gill and Pant added 100 in the final session before Gill was bowled by Jacob Duffy just before stumps. Duffy finished with 1-180 from 29 overs, the fourth most expensive figures in New Zealand's Test history, AFP said.
The pitch, green on day one, flattened out. "We expected a lot of grass on the wicket, we expected a lot of movement and it has probably not panned out that way," Padikkal said.
New Zealand were all out for 368 in their first innings.
The two-match series ends next week in Christchurch.
Death toll from suspected spurious liquor in Manipur's Chandel rises
At least 14 people have died and more than 200 have been hospitalized after drinking suspected adulterated liquor in Manipur's Chandel district.
At least 12 people remain in critical condition, local media reported.
The victims drank the liquor in the Chakpikarong area, about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from the state capital city of Imphal, and deaths were reported between November 18 and 20.
Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited the hospitals where most patients were being treated on Friday. He ordered an inquiry and said the culprits would be arrested soon.
Police said the liquor came from Sugnu in neighboring Kakching district, with no known local brewing in Chandel. A case has been filed, and two people have been arrested.
The local administration has advised residents not to drink liquor from questionable sources and asked anyone who consumed liquor from the same source to get a medical check-up, even without symptoms.
US judge jails Indian national in foiled plot to kill Sikh separatist, New Delhi denies involvement
A US federal judge sentenced an Indian national on Friday to 19 years and seven months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
"I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he said in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.
Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited Gupta in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.
Gupta paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.
Prosecutors also said Gupta had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.
His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.
"There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she said. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.
India denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. New Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.
Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and said outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay."
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to our weekend coverage!
This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest news from and about India.
An Indian national has been sentenced to 19 years and seven months in prison by a US federal judge for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.
Several people have died and more than 200 hospitalized in the northeastern state of Manipur after consuming toxic liquor.
And India has taken a 118-run lead over New Zealand, reaching 486-4 at stumps on day 3 of the first Test against the Black Caps.
For this and more, follow our blog.

noticias.titulo: Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory
noticias.resumen: A fire at a confectionery factory in Indonesia's Banten province has killed at least three people. Dozens are also unaccounted for after the blaze, which destroyed large parts of the facility.
noticias.texto:
Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory
November 22, 2026
Indonesian rescue teams are searching for 36 workers who remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy-making factory killed at least three people, officials said on Sunday.
The fire occurred at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, around 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of the capital, Jakarta, in the Serang district of Banten province.
What do we know about the Indonesian confectionery factory fire?
The factory caught fire on Saturday afternoon, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said.
"All elements of the joint SAR (search-and-rescue) team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritizing the safety of personnel in the field," he added.
Rizky said four people injured in the blaze had been taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic. Eleven more were said to have been rescued alive.
The governor of Banten province, Andra Soni, told reporters overnight that 60 people were believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out.
Drone footage shows the fire destroyed large sections of the three-story building, bringing down the roof in some places.
Survivors said the fire started in a cooling unit on the third floor.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products.
Deadly industrial fires in Indonesia
Indonesia has seen a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising questions about the country's workplace safety standards into question.
Among other disasters, at least 22 people were killed in a fire last December that broke out in a seven-story building in Jakarta after a suspected drone battery explosion, police said.
An explosion in a nickel-processing plant in the east of the country killed at least 13 people in 2023.

noticias.titulo: COP31: Fossil fuels still missing from draft deal at UN climate summit
noticias.resumen: The climate summit is in its second day of overtime, despite weeks of negotiations. Nations are now mulling over a new draft text that still doesn't mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
COP31: Fossil fuels still missing from draft deal at UN climate summit
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 22, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached
- The latest COP31 draft deal still fails to mention fossil fuels, raising the possibility that the summit could end with no deal
- Fossil fuels are a major flashpoint at this year's summit, which comes amid soaring energy prices and tensions over the US-Israeli war with Iran
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:
EU cannot accept deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels': Irish minister
Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien has said the European Union is "profoundly disappointed" with the current draft deal on the table at COP31 because it "fails to meet the moment" and that the bloc will not agree to it.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5°C within reach," O'Brien said.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels," he added.
Former Greenpeace chief says no deal is better than current deal
Former Greenpeace executive Jennifer Morgan said it would be better to end the COP31 summit with no deal than a watered-down declaration.
Her remarks come amid deep divisions over the omission of fossil fuels from the draft declaration.
Morgan rejected the notion that it would be better to accept the current draft than have no resolution at all, as the Turkish COP president has suggested.
"I think this is the day for the first time in my 31 COPs that I thought it was better not to have a decision that sets us back, that goes against what small islands and vulnerable people are saying," Morgan added.
She praised Germany for standing up to pressures to accept the current deal.
"Of course it would have been better to have a strong outcome here with everyone moving forward, but I agree with the German minister who just said if the text stays the way that it is, then it should not be accepted," Morgan said.
The US climate activist blamed oil-producing nations for the impasse.
"Saudi Arabia's fingerprints are all over" the current draft proposal, she said.
The omission has created a deadlock at COP31, which was due to conclude on Friday but has been extended as delegates seek consensus.
Morgan also blamed this year's Turkish presidency for failing to bring everybody together and instead letting countries that rely on fossil fuels dictate the terms of the agreement.
"Last year we had Brazil with a very strong presidency. They worked all year to bring countries together and they managed. It was not easy last year," Morgan said.
"This year we had presidencies that, in my view, were not well prepared. They did not bring countries together (...) it's been shuttle diplomacy with no text for four days. That's not the way you get an agreement here," she added.
Germany rejects 'unacceptable' draft deal
German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider has said the latest version of the draft agreement is "not acceptable."
Schneider said that the draft decision "not only fails to provide an adequate response but actually takes a step backward. A step backward from previous decisions on climate protection is the last thing Germany can support."
Schneider said that delegates had been working hard for days to reach a unanimous decision on "the world's greatest challenge: human-induced climate change," noting that this summer had "shown that the nature of this warming not only costs lives — as in Nepal — but also changes our world for the worse."
"It is up to us, as humanity, to do something about it. That is why a conference dedicated to climate protection — whose sole purpose is to protect the climate — must send a clear signal that we are taking action against this threat."
Schneider said he still believed most nations are willing to work to enact climate protection, but singled out those who still rely on fossil fuels to power their economies.
"The overwhelming majority of nations are committed to climate protection. Some, however, are still making huge profits from oil and gas and are unwilling to scale back their production or to pioneer a clear roadmap for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in this area," he added.
France criticizes draft deal as 'backward' step
France has called a new draft deal proposed at COP31 a "backward" step.
French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut criticized the deal for failing to mention fossil fuels, casting fresh uncertainty over whether nations will be able to reach an agreement.
"Time is ticking and we are not there yet," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said in a statement.
Turkish COP31 president calls for resolution to be adopted
COP31 President Murat Kurum has expressed his frustration over the deadlock at the summit.
The latest version of the draft deal again fails to mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Over 40 hours after its scheduled conclusion and with no compromise in sight, the summit risks losing the numbers required to make any decision as delegates leave for home.
"If it is not adopted, I believe those who push the COP process into a deadlock will need to reflect on their position," Kurum said.
"It is our wish that this resolution be passed. We shall shortly be expressing our determination to ensure that this resolution is passed at the general meeting," he said.
"It is up to the parties involved. If there is sincerity here, and if there is a genuine desire to get things done, I believe that this can be achieved in this chamber. We shall see about that in a moment," Kurum added.
What we know about the latest COP31 draft deal
The third draft makes no mention of the words "fossil," "oil," "coal," or "phase out."
However, as in the second draft, the latest version retains a goal to boost electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, as well as efforts to expand the use of "clean energy."
The draft text also does not stipulate that the "35-by-35" electrification target should be met using renewable energy sources.
It also urges countries to "accelerate" carbon capture and storage — a controversial technology backed by the fossil fuel industry.
Fossil fuels still missing in latest COP31 draft deal
Welcome back to our coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
The latest, and potentially final, version of the deal still makes no explicit mention of fossil fuels.
It does refer to a 2023 agreement that committed the world to transitioning away from fossil fuels — but stops short of naming them directly.
The third and presumably final draft text to emerge from negotiations at COP31, which lacks any mention of fossil fuels or how to transition away from them, has been rejected by NGOs.
In a statement, Teresa Anderson, Climate Justice Lead at ActionAid International, said the people who will benefit most from the new "35-by-35" electrification targets and carbon capture "are the fossil fuel, nuclear, data and CCUS (carbon capture, use and storage) industries.
"This text will help elites to profit while leaving people in the dark," Anderson said.
Brandon Wu, AAUSA's Director of Policy and Campaigns, said: "Rich countries came to the COP31 talks with nothing to offer other than red lines.
"They put forward meaningless fossil fuel transition roadmaps that were nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy, then hypocritically blamed developing countries for failing to take action on phasing out fossil fuels.
“This is the behaviour of an arrogant bully who cares about nothing but himself and it is no way to have a proper negotiation. COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it’s because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise."
We're pausing our coverage
As COP31 extends into a second day of overtime, we are pausing our coverage.
In the early hours of Sunday, COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum informed delegates at a plenary that a third and "final" text would be sent to them for review.
He added that negotiators would have until 6:00 am (0400 GMT) "to come to us with agreement on the text" and that a closing plenary would then be convened at 9:00 am local time.
Stay tuned for more news in the coming hours.
IN DEPTH: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
The shift to green tech is already in full swing, including electric cars, electric buses, solar panels and heat pumps. But what is so electrifying about the latest wave of electrification?
Climate activist blames rich countries for COP failure
Harjeet Singh, the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, said that COP31 could be a failure due to a lack of funding.
"COP31 is stuck for one simple reason: money. Europe and other rich countries came to Antalya with empty pockets," he wrote in a statement shared with multiple reporters.
"They've spent two weeks pushing electrification targets and demanding more ambition from developing countries, while refusing to pay for any of it," he added.
Singh accused wealthy countries of blocking a just transition mechanism and of ignoring calls to increase funding for the Adaptation Fund and the Loss and Damage Fund.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he wrote.
The climate activist stressed that the reason this COP failed wasn't a lack of solutions. It was due to "a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis," he said.
IN DEPTH: Why is carbon capture not moving faster?
Carbon capture technology works, but its real-world capabilities are nowhere near to moving the needle on climate change. So what's the hold-up?
IN DEPTH: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
Attacks on climate science and disinformation seem to be delaying key decisions as the UN climate talks draw to a close in Antalya.
IN DEPTH: Africa at COP31 — Will climate cash finally flow?
Leaders from Africa, one of the continents worst hit by climate change, have spent years lobbying for hundreds of billions of dollars to help adapt to the rising impacts of global warming.
The rest of the world relies on African nations for their abundant natural resources, many of them used in clean energy production.
Yet at COP31, wealthy nations have so far failed to commit to the financing needed to help developing nations make a just transition.
Read our report from DW's Kathy Wood.
Peru blames 'geopolitical divisions' for lack of COP31 progress
The head of Peru's delegation at COP31, Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, warned that the UN climate summit was unlikely to end with a concrete deal on climate financing or cutting fossil fuel use.
Garrido Sanchez lamented that the outcome "would be very limited."
He reiterated how "geopolitical divisions" were stopping any final deal from mentioning reducing reliance on oil, gas and coal.
The Peruvian delegate singled out major oil producers, such as Gulf Arab states and Russia, as showing significant opposition.
He noted that while Latin American neighbor Panama had also signaled objection to including the term fossil fuels in the final text, Peru was "not so radical" and is keen to attract investment to "ensure our energy security" through renewables.
China throws weight behind '35-by-35' pledge
China has backed a plan proposed by COP host Turkey to raise global electricity demand to 35% by 2035 — up from the current 20%.
In a joint statement with Australia, which is leading negotiations between almost 200 nations at the COP31 summit in Turkey, Beijing said it welcomes "growing international ambition and cooperation ... to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 on a voluntary basis."
The statement goes on to highlight the benefits the transition can bring for the economy, jobs, energy security, public health and households.
The two partners also "acknowledge the importance of inclusive climate action that ensures no one is left behind," the text continued.
Dozens of countries, including EU states, Japan, South Korea and Canada, have so far signaled support for the voluntary goal, which aims to boost clean energy use.
Yet, environmental groups have warned that the draft text doesn't stipulate the use of solar, wind and other renewable energy sources, which could allow power plants using natural gas and coal to be included.

noticias.titulo: NPR's Senior Podcast Challenge: Early entries we love
noticias.resumen: People 65 and older have been submitting stories for a chance to win our grand prize — a visit to NPR watch your podcast air live on Weekend Edition . There's still time to enter!
noticias.texto:
NPR's Senior Podcast Challenge: Early entries we love
Once people hit retirement age, there are so many questions: Who am I without my job? What do I do to fill this time? How are my relationships changing?
This fall, for the first-ever NPR Senior Podcast Challenge, we asked those of you in the over-65 crowd, to tell us about all this, and you've been sending in your answers.
The competition flips the story line on our popular NPR Student Podcast Challenge – since 2018 more than 90,000 young people have sent us their stories, in their own voices.
Now, we're hearing from listeners with a lot of experience, hopefully some wisdom, and perhaps more grey hair.
While the contest is still open for a few more weeks — you have until November 30 to enter — we've been listening to more than 100 podcasts that have come in so far.
Here's a sample of some of our early favorites:
Lou Ann Baylock, of Sarasota, Fla., told us she wasn't too happy about the title of our contest: the "senior" part.
"I'm 68, but I'm NOT a senior, am I?" she asks in her podcast, Talk to Me.
"I thought seniors were people in their 80s," she says. "I mean, I see my body changing. I know I'm getting older. But am I really a senior?"
Baylock ends up deciding she's OK with that term: She's still working, and as a therapist she tells us in her podcast she has some ideas that might help other people her age.
Finding the joy
Many of our podcasters took up the issue of life after retirement. Some of you are telling us you're having the best time of your life. Others, not so much.
For Martin Goldsmith, 78, of Tacoma, Wash., retirement means not letting his age keep him doing the things he loves.
"The back, the legs, and the joints aren't what they used to be," he says in his entry Joy Filled Retirement. "So for me, the running and skiing are out and the hearing aids are in."
But, he adds, "I can still play my guitar."
Music, Goldsmith tells us, has always been in his DNA. He grew up jamming with his dad on the clarinet and mom on the viola. And he's now playing his guitar at the children's hospital, and he ends his story playing and singing an old favorite, Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out.
Putting yourself out there
And then, there's dating. We've received quite a few podcasts about life post-divorce, or after losing a partner.
Our podcasters are reminding us that it never gets easier, and many of them including George Smith have told us some version of this: "I never thought I'd be here."
Smith lives with his daughter in Wildomar, Calif., and when it came to figuring out the modern dating scene, he says:
"After almost three decades of marriage, I found myself in my mid-60s, divorced, alone in a cafe, and about to meet a woman from a dating app for the first time in my life. Little did I realize," he tells us, "my teenage daughter Shannon would become my dating navigator."
Smith's podcast is aptly called Swipe Right, Dad, and he tells us about three very different online dates he goes on.
Want to enter? Here are the details
Our competition, will close on Nov. 30. You can submit here.
Podcasts submitted must be completely original work, no longer than eight minutes in length. We encourage stories of all kinds – from personal narratives to in-depth interviews to fully reported audio journalism.
Some key rules: No copyrighted music. And, this should come as no surprise: keep AI out of your writing and presentation.
See the rules page for exact requirements and restrictions.
You can submit multiple podcasts. Please fill out a separate form for each entry.
We'll choose several finalists and our grand-prize winner early in the new year and air the winning podcast on Weekend Edition Sunday in January or February.
If you have no idea where to get started, don't worry! You don't need to be an audio expert, and you can make a podcast with nothing more than a smart phone, a computer, and some easily available editing software. You can check out our student podcasting resources page, which includes step-by-step instructions, from choosing a good story, conducting interviews, writing a script, and tips for editing and mixing. And you cansubscribe to our newsletter for the latest from the contest team.
And finally, if you have questions about the Senior Podcast Challenge, email us at seniorpodcastchallenge@npr.org.

noticias.titulo: He expected a small-business loan. It turned out to be a trap
noticias.resumen: America's fastest-growing source of funding for small businesses is also one of the least regulated. One man has waged a long, lonely fight to recoup its punishing cost.
noticias.texto:
He expected a small-business loan. It turned out to be a trap
