GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after.
A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.
It was 2019, and Shahinian's company soared, like a miniature Live Nation-Ticketmaster, selling tickets and producing concerts around Los Angeles and beyond. He imagined how much he could do with stable funding.
The pitch had a catch: Shahinian would first accept a third of the sum and start paying it back immediately, in daily installments of $3,600. After 30 days, he could access the rest of the money. He crunched the numbers, followed up with questions — and took the deal.
Shahinian sent the daily payments, he says, for 30 days. Then 40. Then 50.
The line of credit never came.
"From that day," he says, "it's been one long day, one long nightmare."
For seven years, Shahinian has been mired in the shadowy industry that is now the fastest-growing source of funding for small business in the United States. It's largely unregulated, promising fast money at a tremendous cost. And Shahinian's lawsuit against his funders could become one of the first of its kind to go to trial.
A business in need
Before the "incident," as Shahinian calls his fateful deal, he'd been in business for 15 years, building his company from a side hustle into his main source of income.
Educated as a computer scientist, he'd spent years programming satellites as an aerospace engineer. In 2004, he also developed a site for something he loved in his spare time: community events. Shahinian called his platform for ticketing and seating charts It's My Seat.
Over a decade, Shahinian grew his business from selling tickets to galas and festivals to producing his own shows: booking artists and venues, promoting and marketing. His first concert, by a flamenco guitarist, sold 400 seats. The next, 700. Three years later, 1960s crooner Engelbert Humperdinck performed for 3,000. In 2015, Shahinian expanded again, into touring.
Like most U.S. small businesses, Shahinian says, he self-funded for years. Entrepreneurs like him often dip into savings, family money or home equity; many run up credit cards and reinvest profits.
Shahinian says he had qualified for several generous credit cards, including an American Express with essentially no spending limit. Later, Amex also repeatedly approved him for special merchant financing: instant short-term loans with a low interest rate of 6%.
"All my life," Shahinian offers as his frequent disclaimer these days, "I had never had one missed payment."
By 2018, Shahinian says, he had built his retirement plan: His ticket sales climbed toward $5 million a year, his profits $250,000.
Booking his biggest tour yet, with a 1980s German superstar, Shahinian sought his fifth round of Amex merchant funding.
Except this time, Amex said no. The company was phasing out the program.
All Shahinian could think was: "Whoa." Tours are costly affairs with down payments to venues, marketing, airfare, lights and sound. He'd left himself no time to maneuver — two weeks to acquire about $200,000.
Enter merchant cash advances.
A funding void
Small businesses in the U.S. consistently say they turn to merchant cash advances, MCAs, because they find few alternatives, especially in an emergency.
Most traditional lending takes months and vigorous vetting. The Small Business Administration has tightened its lending rules. Big banks reject about 20% of business loan applications, according to the Treasury Department, and respond to a quarter with only partial funding. A recent Federal Reserve survey found even lower odds.
MCAs, by contrast, present themselves as a lifeline, offering large sums within hours.
Their fees, however, run from 25% to 200% and more, when translated into an annual rate. MCA firms argue they charge a lot because they take on big risks.
They also face almost no regulatory oversight.
MCAs escape most lending laws because, technically, they are not loans. An MCA is meant to be a purchase of future sales — a business gets cash in exchange for a steady cut of its earnings later. MCA funders generally aren't required to be licensed and face no legal limit to how much they can charge.
The industry runs the gamut: A funder could be a firm recommended by Amazon, or the latest fintech startup, or a former subprime mortgage lender. Some rely on brokers to drum up deals. Most collect payment by withdrawing directly from their borrowers' bank accounts — often daily.
Shahinian, scrambling after the Amex rejection, lined up two cash advances for a total of $250,000, he says, owing back almost $400,000. This saved his concert tour but cost him all the profits.
"It was my fault — I waited last minute," Shahinian says. "I'm talking to myself, 'Vahe, you had to do it this time. You're never going back to MCAs.'"
A fateful offer
But MCA pitches never stop. Sometimes, Shahinian replied that he wanted only a traditional loan, something along an 8% interest rate.
Before he even went hunting, the offer came to him — the pitch that changed his life: The line of credit up to $750,000 at an annual interest rate just under 9%. Finally, Shahinian thought, someone recognized the quality of his business.
"It's like the puzzle fit, you know?" he says.
This encounter took Shahinian beyond the MCAs' unforgiving fees into what he alleges was fraud.
As he weighed the offer's condition — 30 days of daily $3,600 payments — he didn't recognize it as a merchant cash advance.
On the phone, the broker presented it as a routine test, Shahinian says, to show his dependability before he'd qualify for his preapproved line of credit. Shahinian had no lawyer or adviser to consult then. He looked up the finance firm, Wall Street-based EIN Cap; it advertised itself as a "provider of working capital to local businesses."
"I was assured that 'We've done this for years. We don't care about a 30-day program — our goal is long term,'" Shahinian says. "The whole setup was to make someone like me feel assured, feel safe — and I felt safe to go in it."
From the start, Shahinian says, he received $228,000 instead of the promised $250,000. The difference was withheld as an initial fee, a common feature of MCAs. He set aside almost half the funds to secure his daily $3,600 payment. The rest vanished into down payments for venues and other tour investments.
After 30 days, when the line of credit didn't materialize, Shahinian says the broker portrayed the delays as technical. His emails grew urgent.
"I had calculated and planned everything based on the 30-day plan."
"I planned massive tour projects based on this solid word. This is not a joke."
"I don't think you understand the urgency of this situation. I'm basically out of time."
EIN Cap later in court argued it never promised Shahinian any loans or lines of credit — only a merchant cash advance, which it delivered. EIN Cap said it was the brokers — the middlemen — who had arranged the deal and made promises. Much of what the company had to say about its ties to those brokers is in sealed depositions.
After 40 days of daily payments, Shahinian says, for the first time, his bank account hit zero.
A spiral of debt
Shahinian's lawyer, Shane Heskin — who has been clashing with MCA companies for a decade — calls what happened here "carroting." As in, a carrot gets dangled in front of a small-business owner in the form of an attractive financing deal — a low-interest loan — in a bait and switch to sign an unsolicited MCA.
"I see two or three a week," Heskin says about such cases. "They're exploding."
Heskin says common targets are first-time business owners, first-time borrowers and especially immigrants.
NPR spoke with several entrepreneurs who were "carroted" in similar ways. One described falling into a deep depression; another declared bankruptcy. None, except Shahinian, wanted to speak on the record.
Shahinian says he paid his unwanted MCA to the end, hemorrhaging cash.
"That's just who I am, you know?" he says, explaining his choice. "Who I was."
In fact, had he stopped paying, his funders might have sued him for debt collection — a common consequence with MCAs.
Days before his biggest concert tour yet, with his accounts empty, Shahinian assessed costs: venues still half-paid, airfare unbooked and rising in price, thousands of tickets undermarketed and unsold.
He did what many business owners do when they struggle to stay afloat with merchant cash advances: He took out more cash advances.
A collapse
Shahinian says his two new MCAs, totaling around $250,000, evaporated into expenses in half a day.
"From here," he says, "the avalanche of money over money, over money, over money started."
He tapped his credit and then home equity — his own, his parents' and his best friend's. Within weeks, Shahinian says, he was more than $1 million in debt to friends and family.
"He asked me for some money, and, I mean, I could see he's drowning, you know?" says Zorik Yeghikian, who did lend to Shahinian later on. He's a restaurant owner whom Shahinian had helped win a catering contract for a local concert venue.
Yeghikian knew the trap of MCA payments. They had nearly capsized his own business, he says, when he'd borrowed about $30,000 and owed nearly triple. Yeghikian slept at his restaurant and worked double shifts alongside his wife, both forgoing pay.
"I lost my hair," Yeghikian says. "I went through hell those years."
The exact scale of the MCA industry is unclear, but it's ballooning. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City reports that businesses are increasingly turning to MCAs to cover basic expenses like payroll. MCAs are a frequent feature in small-business bankruptcies, which have been rising.
Shahinian canceled several concerts of his tours, costing him six-figure losses. Many shows went underpromoted and undersold. They might have seemed OK to the audience but did little to save him.
He began to default on his debts.
Shahinian watched himself become someone who lost count of overdue bills and unpaid invoices. He tapped more emergency MCAs and raked in collections notices. Some of his clients received lien letters, asking them to redirect any payments meant for Shahinian to his funders instead. His business relationships wore thin. His social circle shrunk.
He huddled in his home office with his tuxedo cats, Koby and Toby, and faced the existential dilemma: fight or flight?
A fight or a fold
Shahinian's choice — to fight — is rare. Borrowers often struggle to afford lawyers, let alone find one familiar with the MCA industry.
And MCA firms can be difficult to pin down. Shahinian says he had to hire a private investigator to reach his funders to serve his lawsuit.
He sued EIN Cap and the brokers in 2019. Three years later, he settled his claims against the brokers to focus on EIN. His remaining case in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles accuses EIN of fraud.
"EIN Cap denies Mr. Shahinian's claims, and its position is set out in its public court filings," Levi Silver, counsel for EIN, said in an emailed statement, declining any further comment due to the pending case.
As Shahinian's lawsuit plodded through the legal system, he descended down its rabbit hole.
"Most people settle, but no one depended on this promise like I did, to this magnitude," Shahinian says. "There's no way I was gonna go down. I decided to fight it to the end."
He scoured the web for people associated with his lending deal.
He found his broker, who'd introduced himself as Bryan Stein, used different names and been indicted for financial crimes. The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office told NPR that the man, Boris Shteyngart, pleaded guilty in 2012 to grand larceny; public records show he served time in prison.
Shahinian spent a year tracking down some 700 business owners who'd been sued by EIN for debt collection.
Most did not want to revisit that chapter. Shahinian says that he connected with 70 and that many "came to tears" because "someone is standing up to bullies."
In the past decade, EIN has faced several lawsuits in at least nine states, records show. Most cases related to bankruptcies by its MCA borrowers, and most were settled or dismissed. In one case in Washington state, EIN was ordered to return the daily fees it continued to withdraw from a business that was already insolvent.
Last year, a U.S. district judge in Illinois ruled against EIN in a case over its 2019 MCA funding to a firm that federal regulators accuse of running a Ponzi-like scheme. The judge wrote that EIN "propped up" and "prolonged the Ponzi scheme" by either failing to conduct due diligence or ignoring its findings, and must return profits of $184,854.
Meanwhile in California, Shahinian's trial was delayed by another nine months. Shortly after, he lost his house to a foreclosure.
A suspended reality
For 16 years, Shahinian lived in a lush suburban cul-de-sac in the vibrant Armenian American community of Glendale, north of downtown Los Angeles. In front of his former house is an ancient oak tree; the backyard spills onto the foot of a mountain.
At age 51, Shahinian sold off belongings, packed up his cats, computer screens, ticket printers and prized sound system — and moved in with his elderly parents.
Every dollar from the foreclosure sale, Shahinian says, went to pay mortgage debt and part of the debt to his best friend.
Several friends have urged him to move on from his costly seven-year legal fight, perhaps declare bankruptcy. To him, that's admitting defeat.
"My fault," he says, "was only believing in a promise that I could have never imagined to be false."
In recent years, a handful of states, including California, have started requiring MCA companies to be clearer, in writing, about their fees. And California recently also passed a law that, starting in 2028, will require funders and brokers to be licensed and undergo background checks and inspections.
It's too late for Shahinian.
His business is now back to basics: ticketing, mostly for local shows, and coding bells and whistles for his marketing software. He hopes his lawsuit will recoup more than $5 million — all the debt Shahinian estimates he has accrued since his "incident," including some $3 million in interest and fees.
He lays blame for its entirety at the feet of his funders, with a car-accident comparison. "You're being rear-ended," he says. "The 12-wheeler rear-ending you, you lose the steering wheel, and you smash into a bunch of cars, and everyone's focus is: Why did you smash into a bunch of cars?"
Heskin, Shahinian's lawyer, says the best-case scenario would be a multimillion-dollar judgment with punitive damages, "and then it's good luck collecting on it."
He's not sure what assets EIN or its employees named in Shahinian's lawsuit still have. NPR asked EIN's lawyers whether the firm still operates; they didn't respond. The firm's investors are unknown.
Shahinian argues any win would be meaningful.
"It would show everyone [whom] I affected these years that I'm in the right," he says. "Hopefully it would be a case for the industry to self-heal, self-correct. Maybe. And it'll be hope for others who are stuck — give them motivation."
"Don't give up, you know?" he says. "Don't be on path of least resistance. Go fighting."
He chuckles and pumps his fist up in the air.
NPR's Will Chase contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: 14 people missing after Russian drone strike on Kyiv region
noticias.resumen: Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said the body of one person had been recovered from the rubble and that three people had been injured.
noticias.texto:
Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said the body of one person had been recovered from the rubble and that three people had been injured.
Fourteen people are missing after a Russian drone strike destroyed part of a five-story apartment building in the Kyiv region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday.
Search and rescue operations are underway at the scene of the attack in Dymer, north of the Ukrainian capital.
"Nine people have already been evacuated, and the fire has been contained. But unfortunately, people may still be trapped under the rubble – 14 people remain unaccounted for," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.
Images from the scene show emergency crews picking through the debris as they work to find survivors.
Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said the body of one person had been recovered from the rubble and that at least three people had been injured.
He added that a command centre had been set up to help coordinate a response to the attack, with social services and psychologists working out of the site.
It comes after Russian forces fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles at Ukraine from Thursday night into Friday morning, which Zelenskyy called "one of the largest attacks" of the war so far.
At least seven people were killed in Kyiv in those strikes, while key bridges across the Dnipro River were also damaged.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian forces had launched around 2,700 drones, close to 1,460 aerial bombs, and 165 missiles at 20 Ukrainian regions this week.
"A significant number were ballistic missiles, including North Korean ones, which the Russians are constantly helping Pyongyang modernize to improve their accuracy," Zelenskyy said, as he renewed calls for allies to speed up deliveries of interceptor missiles.
"It is particularly difficult to understand the delays in supplying anti-ballistic interceptors to Ukraine," the Ukrainian leader added, urging Washington to authorise transfers of interceptors already paid for through NATO's PURL initiative.
Ukrainian forces reportedly also carried out their own strikes overnight, targeting a Russian National Guard facility in Krasnodar.
Five people are reported to have been injured in the strikes on Krasnodar, including four in Afipsky, a settlement home to an oil refinery that has previously been targeted by Ukraine.

noticias.resumen: Mongolia is preparing for its first early presidential election after President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa resigned amid corruption allegations, having called for constitutional reform before leaving office.
noticias.texto:
Mongolia is preparing for its first early presidential election after President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa resigned amid corruption allegations, having called for constitutional reform before leaving office.
Mongolia will hold a snap presidential election after President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa resigned amid corruption allegations.
Mongolia’s parliament, the State Great Khural, approved the president’s resignation on Thursday, with 96 of the 104 lawmakers present voting in favour of the motion, according to state news agency MONTSAME.
This marks the first time a sitting Mongolian president has resigned before completing their term.
On Tuesday, the 58-year-old president announced his resignation to allow him to prove his innocence in relation to corruption allegations. Khurelsukh denies any wrongdoing.
“I have never lied, stolen or deceived others,” Khurelsukh said at a press briefing on Tuesday, according to MONTSAME.
Khurelsukh has been accused by Nyambaatar Khishgee, former mayor of Ulaanbaatar and a member of a rival faction within the ruling Mongolian People’s Party (MPP), of taking $25 million (€23 million) in bribes.
The allegations concern a railway contract awarded to Bodi International, a Mongolian conglomerate, in 2019, when Khurelsukh was serving as prime minister.
The project involved the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway, which connects Mongolia’s coal-producing region to the border with China.
Bodi International has denied paying bribes to government officials.
Calls for constitutional reform
Before leaving office, Khurelsukh called for a constitutional referendum alongside the upcoming presidential election.
He suggested either introducing a bicameral parliament that would elect the president or shifting to a presidential system with greater executive powers.
Parliament has yet to announce a referendum on the proposed constitutional changes.
A new presidential election must be held within four months of the president’s resignation. Until a new president is elected and sworn into office, Parliamentary Speaker Byambatsogt Sandag is exercising presidential powers.
Parliament must announce the election date within 20 working days of the vacancy, and at least 70 days before the election.
Originally, the next presidential election was to be held in the summer of 2027. The winner of the early election will serve a single six-year term.
This means they will serve beyond Mongolia’s next two parliamentary elections, expected in 2028 and 2032 under the regular electoral cycle.
Political instability
Mongolia has experienced several high-profile political resignations in recent years.
In June 2025, former Prime Minister Luvsannamsrai Oyun-Erdene resigned after losing parliamentary support amid corruption allegations, which he denied.
In March 2026, Oyun-Erdene’s successor, Zandanshatar Gombojav, also resigned amid rising tensions within the ruling MPP and a parliamentary boycott by the opposition.
Relations with Europe
Mongolia has been seeking to improve relations with international partners other than its two powerful neighbours, China and Russia.
The country has long followed a foreign policy known as the ‘Third Neighbour Policy’, with the aim of improving relations with international partners, including the European Union.
Just one month before his resignation, Khurelsukh went on a state visit to Germany. During this visit, he met German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.
As part of the visit, Mongolia and Germany signed a joint declaration to strengthen their existing strategic partnership. This includes cooperation on renewable energy, education and security.
In a statement following a meeting in Brussels on 29 June, the EU reaffirmed its support for Mongolia’s Third Neighbour Policy.
The EU described its partnership with Mongolia as based on democracy and the rule of law, while reaffirming its support for the country's economic diversification.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine: Up to seven feared trapped beneath rubble near Kyiv after Russian attack
noticias.resumen: A Russian strike partially destroyed an apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, on Sunday. Nine people, including a child, were evacuated as rescuers searched the rubble for up to seven others feared trapped.
noticias.texto:
Emergency workers rushed to the scene in Dymer, near Kyiv, where a Russian drone strike had destroyed a section of a five-storey residential building from the first to the fifth floor. Footage released by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service showed rescuers using an extended fire ladder and an aerial platform to help residents escape from the damaged structure, while other teams searched through piles of debris for possible survivors.
According to Ukrainian authorities, nine residents, including one child, had been evacuated. The State Emergency Service initially said that up to seven people could be trapped beneath the rubble. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said that 14 people were unaccounted for.
The attack was part of a wider wave of Russian drone strikes reported across Ukraine overnight. Ukraine’s Air Force said 186 attack drones were launched, of which 161 were shot down.
In Kharkiv, a strike drone hit the Kyivskyi district and started a fire. In Chernihiv, a Russian strike set a wood-processing plant ablaze, while in Zaporizhzhia three people, including two children, were injured in an evening attack.
The extent of the destruction in Dymer raised fears for residents who might still be beneath the collapsed sections of the building. Rescue workers remained focused on removing debris and reaching potentially trapped people, with no confirmed outcome for those still missing at the time of the initial reports. The latest strikes once again exposed the dangers faced by civilians in residential areas as Russian aerial attacks continue across Ukraine.

noticias.titulo: Euronews' Attila Kert tapped to lead Hungary's public broadcaster
noticias.resumen: Euronews Hungary head Attila Kert has been tapped to run Hungary's public broadcaster, which faces an overhaul after years of bias criticism under Viktor Orbán. He pledges to restore credibility, launch streaming and probe Russian influence.
noticias.texto:
Euronews Hungary head Attila Kert has been tapped to run Hungary's public broadcaster, which faces an overhaul after years of bias criticism under Viktor Orbán. He pledges to restore credibility, launch streaming and probe Russian influence.
Euronews journalist Attila Kert has been selected as chief executive of Hungary's public broadcaster, Hungarian Radio and Television (MRTV).
Kert has led Euronews' Hungarian team in Budapest since 2013.
Under the previous government, led by Viktor Orbán, the national broadcaster was criticised by NGOs and the European Union for political bias. The institution now faces a reorganisation aimed at delivering objective, independent coverage and completing its digitalisation.
Twenty-seven candidates applied for the post, of whom 14 were found eligible. They set out their plans at a hearing earlier this week, ahead of the decision by the Independent Public Media Board, the body overseeing the transition.
"I am proud to have worked with Euronews for over 13 years. The experience I gained here has helped me a lot in my application for the new position. Without Euronews, I would be less. I am grateful to all my colleagues and thank them," Kert said.
In his presentation, Kert vowed to restore the broadcaster's credibility while reorganising it to become financially sustainable. His plans include setting up a streaming platform and investigating possible Russian influence.
Editorial Director of Euronews, Claus Strunz, said the decision is proof of the journalistic quality and editorial independence of Euronews in Hungary.
“Attila Kert believes in freedom of expression and the power of images and knows how to exercise both responsibly in every situation.
Over the past 13 years as head of our Hungarian service, he has played a pivotal role in safeguarding and strengthening Euronews’ independence and editorial neutrality, both internally and externally, in a highly polarised political and media environment.
His move from a renowned private media organisation to public-service broadcasting therefore marks a significant moment in the history of Hungarian media. Euronews is losing one of its finest journalists, while Hungarian public-service television is gaining in journalistic quality, stature and profile.
We also view his appointment to this important position as a testament to the journalistic quality and independence of Euronews in Hungary,” Strunz said.
Public broadcaster faces reorganisation
The Hungarian public broadcaster faced years of criticism under the Orbán government over bias and disinformation.
The Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) found that MRTV's coverage was systematically skewed, with news programmes "openly and disproportionately" supporting the ruling parties' narrative while marginalising or negatively portraying opposition voices.
After his landslide election victory in April, Péter Magyar vowed to shut down the organisation and create an independent, objective outlet.
In July, the broadcaster went off air for one day, replaced by an on-screen apology: "Public media cannot lie. We apologise because we did this anyway."
Before joining Euronews, Kert held several senior roles in Hungarian media. He was editor-in-chief of the commercial networks TV2 and ATV, and later head of news at the national broadcaster.
He was appointed to lead the Hungarian-language edition of Euronews in February 2013.
In 2026, the independent Italian media research institute Osservatorio di Pavia published an audit of Euronews Hungary's coverage of the election campaign. It scored the channel 99% for editorial independence and 98% for balanced coverage.

noticias.titulo: Japan: Mascot mania takes over Saitama with 200 colourful characters
noticias.resumen: More than 200 colourful mascots gathered in Saitama, Japan, delighting tens of thousands of fans with dancing, parades and photo opportunities. Among the stars was Kumamon, the country's famous black bear mascot.
noticias.texto:
From giant cuddly animals to quirky cartoon figures, mascots danced on stage, paraded through the venue and posed for photographs with enthusiastic visitors. Crowds armed with smartphones captured the playful encounters, while some fans waved excitedly as their favourite characters passed by. Among the biggest attractions was Kumamon, the black bear representing Kumamoto Prefecture, who entertained spectators with an energetic dance performance on stage. One mascot even travelled through the festival aboard a traditional rickshaw.
Mascots are an important part of Japanese popular culture, where they are widely used to promote towns, regions, public services and private businesses. Known as yuru-chara, these often deliberately quirky characters help organisations connect with the public through humour, charm and distinctive designs. Their roles extend far beyond entertainment, representing everything from railway companies to prisons and local tourism campaigns.
Some have become national celebrities, attracting devoted fan bases and generating significant interest in the places they represent. Kumamon is one of the best-known examples, having achieved widespread recognition across Japan and beyond. The annual Saitama gathering offers fans a rare opportunity to meet dozens of their favourite characters in one place, celebrating a distinctly Japanese phenomenon that blends entertainment, regional identity and promotion.

noticias.titulo: Tracking site says Iranian tanker reportedly sailing through Strait of Hormuz does not exist
noticias.resumen: The US military said Saturday marked 130 consecutive days of its naval blockade against Iran, which it says is preventing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from exporting "billions of dollars in crude oil."
noticias.texto:
The US military said Saturday marked 130 consecutive days of its naval blockade against Iran, which it says is preventing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from exporting "billions of dollars in crude oil."
Amid growing speculation that Iran could attempt to break the US' naval blockade of its ports, MarineTraffic data appeared to show an Iranian tanker called "Khat-Shekan" sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.
However, the tanker-tracking site TankerTrackers has said it was a "spoof" and that the vessel does not exist.
"All of the data supplementing that AIS transmission is wrong and there's nothing on satellite imagery to corroborate those movements," TankerTrackers said in a post on social media, adding that the "Iranians know better than to attempt to ship out a VLCC right now given how many were fired upon in recent months."
The reported movement came as satellite images and ship-tracking data published in recent days showed more than 14 oil tankers had gathered around Kharg Island, a key Iranian export terminal.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Friday that the US' naval blockade "must be broken."
"We are making every effort to export oil and to conduct negotiations, and the blockade must be broken," he said.
The US military said Saturday marked 130 consecutive days of its blockade against Iran, which it says is preventing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from exporting "billions of dollars in crude oil."
US President Donald Trump has called the blockade, which focuses on restricting shipping to and from Iranian ports in the waters surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, an "impenetrable steel wall."
The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial oil and gas transit chokepoint that has been at the heart of tensions between Washington and Tehran since the Iran war broke out in late February.
The strategic waterway usually carries around 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade.

noticias.titulo: Portugal: Workers brave downpours to demand a more affordable life
noticias.resumen: Thousands of people marched through Lisbon, Portugal, on Saturday 21 November 2026, braving heavy rain to demand higher wages, better pensions and measures to tackle the rising cost of living. The demonstration came just days before Portugal's parliamentary budget vote.
noticias.texto:
Carrying umbrellas and banners, demonstrators filled the capital's main avenues, chanting "Higher wages, better pensions" and denouncing the growing gap between household expenses and salaries. Placards reading "Everything increases except salaries" highlighted concerns over housing, food, energy and fuel prices. Organised by Portugal's main trade union confederation, CGTP, the nationwide demonstration brought together workers from across the country.
Housing affordability emerged as a central concern, with protesters warning that rising rents were making it increasingly difficult to cover basic expenses. The demonstration took place ahead of the final parliamentary debate on Portugal's budget for 2027, with a vote scheduled for Tuesday 24 November. Further protests were announced as unions sought to increase pressure on the government over wages, pensions and living standards.

noticias.titulo: Reported FBI hack 'not good' but could have benefits, Trump says
noticias.resumen: The reported breach comes amid a wave of tech outages in the US, which have impacted travel, communications and banking, as well as an internal system used by the National Security Agency.
noticias.texto:
The reported breach comes amid a wave of tech outages in the US, which have impacted travel, communications and banking, as well as an internal system used by the National Security Agency.
US President Donald Trump has said that a reported hack of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) criminal justice database was "not good" but that it could have some benefits.
US media outlets reported earlier this week that the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) appeared to have been breached by hackers and that the agency had launched an investigation.
Asked about the subject on Saturday, Trump told Fox News: "We just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that."
"But maybe we'll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise," he continued, before referring to the "Russia hoax," the "Ukraine hoax," and alleged voter fraud.
"Maybe we'll learn about them, maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," Trump said. "I always like to put things in a positive spin."
The NCIC is a computerised index of criminal justice information and includes records on criminal history, fugitives, missing persons and stolen properties, among other topics.
The reported hack comes amid a wave of tech outages in the US, which have impacted travel, communications and banking, as well as an internal system used by the National Security Agency.
National cyber director Sean Cairncross was ousted from his role as the issues mounted, with Trump telling reporters on Friday that he "didn't think that person was good enough." The national cyber director is tasked with advising the president on cybersecurity policy and strategy, including information security and data protection as well as deterrence of "malicious" activity.

noticias.titulo: Hot freezers, lost GPS and fake bombs: Europe's month of cyberattacks
noticias.resumen: Only three of the incidents tallied by Europe's main tech industry group have been linked to a culprit, and that ambiguity may be the attackers' strongest weapon.
noticias.texto:
Only three of the incidents tallied by Europe's main tech industry group have been linked to a culprit, and that ambiguity may be the attackers' strongest weapon.
On 2 and 3 November, supermarket freezers across Europe started switching themselves into defrost mode. In some stores, attackers set the temperature as high as 50°C.
Shops in Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Romania and Sweden threw away spoiled meat and frozen food, while several blood banks in France were also hit. The UK reported attacks too.
EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen called it a "deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain". Nearly three weeks later, nobody has claimed responsibility and the motive remains unclear.
One month, 16 incidents
The fridge attacks were one of 16 incidents mapped by DigitalEurope, the trade association for Europe's digital technology industry, based in Brussels, Belgium, between 18 October and 18 November.
Eleven were cyberattacks. Hackers took an energy company's IT systems in Norway, closed a district hospital's emergency room in Germany and stole data from a tunnel builder working across Denmark and Germany.
At an unnamed EU institution, HR, payroll and medical systems were knocked offline. The personal data of 18 senior officials from Italy, Germany and the Netherlands was published, and espionage malware was found in Romanian government email.
About €100 million was taken from a French bank through one of its suppliers, more than 700 fintech customer accounts were exposed in Italy, and a Danish shipping group's legacy system was raided for data.
The other five incidents were physical, including two sabotage plots. About 80 aircraft lost GPS over the North Sea, drones forced Moldova to close its airspace, and hoax bomb threats hit more than 35 flights across Europe.
"Resilience is no longer just an IT department job," said Cecilia Bonefeld-Dahl, DigitalEurope's director general. "It is security policy and industrial policy."
The group says its list is not exhaustive. Ransomware gangs alone list dozens of European victims every month.
The password is 12345
The November wave was not the first. In mid-October, hackers took over refrigeration units in at least 350 supermarkets in France, including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché and Coopérative U stores, and manually overrode their temperatures.
France's cybersecurity agency said the units ran software from Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell systems. Danfoss said many had reached the end of their life, no longer received security updates or ran outdated firmware.
Supermarket refrigeration is often connected to the internet so contractors can monitor and repair it remotely. Security firm Forescout found nearly 13,000 refrigeration control services openly reachable online in 99 countries.
In November, attackers exploited weak security and known flaws in Danfoss's AK-SM system manager. Many systems still used factory-default logins such as "Supervisor" and "12345".
George Nott, technology editor at trade magazine The Grocer, said the attackers found exposed login pages and used vulnerabilities that had already been patched. In Sweden, the Coop chain said the equipment in its seven affected shops was connected over old 4G mobile networks.
Xavier Bellekens, chief executive of cybersecurity firm Lupovis, said routing the controllers through VPNs would largely have removed the risk.
Who did it?
Of DigitalEurope's 16 incidents, seven have no named culprit. Attackers claimed four themselves, investigators suspect an actor in two without formally naming it, and only three have been publicly attributed by a government or researchers.
"That is what makes hybrid attacks work: cheap, deniable and hard to pin on anyone," the group said.
The fridge attacks show how hard the question is. Lupovis said its decoy systems recorded more than 276 attempts by 91 threat actors to probe Danfoss controllers over 10 days, peaking on 26 October and stopping at the end of the month.
The activity was traced to "bulletproof hosting" services, built to resist takedowns and law enforcement, some of which Russian groups have used before. Bellekens said that did not prove Russia was responsible, but there was "a bit of a pattern". The coordination within about 24 hours pointed to a well-planned operation, possibly by a state, he added.
Others are less sure. Dan Cimpean, director of Romania's National Cyber Security Directorate, called the attacks "semi-amateurish" and said he did not suspect a state actor. After the French attack, Ken Munro of British firm Pen Test Partners said it could be "kids messing around".
No ransom was demanded, which investigators found puzzling: criminal and hacktivist groups usually move quickly to profit from or publicise an attack. Agencies cannot even agree on what to call it. Belgium, Italy and Estonia labelled it a cyberattack, Sweden and Ireland a "cyber incident", while the EU's cybersecurity agency ENISA stopped short of calling it an attack.
Same targets, different weapons
DigitalEurope's tally suggests the line between online and offline attacks is blurring. In the same month, one military drone maker in Germany was hit through a hijacked software update, while an arson attack on another in Estonia was foiled.
The group also counted a plot to start fires next to a railway and a power line in Germany.
"Digital and physical attacks hit the same targets," it said. Its map shows the incidents stretching from the North Sea to Romania and Moldova.
Find, fund, buy
Bonefeld-Dahl wants Europe to go further. "Europe needs the technology to detect, deter and recover – and it must FIND. FUND. BUY," she wrote on LinkedIn.
DigitalEurope is calling on EU leaders to spend at least 25% of the next EU budget, worth almost €2 trillion, on technologies to deter, defend and recover. It says only 14% currently goes to digital.
"There is no more time to waste," Bonefeld-Dahl wrote, in a message addressed to the bloc's prime ministers.
The 14% figure is the digital share of the EU's 2021–2025 spending, including its post-pandemic recovery fund, rather than of the budget now being negotiated. And as an industry lobby, DigitalEurope speaks for many of the companies that would sell Europe that technology.
In Brussels, the response is taking shape in the revision of the EU's Cybersecurity Act, led in the European Parliament by Czech MEP Markéta Gregorová.
What next?
Experts warn that fridges are only the start. Nott said heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems, electronic shelf labels and even floor-cleaning robots could have similar weaknesses.
Kumar Sokka, chief executive of Acre Security, said the same type of controller can run doors, access control, cameras, alarms and building climate systems. Organisations often leave them to facilities teams rather than treating them as part of their obligations under NIS2, the EU's cybersecurity law, he said.
Artificial intelligence could make the problem worse. Gianni Cuozzo, founder and chief executive of Exein, said AI was shortening the time between finding a vulnerability and building an attack, so connected devices needed to defend themselves as they run.
Bonefeld-Dahl will discuss Europe's response in Vilnius, Lithuania, next week. She ended her post with a question: "What's the next critical target?"

noticias.titulo: New COP31 draft deal tabled as countries scramble to salvage climate talks
noticias.resumen: The latest draft again failed to mention fossil fuels, which have become a flashpoint at the talks.
noticias.texto:
The latest draft again failed to mention fossil fuels, which have become a flashpoint at the talks.
A new COP31 draft agreement was published early on Sunday as nations continued to struggle to reach a climate deal.
The new draft, published deep into overtime, kept a much-sought goal to electrify the global economy but again failed to mention fossil fuels, deepening divisions at the UN conference - which is being held in Antalya, Turkey.
The latest text needs consensus approval from almost 200 nations at a closing session on Sunday.
An EU official told the AFP news agency that the draft was a "backwards" step and warned that there was a "very real possibility" of the talks ending without a deal.
"I am more pessimistic today than I was yesterday," they said.
"The situation is difficult, and the outcome is uncertain. The oil-producing countries are putting up a fierce fight," a German official added.
Planet-heating fossil fuels have become a flashpoint at the talks, which come amid soaring energy prices and simmering global tensions stemming from the Iran war.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week had called for a sped-up phasing out of fossil fuels. But a second version released on Thursday removed all mentions of the energy sources, forcing negotiators back to the bargaining table.
A group of countries including France and Panama had released a letter on Friday insisting that a deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels."
The latest offering acknowledged a previous global deal to transition away from fossil fuels but stopped short of naming them explicitly.
It also kept a contentious push to expand carbon capture and storage, a technology backed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised by opponents as costly and ineffective at reducing emissions.
"We are very disappointed with how the text looks," Michael Joseph, the environment minister of Antigua and Barbuda, told AFP.
"I can't honestly say that I'm okay with it passing" as it is, Joseph said, adding that the draft was "quite silent" on fossil fuels.

noticias.titulo: Gadi Eisenkot invites Netanyahu's Likud party for 'marathon' coalition talks
noticias.resumen: Gadi Eisenkot has until early December to form a new government after both his and Netanyahu's blocs fell short of a majority in Israel's October legislative elections.
noticias.texto:
Gadi Eisenkot has until early December to form a new government after both his and Netanyahu's blocs fell short of a majority in Israel's October legislative elections.
Gadi Eisenkot has invited the right-wing Likud party of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for "marathon" coalition talks as he continues to work to form Israel's next government, his party said on Saturday.
The talks are due to begin on Sunday and represent a "sincere and genuine effort to form a government that is as broad as possible," the centrist Yashar party said.
"The Yashar negotiating team will leave no stone unturned, enable bold moves and bring about a breakthrough that will lead to the formation of a government," it added.
Eisenkot has until early December to form a new government after both his and Netanyahu's blocs fell short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset in Israel's October legislative elections. Netanyahu's camp finished on 53 seats, while the opposition, led by the Yashar party, ended on 48.
In Israel, a candidate tasked with forming a government has 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.
Likud on Saturday outlined its position on forming a national unity government, which Netanyahu has been pushing for, including demands to halt "all personal attacks and incitement" as well as political "boycotts" against Netanyahu and the government.
It also called for a joint declaration committing to a unity government comprised of "all parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people" and without the involvement of Arab parties - which secured a record 19 seats between them in last month's elections.
"As for the talks with the Likud, we are making sincere and genuine efforts, but unfortunately there is a wide gap between rhetoric and actions, and between the Likud’s rhetoric and its actual willingness to cooperate," Eisenkot wrote in a post on social media on Friday.
He added that he intended to continue trying to "achieve a breakthrough in each of the options before us for forming a coalition that is as broad as possible" but that he did not plan to "drag this out."
"They must understand that, at the right time, I will bring a new and strong government headed by me to the Knesset for approval," he said.

noticias.titulo: Madeira's ocean survey finds evidence protection works – and some worrying signs
noticias.resumen: A survey by more than 200 specialists found that Madeira's marine reserves are working – but some species are still in peril.
noticias.texto:
A survey by more than 200 specialists found that Madeira's marine reserves are working – but some species are still in peril.
Madeira's waters sit at an ecological crossroads in the North-East Atlantic. Migrating whales, seabirds and turtles pass through, and the archipelago is home to cold-water corals and one of the world's rarest seals. Yet large stretches of the sea around the Portuguese islands have never been properly studied.
The Madeira Ocean Expedition, which ran throughout October, set out to fill those gaps. Its findings will feed into decisions on how to manage and expand Madeira's marine protected areas, as the region works towards protecting 30 per cent of its sea by 2030, with at least 10 per cent fully protected.
"We cannot protect without understanding how the biodiversity functions and works," says João Canning-Clode, director of the MARE-Madeira research centre.
A health check at sea: 500 dives in Madeira's ocean
Madeira's regional government organised the expedition with the Oceano Azul Foundation, National Geographic Pristine Seas, the regional research agency ARDITI and Oceanário de Lisboa. Teams worked from the historic tall ship Santa Maria Manuela and a fleet of smaller boats around Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas Islands.
"In an expedition like this, we want to take a snapshot about the health of the marine environment," says Emanuel Gonçalves, chief scientist at the Oceano Azul Foundation.
Scientists completed nearly 500 dives, lowered more than 300 baited cameras, filtered seawater for traces of DNA, mapped the shoreline with drones and sampled for microplastics.
With no research vessel of its own yet, MARE-Madeira also hired a fishing boat. "The fishermen could see for the first time live images of some of the biodiversity that they are actually fishing," Canning-Clode says. "On the other hand, the scientific community can see firsthand how difficult their life is."
Signs that Madeira's ocean protections work
Early results suggest Madeira's reserves are making a difference. Limpets – grazing sea snails harvested as a local delicacy – were bigger and more abundant inside protected areas, a sign that limits on collecting them are working, and the largest groupers were recorded there too.
"The good news is that we have the science to show us that when we fully protect the ocean, the ocean responds," Gonçalves says.
The Mediterranean monk seal is another case in point. Hunted for centuries, it had almost vanished from Madeira by the late 1980s, when only six to eight animals were thought to remain. The Desertas Islands became a nature reserve in 1990, partly to protect it. Today the species "is a beacon of hope", Gonçalves says. "The population is increasing in numbers. Now that increase is very slow because they are very slow breeders."
The expedition also achieved the first-ever satellite tagging of a Blainville's beaked whale in the North-East Atlantic. Early tracking data show the animal favouring waters south of the Desertas, close to the fully protected area.
But one finding stands out for the wrong reason. Fewer than 10 sharks were recorded across the entire expedition. The organisers call this scarcity concerning and in line with wider worries about sharks in the Atlantic.
Into the deep: The difficulties of exploring Madeira's ocean
By area, Madeira is mostly deep sea. "It's an ocean state, a deep ocean state," says Diva Amon, a marine scientist on the Oceano Azul Foundation's board. "And the deep sea is a very difficult place to study."
Drift cameras developed by researchers in the Azores and lowered from a fishing boat reached 1,060 metres. They revealed sponge fields and large black corals that may be several hundred years old – alongside lost fishing lines and a glass bottle.
Closer to the surface, the habitat-mapping team's highlight was a dense black coral garden off Porto Santo, known as Ariel's Garden after the team's pink underwater robot. "Our torpedo is pink, so by majority vote it's called Ariel, after the little mermaid from the Disney film," says João Monteiro, a researcher at MARE-Madeira and the University of Madeira.
A second expedition in 2027 will explore the deepest waters. Amon hopes it will reveal "places that are as iconic as the Grand Canyon or the Okavango Delta".
For Paul Rose, head of expeditions at National Geographic Pristine Seas, Madeira's location matters. "People think about ocean protection, they think about the Pacific... It all seems a bit remote," he says. "But if they see huge, beautiful, functioning, proven marine protected areas in Europe, it's closer to home."
Just over 10 per cent of the global ocean now lies within protected areas, according to IUCN and UNEP-WCMC – a third of the way to the 2030 goal. "We've really got to protect 30 per cent or we're in big trouble," Rose says.

noticias.titulo: Is Europe ready to judge workers by skills, not just diplomas? Who leads skills-first hiring?
noticias.resumen: Employers across Europe increasingly value skills while formal qualifications are still significant. Euronews Business takes a close look at which countries are most ready for a skills-first approach with experts explaining the gaps.
noticias.texto:
Employers across Europe increasingly value skills while formal qualifications are still significant. Euronews Business takes a close look at which countries are most ready for a skills-first approach with experts explaining the gaps.
The labour market is constantly changing. New jobs are emerging and new skills are required. Degrees still matter in Europe’s job market, but employers are paying more attention to what people can actually do, experts say.
“The currency of the labour market is shifting from traditional credentials alone towards a stronger focus on skills,” OECD’s ‘A Skills‑First Labour Market’ report says.
This is known as a skills-first approach.
“In practice, skills-first hiring is not about replacing degrees altogether, but about giving greater weight to individuals’ demonstrated skills, wherever they were acquired, to improve the matching of talent to jobs,” Glenda Quintini, senior economist at OECD, told Euronews Business.
Dr Soon-Joo Gog, senior director at the Centre for Skills-First Practices at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, emphasised that skills-first does not mean skills only. It is an operating principle. Individuals and employers use demonstrated skills, alongside qualifications.
The OECD’s Skills-First Readiness and Adoption Index measures how ready each country is for this approach.
How does the index work?
The index gives each country a score between 0 and 1. A higher score means a country is better prepared for skills-first practices and uses them more widely.
The index looks at how well countries identify, develop, recognise and reward skills. This includes adult learning, the use of skills data, public support for training and how far employers value what workers can show they are able to do.
Sweden and France lead the way
Sweden has the highest score in Europe at 0.70, followed by France (0.69), the UK (0.65) and Belgium (0.64).
“Countries such as Sweden and France perform strongly overall, although there is no single pathway to building a skills-first labour market,” Quintini said.
“Sweden, for example, stands out for its strong enabling framework, including the use of skills intelligence data and public support for skills development.” she added.
Finland (0.63), Czechia (0.61), Norway (0.61) and Latvia (0.61) also score above the European average.
The average across 23 European countries is 0.58. Spain (0.59), Denmark (0.58), Portugal (0.58), Italy (0.58), Lithuania (0.58), Poland (0.58) and Austria (0.58) are close to this average.
Germany (0.57), Switzerland (0.57) and the Netherlands (0.56) are slightly below it.
Hungary (0.45) and Greece (0.46) have the lowest scores. Turkey (0.52), Slovakia (0.54) and Slovenia (0.54) also score low.
Quintini noted that countries at the lower end of the index often face greater barriers related to adult learning participation and the development of broader learning ecosystems.
“The gap is therefore not simply about education systems, but it reflects how effectively countries identify, develop, recognise and reward skills in the labour market,” she said.
The US scores slightly above the European average at 0.60. Canada (0.55), Japan (0.51) and South Korea (0.48) are below it.
Gog pointed out that most European countries have laid the foundations but the harder step is to make these practices routine.
“That takes time and requires coordinated effort across the system,” she said.
Degrees still matter, but they are not the only signal
Experts agree that degrees remain important. But employers increasingly want to see skills as well.
“Degrees continue to matter in OECD labour markets, particularly because they remain a widely recognised signal of knowledge and capabilities,” Quintini said.
“However, employers are increasingly looking beyond formal qualifications and paying greater attention to the actual skills that workers possess and can demonstrate.”
She said skill shortages are driving this shift. Firms also need to find talent from a wider range of backgrounds, and skill needs are often changing faster than education systems can adapt.
As of 2025, more than 70% of employers across OECD countries report difficulties filling vacancies because of a lack of skilled talent. At the same time, around a third of workers say they are either over-skilled or under-skilled for their current job.
Significance of degrees varies by occupation
“Degrees still matter but their importance varies considerably by occupation and the real requirements are not always made transparent to jobseekers,” Pawel Adrjan, director of economic research at Indeed, told Euronews Business.
Indeed research found that only 14% of UK job postings explicitly mention formal education requirements, compared to 50% in the US.
He underlined that degrees remain important in specialist and highly regulated professions in practice.
“The key distinction is that a degree remains a valuable signal of knowledge and capability but it is not necessarily the only way candidates can demonstrate the skills required to do a job,” he added.
Skills need to evolve rapidly
Anna Toni, senior specialist at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment in Finland, emphasized that stakeholders increasingly recognise that valuable skills are acquired not only through formal education, but also through work experience, volunteering, hobbies and other life experiences. New tools and methods are being developed to identify and validate these skills.
“Labour markets are changing faster than before, driven by factors such as digitalisation, the green transition and AI. Skills need to evolve rapidly, and education and employment policies must adapt accordingly,” she told Euronews Business.
Skills or degrees: Which pays more?
The OECD found that on average, extra education raises wages by about 16%, while better numeracy skills raise them by about 9%, when comparing gaps of similar size.
This finding shows that employers still place substantial value on educational credentials as signals of productivity, especially when information on workers’ skills is limited according to Quintini.
In the OECD index, below 1 means education pays more than skills. France is the only European country above 1 at 1.33. This means a numeracy gap pays about a third more than an education gap of the same typical size.
“This [in France] may reflect a labour market and policy environment that is more conducive to recognising and valuing demonstrated skills,” she said.
Gog warned that the test covers numeracy only, so it misses the technical, social and job-specific skills that many jobs need.

noticias.titulo: Suffolk village votes to ‘leave UK’ in protest over asylum seeker plans
noticias.resumen: Residents of Barnham back symbolic independence vote after government proposes accommodating around 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former RAF base.
noticias.texto:
Residents of Barnham back symbolic independence vote after government proposes accommodating around 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former RAF base.
A village in eastern England has voted overwhelmingly in favour of symbolically leaving the United Kingdom in protest against government plans to accommodate hundreds of asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.
Residents of Barnham, in Suffolk, voted 257 to 16 in favour of seeking a special status similar to that enjoyed by the Crown Dependencies of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man. One ballot was spoilt in Saturday’s vote, in which around 500 residents were eligible to take part.
The vote is purely symbolic and has no legal force. It does not mean Barnham can leave the United Kingdom or acquire Crown Dependency status. Any such change would require formal agreement and constitutional action by the UK authorities.
The former Royal Air Force site has been identified as a potential location for accommodating around 930 asylum seekers while their applications are processed. The government is seeking to move away from using hotels and towards accommodation at former military sites.
No final decision on RAF Barnham asylum plans
The government has stressed that no final decision has been made on whether RAF Barnham will be used to accommodate asylum seekers.
It said that, should the plans go ahead, it would work closely with local authorities and Suffolk Police to ensure the safety and security of the community.
The Home Office also cited the example of Wethersfield in Essex, where male asylum seekers have been accommodated since July 2023, saying there was “no evidence of rising crime in the area”.
A Home Office spokesperson said the government was pursuing a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country and had saved more than £1bn (approximately €1.19bn) in costs since the general election.
The plans include closing all asylum hotels and relocating people to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.
The spokesperson added that the proposed facilities would be self-contained and equipped with round-the-clock security and CCTV to minimise the impact on surrounding communities.
Residents protest over lack of consultation
The proposal has prompted protests among residents, who say they were not adequately consulted about a development that could have a significant impact on their small community.
A similar vote took place in Piddington, Oxfordshire, in September, where residents also backed a symbolic move to leave the UK in protest against plans to accommodate more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.
Piddington’s symbolic vote failed to halt the plans, and the village is now preparing a legal fight after the government granted planning permission.
