noticias.titulo: A five-star stay in Qatar: Luxury hotels and resorts to book
noticias.resumen: From beachfront resorts to skyscraper hotels overlooking the Arabian Gulf, Qatar is home to a growing portfolio of luxury properties.
noticias.texto:
From beachfront resorts to skyscraper hotels overlooking the Arabian Gulf, Qatar is home to a growing portfolio of luxury properties.
When Qatar hosted the FIFA World Cup in 2022 it wasn’t just its sporting infrastructure that got an upgrade – but also its collection of hotels and resorts.
Now, Qatar’s luxury hotel portfolio has grown with five-star properties extending from the centre of the capital city Doha to the country’s islands and coastline.
For travellers seeking a high-end stay, the choice extends beyond location, with properties offering everything from private beaches and spas to fine dining and stunning views of the Arabian Gulf.
Looking for a five-star stay in Qatar? Here are some of the best luxury hotels and resorts to consider in Doha and Lusail.
The Chedi Katara Hotel & Resort
Opened in November 2022 in Katara Cultural Village, The Chedi has 91 rooms, suites, and villas with Mughal- and Ottoman-style interiors and sea views. Each of its 32 villas has a private garden and pool.
It features a private beach with water sports and two pools – a 60-metre-long infinity pool and a 35 metre family pool. Its Eastern-inspired spa includes a couples’ room and separate hammams for men and women.
Dining options include overwater restaurant La Marsa, which is reached by jetty.
Fairmont Doha
Fairmont Doha shares the landmark Katara Towers with its sister property, the Raffles Doha, in Lusail Marina. Both opened in November 2022 for FIFA World Cup guests and VIPs.
The hotel’s 362 rooms and suites take inspiration from sleek megayachts, while a 57-metre “crystal swirl” chandelier runs through the lobby.
For active travellers, there’s Fairmont Fit and a climbing wall. For a more relaxed stay, Fairmont Spa features nine treatment rooms and a traditional hammam. There is also a main outdoor pool, a 25-metre indoor lap pool and a private pool for Fairmont Gold guests.
The hotel offers five dining options, including Provok, a pan-Asian restaurant with sweeping rooftop views.
Four Seasons Hotel Doha
On the Corniche in West Bay, the Four Seasons Hotel Doha originally opened in April 2005. After a complete interior design overhaul by French designer Pierre-Yves Rochon, it reopened in 2020 with renovated guest rooms, suites, floors, lobby and dining outlets.
As well as 237 rooms and suites, the hotel has a private beach and five pools, including grotto pools and pools with slides. Its three-storey spa and wellness centre has 11 treatment rooms and a large hydrotherapy area with an ice room.
Nobu Doha, one of the hotel’s culinary highlights, is located on a private peninsula overlooking the Arabian Gulf and Doha skyline.
Four Seasons Resort & Residences at The Pearl-Qatar
Opened in November 2023 on The Pearl island, the second Four Seasons property in Qatar combines a beachfront resort with private accommodation. It has 161 guest rooms and 84 private residences.
The resort has a private beach and three pools, including a 25-metre indoor pool. Guests can also use the luxury Loulou spa, with aqua-thermal facilities, while younger guests have access to the Kids for All Seasons programme, with activities for children aged 4-12.
Dining options include Chicago Rare, a modern steakhouse with views of the Gulf and live jazz.
Mandarin Oriental, Doha
Mandarin Oriental, Doha opened in March 2019 in the heart of Msheireb Downtown, with the popular Souq Waqif just a short walk away.
It includes 117 rooms, 41 suites and 91 serviced apartments, offering views of Barahat Msheireb town square and the city landscape.
The hotel has two rooftop pools, including a 25-metre lap pool. Its spa offers a signature “Singing Sand Dunes” treatment inspired by the desert dunes in Qatar.
Dining facilities include Mosaic, which has nine open kitchens serving dishes inspired by the Silk Route.
Marsa Malaz Kempinski, The Pearl-Doha
Opened in December 2014 on its own private island at The Pearl, Marsa Malaz Kempinski blends palatial Arabian and European design across its 281 rooms and suites. It is also just a short walk from Qanat Quartier’s colourful buildings and canals.
Guests can take part in water sports from the private beach and jetty, while children have their own pool and the Titan Tikes playroom. The outdoor pool area also has a large whirlpool, while the Marsa Malaz Spa offers a private indoor pool.
Dining options include the Doha outpost of Harry's Dolce Vita, an Italian restaurant that serves classic dishes.
The Ned Doha
Located in the former Ministry of Interior building on Doha’s Corniche, The Ned Doha opened in 2022. Its 90 rooms and suites feature 1970s-inspired interiors, with balconies overlooking the Arabian Gulf or neighbouring Al Bidda Park.
Ned's Club includes a health club with a spa, a traditional Moroccan hammam and a 30 metre heated outdoor pool, while the hotel's central atrium hosts live performances.
Millie’s Lounge, one of several restaurants and bars, has curved booths and views of Doha's skyline, while Electric Diner is styled as a 1950s American diner.
Raffles Doha
Raffles Doha opened in November 2022 in Lusail’s landmark Katara Towers, whose curved design is inspired by Qatar’s crossed swords.
The hotel has 132 suites, each with dedicated butler service. The hotel’s 55-metre outdoor pool has private cabanas, while Raffles Spa has five private spa suites, each with its own hammam, jacuzzi, outdoor pool and treatment space.
Dining includes ALBA, an Italian restaurant that earned one star in the 2026 Michelin Guide Doha.
The Ritz-Carlton, Doha
Set on its own private island between The Pearl and Lusail, The Ritz-Carlton Doha has been a mainstay in the hotel scene since 2001.
It has 374 rooms and suites, with a beach offering watersports and cabanas. The resort also has a 25-metre indoor pool and active guests can use the two indoor tennis courts and a squash court.
Families can explore the Ritz Kids garden, where children can learn about local flora and sustainable gardening.
Dining includes STK Doha, a modern steakhouse with skyline views that also hosts the 3D Le Petit Chef experience.
Rosewood Doha
Officially opened in January 2026, Rosewood Doha is just steps away from Lusail's marina and boardwalk. The hotel offers 155 rooms and suites, 162 apartments and 276 residences, with the Reef Suite offering a butler service.
Asaya, a wellness club open to members, hotel guests and residents, features anti-gravity heated loungers and a padel court, along with a 25-metre lap pool and a family pool with a dedicated children's area.
Koo Madame, inspired by Madame Wellington Koo, a former First Lady of the Republic of China, is one of eight dining destinations at the hotel. There’s also The Butterfly Room, a dedicated tea lounge.
The St. Regis Doha
Personal butler service is part of every stay at The St. Regis Doha, regardless of room category. The West Bay hotel has 335 rooms and suites, with views across the Arabian Gulf or The Pearl.
The hotel has a private beach that offers a range of water sports and an outdoor Olympic-sized pool, with private poolside cabanas that include their own plunge pools, kitchenette, and flat-screen TVs.
Dining includes steakhouse Astor Grill and Sarab Lounge, known for its English afternoon tea with live music.
Waldorf Astoria Doha Lusail
Opened for the 2022 FIFA World Cup, Waldorf Astoria Doha sits on a private beach in Lusail, with 429 rooms, suites and apartments.
There’s a waterpark and Aloha Surf Club, which has a dedicated surf pool. The resort also has three swimming pools, including one for families. Children and teenagers have their own clubs, while the three-storey ESPA Life Spa features a private indoor pool, thermal facilities and a hammam.
The hotel’s F&B options include SUSHISAMBA, which has a beach club with a private pool surrounded by cocoon-style cabanas.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine: Dashcam captures massive explosion on Lviv street
noticias.resumen: A dashcam captured the moment a Russian projectile struck a building directly ahead of a car in Lviv, forcing the driver to reverse. The attack killed two people and injured at least 10 others.
noticias.texto:
The footage, recorded by a driver travelling through Lviv on Friday 20 November, shows the moment a projectile struck a building directly ahead of the vehicle. The impact sent debris across the road and forced the driver to reverse sharply before driving away.
Two people were killed and at least 10 others injured in Lviv’s Zaliznychnyi district as a large-scale Russian missile and drone barrage tore across the western Ukrainian city and its surrounding region, igniting fires in residential blocks and garages. According to Ukrainian authorities, the bombardment left a trail of destruction spanning homes, vehicles, a dormitory, a warehouse and critical energy infrastructure, while also damaging a ticket terminal at Sknyliv railway station.
The fallout extended beyond the city limits into the nearby Zolochiv district, where debris from a downed Russian drone damaged three houses and a vehicle, leaving one further person injured.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, in the wider assault. The strikes also affected Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, underscoring the scale of the bombardment and the continuing threat to civilians and essential infrastructure.

noticias.titulo: Salvage operation under way after cargo ship runs aground off French coast
noticias.resumen: French authorities are racing to prevent a stranded cargo ship from capsizing after it ran aground off the south-western coast. The Maltese-flagged vessel, which is carrying more than 100 tonnes of fuel, poses a potential pollution threat as salvage teams prepare to refloat it.
noticias.texto:
French authorities are racing to prevent a stranded cargo ship from capsizing after it ran aground off the south-western coast. The Maltese-flagged vessel, which is carrying more than 100 tonnes of fuel, poses a potential pollution threat as salvage teams prepare to refloat it.
A Maltese-flagged cargo ship remains stranded on the south-western coast of France as authorities work to prevent it from capsizing and causing potential environmental damage.
The 169-metre vessel, named MIRO G, ran aground near Cap de l’Homy, in the Landes department, close to the village of Lit-et-Mixe, shortly before 1am on Friday, 20 November.
The ship had encountered difficulties in severe weather, with wind gusts reaching around 90km/h. Despite dropping anchor in an attempt to stabilise its position, the vessel drifted towards the shore and became stuck on a sandbank.
While 19 crew members had already been rescued, a further 11 people – including the captain and two other crew members, as well as salvage experts and company representatives – were evacuated by helicopter on Saturday ahead of worsening weather conditions. No injuries were reported.
French authorities said the ship was carrying no cargo but remained a potential pollution risk because of the fuel on board. Aerial surveillance carried out by the French Navy found no signs of pollution in the surrounding waters.
Salvage experts have been assessing how to refloat the vessel, but the operation has been complicated by technical problems and worsening weather conditions.
Ballast tanks filled to stabilise stranded vessel
The ship's ballast tanks have been filled with seawater to increase its stability and reduce the risk of it capsizing or shifting further towards the beach. However, the water will eventually need to be pumped out to make the vessel lighter and allow it to be pulled free.
The operation has been hampered by the failure of the ship's two main generators, which are needed to power the pumps. Engineers are working to restore an alternative electricity supply.
The French salvage tug Abeille Bretagne has also arrived in the area, carrying a 1,000-metre towline. However, shallow waters mean it cannot approach closer than around 900 metres to the stranded vessel, making the towing operation particularly challenging.
Strong winds and rough seas are expected to continue, with officials warning that the operation to refloat the ship could take several days or longer.
Access to the beach at Cap de l’Homy has been restricted while the emergency response continues.
The French maritime authorities said they were working to take advantage of the first suitable weather window, but stressed that there was no guarantee the operation would succeed.

noticias.titulo: Iran attacks US bases in Bahrain as its tankers get ready to break the US blockade
noticias.resumen: The “no war, no peace” US-Iran confrontation appears to be moving towards a possible breaking point as Iran increases its military actions in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, while its critical attempt to break the US military naval blockade in the Persian Gulf appears to be imminent.
noticias.texto:
The “no war, no peace” US-Iran confrontation appears to be moving towards a possible breaking point as Iran increases its military actions in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, while its critical attempt to break the US military naval blockade in the Persian Gulf appears to be imminent.
Iran launched two waves of drone and ballistic missile attacks on Saturday night against four US bases in Bahrain, home to the US’ Fifth Fleet headquarters, the Iranian media reported, while Bahrain announced the attacks, warning the population to shelter.
Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency claimed that the Iranian military targeted four US bases in Bahrain, with two of the named as Sheikh Isa and Juffair, in what it called a response to continued US incursions in Iran’s airspace.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed that it struck 2 Patriot defence batteries and a radar system. Bahrain and the US military did not confirm the claims.
Bahrain said that its air defence intercepted several Iranian attacks, calling them a “heinous Iranian aggression”.
Local sources in Bahrain reported loud explosions and Bahrain’s Interior ministry announced that a fire broke out at a civilian industrial compound, with no injuries reported, while local videos showed smoke rising from a fire in an unidentified location.
Right after the attack on Bahrain, reports emerged from southern Iran of explosions in Sirik. The US military has retaliated regularly against Iranian military facilities in recent weeks.
Earlier on Saturday, US Central Command CENTCOM denied Iranian claims that a surface-to-air missile damaged a US F-16 fighter jet on Friday evening.
Meanwhile, at least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.
In a sharp increase of incidents in the Strait of Hormuz over the last week, the UK military’s maritime security center (UKMTO) said two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait. There were no reports of casualties.
The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait and caught fire. State media also said that the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels.
Iran’s army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia warned the US again on Saturday that any attack on Iran will be met with “a decisive and immediate response” as “we are much stronger than in the past,” Iranian TV IRIB report.
“Any new aggression will be met with a decisive, immediate and effective response from the armed forces, and the defence of the country will not be limited to a specific geographical area,” Akraminia said during a visit to Iranian troops in the south of the country.
The Iranian TV showed for the first time the ground troops deployed into defensive positions in the coastal areas of southern Iran on Saturday.
Meanwhile on Saturday, as more than 14 Iranian tankers are reported to be prepared off Kharg Island to break out of the US military blockade in the coming days, Iran’s deputy minister of foreign affairs Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that the US blockade of Iranian ports “is an act of war and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege.”
Iran warned of a “fierce military response” if the convoy was engaged by the US military, threatening with widespread attacks on energy infrastructures across the Gulf region.
Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian also said that Iran is subject to a “silent economic war” which is “tougher than a war with missiles,” adding that Iran has the capability to withstand it.
As Gharibabadi announced that Tehran has warned the United States that the Iranian convoy will sail soon to China, the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War said that “Iranian attempts to run the blockade impose a series of dilemmas on the United States by either collapsing the blockade or returning to a war that imposes unideal political costs on the United States by straining its relationships with Gulf allies.”
Against the backdrop of the intensifying crisis, the diplomatic negotiations between the US and Iran spearheaded by Qatar continue.
Iran’s deputy foreign minister Gharibabadi announced on Saturday that a Qatari delegation held talks with Iranian officials on Friday evening for some two hours, before returning to Doha.
Iranian Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi suggested that a deal is possible when he declared that reopening the Strait of Hormuz would be “not difficult” if the US accepted Iran’s “reasonable conditions,” especially by ending the blockade which he called “completely illegal,” lifting sanctions and Washington acknowledging “past mistakes.”
In parallel, US president Donald Trump told US network Fox News on Saturday that he planned to make a “permanent” deal with Iran to prevent it from acquiring a nuclear weapon and that he was never interested in a regime change in Iran.
“I intend to reach a permanent deal with Iran that prevents them from obtaining nuclear weapons, even if another president takes my place in the future and is unfit for the office,” Trump said.

noticias.titulo: Video shows Mexican forces capturing 'El Chapo Isidro', FBI most-wanted cartel boss
noticias.resumen: Mexican special forces captured drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “Chapo Isidro”, during a raid in Sinaloa, with footage showing soldiers escorting him into an army vehicle.
noticias.texto:
Mexican special forces captured drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “Chapo Isidro”, during an operation in the northwestern state of Sinaloa on Friday night.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
Footage released by Mexico’s Defence Department shows heavily armed soldiers escorting a detainee through a building and into an army vehicle.
Meza Flores was among the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives and is accused of trafficking drugs into the United States and illegally carrying firearms.
Mexican authorities said intelligence provided by the Trump administration helped lead to his capture. The operation was followed by violence in the region, prompting security forces to remain deployed to protect civilians.

noticias.titulo: Thousands take to streets in Portugal, France and Spain over rising living costs
noticias.resumen: Thousands of people demonstrated in Portugal and France on Saturday, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and action to tackle the rising cost of living. In Lisbon, workers marched despite heavy rain, while trade unions, Yellow Vest activists and youth groups gathered in Paris.
noticias.texto:
Thousands of people demonstrated in Portugal and France on Saturday, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and action to tackle the rising cost of living. In Lisbon, workers marched despite heavy rain, while trade unions, Yellow Vest activists and youth groups gathered in Paris.
Protests over living costs and social inequality continued in Europe on Saturday, 21 November, with demonstrations in Portugal, Spain and France.
In France, demonstrations over the cost of living, student rights and police violence continued for a sixth consecutive Saturday. However, turnout was considerably lower than a week earlier.
During the march from Place de la République to Place de la Nation in Paris, demonstrators waved flags and wore T-shirts bearing trade union logos. Others turned out in the movement's distinctive yellow vests.
According to the Interior Ministry, 82,500 people took part in demonstrations nationwide, including 21,500 in Paris. Organisers put the total at 150,000, of whom 45,000 marched in the capital.
A week earlier, the authorities had counted 106,000 demonstrators across France, while organisers estimated the turnout at 200,000.
In Lyon, where demonstrations had been banned across a large area, several unauthorised marches attempted to reach the city centre during the afternoon. Police dispersed the groups using tear gas, according to an AFP journalist at the scene.
In Marseille, 4,600 people took part in protests, according to police, matching the previous turnout. The march later split into two groups, one of which continued as an unauthorised demonstration.
Around 70,000 police officers and security personnel were deployed nationwide. The demonstrations were largely peaceful, although sporadic incidents of violence were reported, including in Marseille.
The latest mobilisation coincided with the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, which began in November 2018 in response to rising fuel taxes before developing into a broader protest against living costs and social inequality.
Thousands march in Lisbon despite heavy rain
In Portugal, thousands of workers took to the streets of Lisbon to demand higher wages and pensions, more affordable housing and better public services. The demonstration was organised by the country's largest trade union federation, CGTP-IN, and went ahead despite heavy rain.
Protesters travelled to the capital from across the country, with special trains arriving from Porto and buses bringing demonstrators from cities including Aveiro and Faro.
The union called on the government to address the growing financial pressures on households, demanding lower prices for essential goods and services, as well as measures to make housing more affordable.
"They talk about the economy, but they don’t know what it’s like to stretch every penny to pay the rent and electricity bills. They don’t know what it’s like to have to choose between buying medicine and putting food on the table,” the CGTP-IN says in a campaign video shared on its Facebook page.
Many demonstrators said their earnings were no longer sufficient to cover everyday expenses, particularly housing, food and energy bills. The mobilisation also reflected growing frustration over the government's proposed 2027 state budget and its approach to public services.
In addition to Saturday's national demonstration in Lisbon, the CGTP-IN has called a further rally outside the Assembly of the Republic for next Tuesday, 24 November, coinciding with the final vote on the 2025 State Budget proposal.
Housing and purchasing power at the centre of discontent
Although the demonstrations in Portugal and France were organised separately, they shared several concerns, particularly the erosion of purchasing power and difficulties finding affordable housing.
In Portugal, house prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new tenancies have risen sharply. Average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 % below the EU average, according to Eurostat.
The demonstrations came a day after a wider wave of student and worker protests swept through more than 20 European countries on Friday, 20 November.
Thousands of people took to the streets of Barcelona on Saturday, with police estimating the turnout at 3,000 and organisers putting it at 5,000. Demonstrators called for more affordable housing, better-funded public education and stronger public services.
In Madrid, a separate demonstration focused on the treatment of elderly people in care homes during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Madrid protesters demand justice for care home deaths
Demonstrators took to the streets, demanding justice for the 7,291 elderly people who died in care homes during the first wave of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020.
The protest, organised with the Marea de Residencias (Care Homes Movement), called for truth, justice and compensation for the victims and their families.
The protesters denounced the controversial protocols introduced under the regional government of Isabel Díaz Ayuso, which restricted hospital transfers for certain elderly care home residents during the pandemic. They also called for care homes to be fully publicly owned and run.
Critics have described the measures as discriminatory, while the regional government has defended its handling of the crisis.

noticias.titulo: Paolo Bulgari, Italian jewellery tycoon, dies aged 89
noticias.resumen: The grandson of Bulgari's founder helped transform the family jewellery business into one of the world's most prestigious luxury brands. He led the Roman maison as chairman from 1984 and remained passionate about jewellery design throughout his life.
noticias.texto:
The grandson of Bulgari's founder helped transform the family jewellery business into one of the world's most prestigious luxury brands. He led the Roman maison as chairman from 1984 and remained passionate about jewellery design throughout his life.
Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari has died in Rome at the age of 89, his family announced on Saturday, 21 November 2026.
The family paid tribute to him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", praising his humanity and his talent as an entrepreneur who loved Italy and served as its ambassador around the world.
Bulgari was the grandson of Sotirio Bulgari, who founded the eponymous jewellery business in Rome in 1884. Born in the Italian capital in 1937, Paolo belonged to the third generation of the family behind the luxury house.
From family workshop to global luxury empire
Paolo Bulgari joined the family business in 1960, initially working alongside his father, Giorgio. He developed a particular expertise in precious stones and became internationally recognised for his knowledge of gemstones.
In 1984, he became chairman of the company, working closely with his brother Nicola and nephew Francesco Trapani to expand the business internationally.
Under their leadership, Bulgari developed beyond its traditional jewellery business, adding watches, perfumes, leather goods and accessories to its portfolio. Its distinctive designs, often inspired by ancient Greek and Roman art, became synonymous with Italian luxury.
The brand became particularly famous for its colourful gemstones, bold gold jewellery and distinctive use of cabochon-cut stones. Among its most celebrated admirers was Hollywood actress Elizabeth Taylor, whose association with the jewellery house helped cement its international reputation.
Sale to luxury giant LVMH
A major turning point came in 2011, when the Bulgari family sold its controlling stake in the business to French luxury conglomerate LVMH in a deal worth approximately €3.7 billion.
Paolo Bulgari later described the decision as painful, but said it was made partly out of responsibility towards the company's employees and concerns about the difficulties of managing the generational transition.
Despite relinquishing family control, he remained closely connected to the brand and continued designing jewellery well into his later years. He also enjoyed occasionally working behind the counter at the company's historic boutique on Rome's Via dei Condotti, sometimes introducing himself simply as a shop assistant.
Philanthropy and commitment to Rome
Beyond the luxury industry, Bulgari devoted considerable attention to social causes, particularly education and opportunities for young people.
In 2019, he founded the Paolo Bulgari Foundation with his wife. The organisation supports educational regeneration and vocational training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods of Rome.
One of its major projects involved the redevelopment of Largo Mengaroni, the main square in the Tor Bella Monaca district, completed in 2023 in cooperation with local schools, associations and the municipal authorities.
Paolo Bulgari is survived by his six children from two marriages. His funeral will take place on Monday, 23 November, at the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome.

noticias.titulo: New documentary: Princess Kate speaks candidly about how cancer changed her body and mind
noticias.resumen: The Princess of Wales opens up about the physical and emotional impact of her cancer diagnosis in a deeply personal BBC documentary. Kate also reflects on her recovery, finding hope amid uncertainty and learning to live with a new perspective on life.
noticias.texto:
The Princess of Wales opens up about the physical and emotional impact of her cancer diagnosis in a deeply personal BBC documentary. Kate also reflects on her recovery, finding hope amid uncertainty and learning to live with a new perspective on life.
Catherine, Princess of Wales, has spoken candidly about how cancer changed her, both physically and emotionally, in a new documentary about her journey through illness and recovery.
"Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically, but there's a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," Kate says in the trailer for the film, titled Heal.
The 30-minute documentary follows the Princess as she reflects on her own experience and meets other people facing serious health challenges.
Kate also discusses the process of finding her way back to everyday life after treatment, describing healing as a journey. "How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty," she says.
Three Peaks Challenge became her own way of ringing the bell
The documentary follows Kate as she takes on the National Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.
She completed the challenge in June 2026 in support of The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, the organisation linked to the London hospital where she received treatment.
The film includes footage of Kate embracing her husband, Prince William, and their three children, George, Charlotte and Louis, after completing the demanding challenge. In another emotional moment, Kate visits cancer patients and watches a survivor ring the traditional bell marking the end of treatment.
The Princess reveals that she did not ring the bell herself when she was told she was in remission.
Her brother James suggests that completing the Three Peaks Challenge may have become her own way of marking the milestone.
Kate's cancer diagnosis and recovery
Kate announced in March 2024 that she had been diagnosed with cancer following major abdominal surgery. She subsequently underwent preventative chemotherapy, completing her treatment in September 2024.
In January 2025, she announced that her cancer was in remission, while emphasising that recovery would take time.
The Princess has not disclosed the type of cancer she was diagnosed with.
Earlier this month, she also spoke about the challenges of recovery in an interview with Country Life magazine, whose latest edition was guest-edited by Prince William.
"I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good and bad days, that it will take time," she said.
Kate also explained how spending time in nature had helped her through the process, describing it as a sanctuary where she could reconnect with herself.
"I think that's because nature offers something unique. It doesn't ask anything of us. It doesn't judge us or expect us to perform. It simply allows us to be," she said.
Documentary aims to help others facing serious illness
Through Heal, the Princess hopes to encourage a more holistic approach to cancer care, taking into account not only physical health but also emotional and psychological wellbeing.
"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," she says in the trailer. "Things can renew and grow. Often it is through pain that we realise there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."
Kensington Palace said the documentary explores the profound impact serious illness can have on patients and those around them, drawing on Kate's personal experience and the stories of others navigating health challenges.
All proceeds from the documentary's distribution will go to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, supporting people living with and beyond cancer. The charity, established in 2002, continues a tradition of philanthropic support for The Royal Marsden, the specialist cancer hospital founded by Dr William Marsden in 1851.
Heal will be broadcast on BBC One and BBC iPlayer on 29 November, with international screenings to follow in the United States, Australia and Canada.

noticias.titulo: Real Madrid outpace Bayern Munich in revenue race as both clubs post record figures
noticias.resumen: Real Madrid have widened the financial gap over Bayern Munich, generating more than €1.2 billion in revenue in the 2025-26 season. The German champions are also approaching the billion-euro mark, while celebrating a record 500,000 members.
noticias.texto:
Real Madrid have widened the financial gap over Bayern Munich, generating more than €1.2 billion in revenue in the 2025-26 season. The German champions are also approaching the billion-euro mark, while celebrating a record 500,000 members.
European football's financial heavyweights are celebrating another record-breaking season. Real Madrid reported operating revenue of €1.221 billion for 2025-26, comfortably ahead of Bayern Munich's €988.2 million.
Real Madrid sets €1.25bn budget after record revenue
Real Madrid president Florentino Pérez announced the record figures at the club's annual general meeting, while presenting a budget of €1.25 billion for the 2026-27 season.
For the first time, the Spanish giants have surpassed the €1.2 billion revenue mark, a figure Pérez described as unprecedented for a sports organisation.
The club also recorded its highest-ever EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation), at €287.4 million. Net profit after tax reached €26 million, an increase of eight per cent compared with the previous season.
Pérez highlighted Real Madrid's international standing, citing Forbes, Deloitte and Brand Finance rankings. According to Forbes, the club is the world's most valuable football club for the fifth consecutive year. Deloitte ranks it first in revenue, while Brand Finance considers it the world's most valuable and strongest football brand.
Pérez said the club's partnerships with companies and technology providers would help it apply new expertise to its operations, particularly its sporting activities.
The figures underline the commercial strength of both clubs, although the Spanish giants remain out in front. Real Madrid's revenue increased by 3.1 per cent compared with the previous season, while Bayern recorded a more modest rise of around one per cent.
The difference amounts to approximately €233 million, although the clubs' published accounting figures are not entirely like-for-like: Real Madrid explicitly excludes player-transfer income from its operating revenue figure.
Real Madrid outstrip Bayern Munich in record revenues
Real Madrid's growth has been driven largely by its commercial operations and the redevelopment of the Santiago Bernabéu stadium.
Marketing generated €539 million, an increase of six per cent, while stadium revenue reached €363 million, up 11 per cent. Television rights and revenue from international competitions contributed a further €319 million.
The stadium's commercial performance is particularly significant: its revenue has more than doubled compared with the final season before the redevelopment began in 2018-19.
Real Madrid have now recorded a profit for 26 consecutive financial years, according to the club.
Bayern close to the billion-euro mark
Bayern Munich are not far behind, having increased their consolidated revenue from €978.3 million to €988.2 million.
The club's sponsorship income was particularly strong, rising by almost €30 million to €268.4 million. Merchandising also reached a record €152.8 million.
However, the financial picture was more mixed when it came to profits. Bayern's operating result (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million, but its profit before tax fell by 16.9 per cent to €35.3 million. The group's net profit declined by 15.9 per cent to €22.8 million.
Bayern explained that the lower profit was largely due to exceptional revenue in the previous financial year from the European Championship and the Champions League final, which did not recur in 2025-26.
CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen nevertheless described the results as another record year (source in German), emphasising the club's financial stability and its continued investment in the men's and women's teams.
Bayern also highlighted a decline in revenue from the Bundesliga's central media marketing, which fell by €10 million to €93 million. Dreesen said German clubs needed to address their competitive disadvantage in international television marketing.
Bayern reach a historic membership milestone
Away from the financial figures, Bayern celebrated another milestone: the club has surpassed 500,000 members for the first time.
According to Bayern, this makes it the largest sports club by membership worldwide. Its membership has doubled over the past 12 years, from around 250,000 in 2014.
The milestone also underlines the difference between the clubs' structures. Bayern is majority-owned by its members' association, FC Bayern München eV, while Real Madrid is entirely owned by its members, known as socios.
At Bayern, members also have voting rights at the annual general meeting, giving them a direct say in the club's affairs.
Two different models of financial success
Although Real Madrid currently have the larger revenue stream, both clubs demonstrate how Europe's leading football institutions are expanding beyond traditional sources of income.
Real Madrid have benefited considerably from their renovated stadium and global commercial reach. Bayern, meanwhile, have built particularly strong sponsorship and merchandising businesses while maintaining a cautious approach to spending.
The substantial difference in turnover does not translate into an equally large gap in profitability. Despite generating around €233 million more revenue than Bayern, Real Madrid reported net profit after tax of €26.3 million, only €3.5 million more than the German club's €22.8 million.
This suggests that higher revenues do not automatically result in significantly higher profits, as operating costs, player salaries, transfer spending, financing and other expenses also play a major role. Both clubs nevertheless ended the 2025-26 financial year in the black, demonstrating their ability to remain profitable while operating on a huge financial scale.
For Bayern, the next major target is clear: breaking through the €1 billion revenue barrier. Real Madrid, meanwhile, have already moved beyond it and are setting their sights on further growth.

noticias.titulo: Estonia-Russia border closure sends residents rushing to cross before deadline
noticias.resumen: Families and travellers are queuing to cross from Russia into Estonia before all five road border crossings are shut on 1 December. The decision follows an alleged Russian-backed sabotage attempt, but has also raised concerns among people with relatives on both sides of the border.
noticias.texto:
Families and travellers are queuing to cross from Russia into Estonia before all five road border crossings are shut on 1 December. The decision follows an alleged Russian-backed sabotage attempt, but has also raised concerns among people with relatives on both sides of the border.
People carrying suitcases, backpacks and plastic bags have been gathering in the Russian border town of Ivangorod, hoping to cross into Estonia before the Baltic country closes its land border with Russia next month.
The queues reflect the impact of a decision that will affect not only cross-border travel but also families with relatives living on opposite sides of the frontier.
Estonia, a member of NATO and the European Union, announced on 20 November that it would suspend road crossings at all five road border checkpoints with Russia from 1 December. The restriction is due to remain in place for six months, after which the government will review the security situation and decide whether to extend or amend it.
Why is Estonia closing the border?
The decision follows an attempted arson attack on the premises of Estonian drone manufacturer Threod Systems in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, on 14 November.
According to Estonia's Internal Security Service, Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was behind the attempted attack. Eight Latvian citizens were detained, with investigators suspecting they had been recruited to carry out the operation. The company's security staff intervened before significant damage was caused.
Estonian authorities described the incident as part of a wider pattern of sabotage (source in Estonian) and hostile activity against the country and other European states. The government said the border closure would make it harder for Russian intelligence services to recruit and influence people crossing into Estonia, as well as help prevent sanctions evasion.
Moscow has rejected the accusations. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the allegations as unfounded, while Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Estonia of infringing the rights of Russian citizens and threatened political and diplomatic countermeasures.
Zakharova also compared the planned closure to the construction of a new Iron Curtain.
Families divided by the border
For people living in the border region, the decision has consequences extending far beyond security policy.
Narva, an Estonian town of more than 50,000 people, lies directly opposite Ivangorod on the other side of the River Narva. The two towns have long-standing family, social and economic ties, with many residents having relatives on both sides.
The crossing has also been used by people travelling from other European countries to reach St Petersburg.
Russia suspended vehicle traffic through the Narva crossing in February 2024, but pedestrians have continued to cross.
Narva Mayor Jaan Toots has called on the Estonian government to consider humanitarian exemptions for residents who need to visit elderly relatives, attend funerals or deal with other urgent family matters. He has also warned of economic consequences for the town, including potential losses for local hotels, restaurants and businesses.
The closure is also expected to affect employment in the region, where border guards and customs officers are among the local workforce.
Crossings have already fallen sharply
The number of people travelling between Estonia and Russia has declined considerably since the start of the war in Ukraine.
According to Estonian public broadcaster ERR, annual crossings fell from more than four million before 2022 to around 760,000 in 2026. Of those, approximately 447,000 were made through the Narva-Ivangorod crossing, according to the figures cited by AFP.
Reuters reported that Russian nationals accounted for 307,000 of this year's crossings, while 175,000 were made by Estonian citizens and 54,000 by Finnish passport holders.
The planned restrictions will apply to all five road crossing points: Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse. Rail freight will continue, subject to existing restrictions and customs checks.
Travellers will have to use alternative routes through neighbouring countries, particularly Latvia, although journeys are likely to become longer and more expensive.
For those without access to a car, travelling by air may become the only practical alternative.
The closure is currently planned for six months, rather than indefinitely. Estonia's government says it will reassess the measure after that period, depending on the security situation.

noticias.titulo: Former Costa Concordia cruise ship captain released from prison on probation after nine years
noticias.resumen: The case dates back to January 2012, when the Costa Concordia ship struck rocks off the coast of Isola del Giglio in the Tyrrhenian Sea. The disaster claimed 32 lives.
noticias.texto:
The case dates back to January 2012, when the Costa Concordia ship struck rocks off the coast of Isola del Giglio in the Tyrrhenian Sea. The disaster claimed 32 lives.
After spending more than nine years behind bars, Francesco Schettino, the former captain of the Costa Concordia cruise ship, left Rome's Rebibbia prison on Friday evening.
According to a report from the Italian outlet Quotidiano Nazionale (QN), the Rome Supervisory Court granted Schettino release under probation after a thorough review of his rehabilitation process and his conduct during his time in prison.
Francesca Carnicelli, a lawyer for Schettino, welcomed the decision, saying prison staff had given an extremely positive assessment of his participation in the rehabilitation programme.
"In our view, all the conditions were in place for this alternative measure to be granted, as it represents the correct continuation of the process after the conviction," Carnicelli said.
The case dates back to January 2012, when the Costa Concordia ship, owned by the Costa Crociere cruise line, struck rocks off the coast of Isola del Giglio in the Tyrrhenian Sea.
The impact ripped a hole around 35.59 metres long in the port side of the ship's hull, causing it to list heavily before it ran aground on a rocky outcrop near Punta Gabbianara, where it partially sank.
The disaster claimed 32 lives, including passengers and crew members.
In the subsequent legal proceedings, Schettino was sentenced to 16 years in prison
The sentence was upheld by the Florence Court of Appeals on 31 May 2016, along with a five-year ban from working in the maritime industry. The provisional compensation awarded to survivors who joined the proceedings as civil claimants also increased to between €40,000 and €65,000 each.
The conviction was finally upheld by the Court of Cassation on 12 May 2017.

noticias.titulo: Raccoon roast as a sustainable alternative to Germany's Christmas goose?
noticias.resumen: A chef from Thuringia serves the furry pest with red cabbage and dumplings, praising its tender meat. Could it become the new Christmas favourite?
noticias.texto:
A chef from Thuringia serves the furry pest with red cabbage and dumplings, praising its tender meat. Could it become the new Christmas favourite?
He first came across raccoons while out fishing. For more than two years now, the small, button-eyed animals have been a permanent fixture on his restaurant menu – despite the fact that he is a vegetarian in his private life.
Chef Steffen Haaßengier now also teaches others how to prepare raccoon meat, offering cookery courses in Weimar, a city in the German state of Thuringia.
In 2025, the 42-year-old processed around 450 tonnes of raccoon meat. On special "raccoon barbecue days", he butchers up to 35 animals. Local hunters bring the raccoons to him after shooting them, and the veterinary authorities test them for diseases beforehand.
Tender meat with a distinctive flavour
In Canada, raccoons have long been considered a delicacy. "The raccoon has a very interesting, slightly sweet flavour of its own, somewhere between game and beef. It is tender, long-fibred meat, and you could also compare it to rabbit", says Haaßengier.
For seasoning, he recommends robust flavours such as rosemary, thyme, paprika, garlic and onion.
He says feedback from his guests is consistently positive. "Most people say they first have to get over the image they have in their heads. Many initially think of this small, cute animal, but there are lots of other small, cute animals, such as lambs, and they are cute too. But in the end, everyone likes the taste, and many even come back several times, bringing family and friends."
To keep his customers interested, he is always coming up with new dishes. One example is his raccoon burger, which has become a firm favourite. It is served with homemade Canadian coleslaw and chips.
On Sundays, he always serves the classic "raccoon leg" with a red wine and lingonberry sauce. By now, he has built up a regular clientele who return every fortnight. He is currently working on a "lovely raccoon ragout".
The main argument in favour of raccoon meat, he says, is sustainability. "There is no factory farming involved, so there is no need for force-fed geese or other animals raised for their meat. There are plenty of raccoons anyway. They have to be culled because they are an invasive species. It is food for a good cause."
As for the price, he says, there is not much difference either.
Invasive species out of control
Originally native to North America, the raccoon is classified as an invasive species in Germany. As an omnivore, it poses a threat to native amphibians, reptiles and birds. According to the German Hunting Association, almost 290,000 raccoons were shot across Germany in 2025.
This "problem animal" can weigh between 3.6 and 13 kilograms and live for up to 16 years. During its lifetime, it can cause considerable damage, particularly to buildings, through faeces and urine contamination, as well as to gardens and native wildlife.
The numbers are also rising in the German capital, Berlin. In the 2024/25 hunting season, 286 raccoons were shot, compared with just 103 in 2022/23. In neighbouring Brandenburg, around 30,000 raccoons were shot in 2022/23.
In East Germany before reunification, another invasive species was also a popular item on the menu: nutria. Its meat was considered a valued foodstuff, mainly available as a by-product of fur farming. The meat of the so-called "swamp beaver" was prepared in much the same way as rabbit or hare – as a roast, stew or pan-fried dish – or made into sausages. Nutria Bolognese was popular in school and workplace canteens.
Can raccoon with dumplings and red cabbage replace the traditional Christmas goose?
In Germany, a festive meal is traditionally a must at Christmas. While many families serve the classic potato salad with sausages on Christmas Eve, 24 December, the main Christmas holidays often feature roast goose, duck or beef roulades, accompanied by red cabbage and potato dumplings.
But does it always have to be the familiar classics? With raccoon numbers on the rise, an unusual alternative could soon find its way on to the Christmas dinner table: braised raccoon leg with dumplings and red cabbage. Could it catch on?
Steffen Haaßengier says it certainly could. "As a braised dish, raccoon leg can easily replace goose leg, roulade or duck." He adds that serving it would not mean abandoning any traditions.
On 6 December, his restaurant, Zum Lindeneck, in Weimar is hosting a St Nicholas feast. Alongside raccoon, badger will also be on the menu at Zum Lindeneck in Weimar, with both dishes offered at special prices.

noticias.titulo: Brazil ex-president Bolsonaro in intensive care over intestinal problem
noticias.resumen: The former Brazilian president was taken to hospital with abdominal pain, accompanied by military police.
noticias.texto:
The former Brazilian president was taken to hospital with abdominal pain, accompanied by military police.
Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro has been admitted to intensive care with an intestinal obstruction, the hospital treating him said on Saturday, marking another health setback for the far-right leader, who was convicted of plotting a coup.
He was escorted to DF Star Hospital Asa Sul, Brasília, the capital of Brazil, by the military police.
According to his doctor, the former president has an "acute obstructive abdomen", Globo reports (source in Portuguese).
Bolsonaro remains in hospital under observation. Doctors have not ruled out the possibility of further surgery.
The hospital said in a medical bulletin that Bolsonaro remained “clinically stable, conscious, alert and breathing without assistance”. Doctors have inserted a gastric tube to provide nutritional support, adding that no date has been set for his discharge.
Bolsonaro taken to hospital after falling ill at home
Bolsonaro’s son Carlos, a senator-elect, described a night of vomiting and severe pain.
“I’m not a doctor, but I’ve never seen him like this,” he wrote on X, raising the possibility that his father could require another operation – potentially his tenth in less than eight years.
According to the Federal District Military Police, the former president, who is under house arrest, felt unwell, prompting a request for a medical assessment. A doctor visited Bolsonaro at home and confirmed that he needed to be taken to hospital.
Bolsonaro was convicted last year of plotting a coup after attempting to remain in power despite losing the 2022 presidential election to left-wing candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. He has denied the charges, claiming he is the victim of a judicial witch-hunt orchestrated by the left.
The former president has undergone several operations and required repeated hospital treatment for health problems linked to the stabbing he suffered during the 2018 election campaign.
Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year-and-three-month prison sentence under humanitarian house arrest, granted by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes in March.
"His health is deteriorating day by day," Carlos Bolsonaro said, blaming his father's condition on his lack of mobility and what he described as "psychological torture" inflicted by the state.
Brazil's Supreme Federal Court will rule in December on the constitutionality of a law that reduces Bolsonaro's prison sentence prison, as well as those of others convicted over the coup plot.
Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Carlos's older brother, lost last month's presidential run-off election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The day after his defeat, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the seizure of his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation.
Flávio Bolsonaro fled to the United States, where he refused to concede defeat. On Elon Musk's social media platform X, the former presidential candidate posted a message calling for support for his father.

noticias.titulo: Mexico captures FBI’s most-wanted cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’, triggering violence
noticias.resumen: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s ten most-wanted fugitives, was arrested in a military operation involving US intelligence cooperation. Gunfire, burning vehicles and panic among civilians followed the raid in northern Mexico. 11 people were killed.
noticias.texto:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s ten most-wanted fugitives, was arrested in a military operation involving US intelligence cooperation. Gunfire, burning vehicles and panic among civilians followed the raid in northern Mexico. 11 people were killed.
Mexican security forces have captured notorious cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, better known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, in the north-western state of Sinaloa, triggering a wave of violence that sent residents fleeing for safety.
At least 11 people have been killed in violent clashes in Mexico’s Sinaloa state following the capture.
Mexico’s Defense Cabinet said on Saturday afternoon that seven suspected cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers died in a fierce gun battle that broke out on Friday night and continued into the early hours.
Meza Flores, who was among the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was one of eight people arrested during the operation, which was conducted using intelligence provided by the United States.
The arrest took place in Guasave on Friday night, 20 November, during an operation involving Mexican military and security forces. The Mexican government said intelligence provided by the administration of US President Donald Trump had contributed to the operation, although it has not disclosed precisely how the two countries co-operated.
The arrest was followed by armed confrontations, burning vehicles and roadblocks. Disturbing footage circulating on social media showed spectators fleeing in panic as gunfire interrupted a baseball match in Guasave.
Military operation and US intelligence cooperation
According to Mexican authorities, security forces used what they described as ‘stealth and surprise’ to apprehend Meza Flores.
The operation involved specialist units from the Mexican National Guard and Army. Officials said their personnel came under attack from armed individuals using firearms and explosives, believed to be cartel operatives.
Following the exchange of fire, security forces entered a property and arrested Meza Flores, along with other individuals.
The detainees were subsequently evacuated aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft to Mexico City, according to the authorities.
The Mexican government acknowledged that intelligence supplied by the Trump administration had played a role in locating and capturing the cartel leader. However, officials have so far provided few details about the intelligence-sharing arrangements or the extent of American involvement.
Mexican news outlet N+ also reported that intelligence agencies from Mexico's Defence Ministry and the United States had co-operated in the operation.
The development highlights the importance of intelligence cooperation between Mexico and the United States in tackling organised crime, particularly given the cross-border nature of the drug trade.
Gunfire interrupts baseball match as residents flee
The arrest quickly turned into a night of violence in Guasave.
Videos and photographs shared online showed civilians running for cover as gunfire erupted during a baseball match. Spectators could be seen leaving the venue in fear as the situation deteriorated.
Other footage showed vehicles set alight and roads blocked, while armed confrontations reportedly spread beyond the immediate area of the operation.
According to Mexican newspaper La Jornada, the violence included shootings, vehicle fires, roadblocks involving burning lorries and clashes between federal forces and armed groups.
Local authorities urged residents to remain indoors and avoid travelling on affected roads.
The scenes illustrate the immediate risks that major operations against organised crime can pose to civilians living in areas where criminal groups maintain a strong presence.
Who is Fausto Isidro Meza Flores?
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, is considered one of Mexico's most significant organised-crime figures.
He is associated with the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation and leads a network also known as the Meza-Flores organisation or the Guasave Cartel.
The group has operated primarily in north-western Mexico, particularly in Sinaloa, and has been linked by US authorities to the trafficking of several illegal drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and marijuana.
Meza Flores rose to prominence following the fragmentation of the Beltrán Leyva organisation and the wider conflicts between rival criminal factions in Mexico.
His organisation has been accused of using violence, intimidation and territorial control to protect its criminal activities.
In February 2025, the FBI placed Meza Flores on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, underlining the importance US authorities attached to his capture.
The US government had offered a reward of up to US$5 million for information leading to his arrest.
What happens next?
Although the arrest is a major achievement for Mexican security forces, it remains to be seen how it will affect the balance of power between criminal organisations operating in Sinaloa.
The capture of a senior cartel figure does not necessarily mean the dismantling of the organisation he leads. Criminal networks can remain operational following the arrest of their leaders, while rival groups may attempt to exploit any resulting power vacuum.
The immediate unrest highlights the continuing challenges facing the country in its fight against organised crime.

noticias.titulo: Russian cargo ship struck by drones in Gulf of Finland
noticias.resumen: The United States announced sanctions against the Sparta II in early May 2022, just over two months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine has also sanctioned the vessel.
noticias.texto:
The United States announced sanctions against the Sparta II in early May 2022, just over two months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine has also sanctioned the vessel.
A Russian cargo ship has been struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland, Finnish and Russian authorities have said.
Finnish Defence Forces detected the attack in international waters on Saturday morning, west of Suursaari, according to the country's defence ministry.
The Sparta II vessel is reported to have sustained damage in the incident, with the Finnish Border Guard saying a fire had broken out on board.
The border agency added that the vessel had drifted into Finnish territorial waters in the eastern part of the gulf but that the situation did not pose a danger to other maritime traffic.
"The Finnish Border Guard is leading maritime rescue and environmental damage control operations on the cargo vessel Sparta II, which is currently in Finnish territorial waters on the open sea south of Loviisa city," it said in an update at around 3 pm local time, while confirming that Russian maritime rescue authorities had been contacted.
"Rescue units are on-site. The crew has not been forced to abandon the ship, and no environmental damage has been detected. The Border Guard is prepared to evacuate personnel and assist in firefighting efforts," it continued.
While it was not immediately clear who was behind the strike, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the incident was evidence of the Ukraine war "spilling over into our neighboring regions."
"Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor," he added.
Aleksandr Drozdenko, the governor of Russia's Leningrad Oblast, said the vessel had been attacked by two drones as it was making its way to Kaliningrad.
The United States announced sanctions against the Sparta II in early May 2022, just over two months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine has also sanctioned the vessel.
The Gulf of Finland is a crucial maritime passage for Russia, connecting Saint Petersburg with the wider Baltic Sea.
Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was also suspected of violating Finnish airspace on Saturday afternoon, off the coast of Loviisa.
“The suspected airspace violation may be related to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that sustained damage in the Gulf of Finland. The Finnish Defense Forces and the Border Guard are handling the situation in cooperation with other authorities," Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen was quoted as saying.
It comes after Polish authorities announced that two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone had crashed in Poland on Friday as allied nations held military exercises in the country, prompting condemnation from European officials.

noticias.titulo: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown kills two people
noticias.resumen: The strike mainly targeted civilian infrastructure, Zelenskyy wrote on X. The attack comes after Russia vowed a 'painful' response to Ukraine's strike on the Crimean bridge.
noticias.texto:
The strike mainly targeted civilian infrastructure, Zelenskyy wrote on X. The attack comes after Russia vowed a 'painful' response to Ukraine's strike on the Crimean bridge.
At least two people were killed and dozens injured in a Russian attack on Kryvyi Rih, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown.
A Russian ballistic missile on the city in central Ukraine killed a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, local authorities wrote. 60 others were injured, including six children.
"A young woman – an emergency medical worker – and a little boy who was just seven years old were killed. His name was Tykhon. He was born in 2019, and, sadly, most of his life was lived during a war like this," Zelenskyy wrote Satuday on X.
"Ordinary homes, offices, and everyday civilian infrastructure in an ordinary city were damaged," he added.
The attack sparked four fires and damaged roughly 25 apartment blocks, a hospital, schools, an industrial facility and businesses and vehicles, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.
Russia also targeted other cities and villages in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipro, Rivne, Chernihiv, Mykolaiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions, Zelenskyy reported.
In the Sumy region, Russian forces struck a railway station in the city of Krolevets, injuring three people, local media reported.
On its end, Ukraine struck an ammunition depot in Crimea and bridge in Luhansk, local media reported, adding that Ukraine's defence forces also targeted two Russian command posts in the Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk regions.
The ammunition depot was near the settlement of Pervomaiske in occupied Crimea, Ukraine's General Staff wrote on Telegram.
"The shells that were supposed to go to the frontline from there will no longer reach the positions of Ukrainian soldiers."
In respone to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's Crimea bridge last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed a "painful" response after holding a summit with US counterpart Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping on Thursday.
Zelensky, who met allies in Berlin Thursday, said Putin's attempts to "redraw the world" with Xi and Trump had been a "failure".
"Putin launched this attack in a highly demonstrative manner – following weak meetings in China and the actual failure of his attempt to somehow “redraw” the world," Zelenskyy said on Friday.

noticias.titulo: EU budget: Costa pitches more cuts, Big Tech tax to break deadlock
noticias.resumen: European Council President António Costa proposes cutting the EU's 2028-2034 budget by nearly €200bn, a 10% reduction, to win over frugal countries. Cohesion funding is cut for the first time. A 3% digital services levy replaces a controversial corporate tax, and debt repayment is slowed down.
noticias.texto:
European Council President António Costa proposes cutting the EU's 2028-2034 budget by nearly €200bn, a 10% reduction, to win over frugal countries. Cohesion funding is cut for the first time. A 3% digital services levy replaces a controversial corporate tax, and debt repayment is slowed down.
European Council President António Costa has presented a new EU budgetary proposal in a bid to win unanimous support by the end of the year. Still, it is already facing significant opposition ahead of a key European Council meeting on Thursday.
Costa took over the sensitive negotiations on the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) after the Irish presidency of the Council proposed significant cuts in October.
Ireland's plan failed to win over the so-called frugal countries, including Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, a powerful bloc of net contributors pushing for a smaller overall budget.
To meet their demands, Costa cut a further €49bn in current prices. The budget would shrink from nearly €2 trillion in the Commission's proposal to €1.78 trillion, a 10% reduction worth €204bn.
Costa's move is an attempt to satisfy the frugals' demand to cut the budget by "several hundred billion euros" and to secure support from all the member states before the end of the year.
"I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement for three reasons. First, this is a budget that matches our ambitions. Second, it keeps national contributions within reasonable limits. And third, it includes a balanced basket of new own resources," Costa said, presenting his proposal.
However, the cut is more modest in 2025 prices, and the proposal includes postponing the repayment of EU joint debt, which the frugals are unlikely to consider a reduction.
An eventual delay in the agreement on the budget would mean several EU programmes would not be ready in time for 2028, and the negotiations would be further complicated by elections in several key countries like France, Italy and Poland.
"The new negotiating framework for the next multiannual European budget is very disappointing," a source from the Élysée told reporters. "As it stands, this proposal from the President of the European Council does not constitute a basis for an agreement."
Meanwhile, the budgetary negotiations have already been made more complex as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said there will be no agreement without unanimous financial support to Ukraine, prompting a backlash from several member states.
Costa's proposal will be the basis for the discussion of EU leaders at the special European Council starting on Thursday in Brussels.
Spending programmes
The fight is not only over the budget's size but over where the money goes. The frugals prefer to be called "modernisers" and want more spending on emerging priorities such as competitiveness and defence.
On the other side, 17 countries from southern and eastern Europe form the "Friends of Cohesion" group, which wants to protect funding for low-income regions through cohesion policy.
Given the group's size, cohesion had barely been touched in earlier compromise proposals. Costa breaks with that for the first time, proposing a €54bn cut for agricultural, fisheries and cohesion funding, around 5% less than the Commission's proposal.
Competitiveness and defence take deeper cuts: €95.5bn, or 16% of the original proposal. Global Europe is hardest hit, losing €45bn, or 21% compared with the Commission's plan.
Administrative costs fare slightly better than under the Irish plan, with a nearly 8% cut to €108bn in current prices rather than 9%.
The Commission's original proposal was already higher than the current budget, so despite the cuts most funding programmes would still see an increase compared with the ongoing MFF.
New digital levy
A key element of Costa's proposal is an ambitious mix of new or revamped EU-wide taxes meant to fill the bloc's coffers with €64bn a year in current prices.
The main novelty is a digital services tax of 3% on annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and monetisation of user data. It would apply to companies with EU turnover above €50 million and global turnover above €750 million.
The European Parliament originally proposed the levy, which already exists in France, Spain and Italy. Costa introduced it to replace the Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE), which met insurmountable opposition from member states because it ran counter to the EU's competitiveness agenda.
Opposition to the digital levy mostly stems from fears of US trade retaliation, as most tech giants of that size are American. The calculus appears to be that a Trump administration weakened by its midterm defeat will be less inclined to retaliate.
"These measures would also help create a level playing field in the single market, where American digital giants often face lower taxes than European firms," MEP Danuše Nerudová (Czechia/EPP) told Euronews.
Parliament estimated the levy could raise up to €25bn a year with a 5% call rate and a wider range of online services. Costa's version stays closer to the Commission's estimate of €5bn a year.
Other EU taxes
With CORE abandoned, the most controversial new own resource is the proposal to channel 30% of Emissions Trading System (ETS) revenues to the EU budget, which still faces strong opposition, most notably from Poland.
The Irish presidency had already proposed phasing it in for member states via the Modernisation Fund. Costa goes further with a gradual start: 0% in 2028, rising to the full rate in 2034.
Costa also keeps the proposal for a minimum tax rate of 15% on tobacco and related products. To address opposition from the most affected countries, it would be phased in, starting at 5%, rising to 10% after three years and reaching 15% in 2034.
The compromise also raises the call rate on non-recycled plastic packaging waste from €0.80 to €1.25 per kilogram in 2028.
A less controversial levy concerns member states' contributions based on the amount of uncollected electronic waste. The compromise raises it from €2 to €2.25 per kilogram.
Arguably the least controversial new resource is the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a tariff on carbon-intensive imports. Costa proposes raising the share of revenues going to the EU budget from 75% in the Commission's proposal to 100%.
The proposal also gives a mandate to explore a new levy on crypto-assets, another Parliament idea. The tax was deemed not ready to generate revenue from 2028 and needs more technical and legal work.
A proposal from Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis, who is also Greece's finance minister, to feed the EU budget with revenues from the allocation of radio spectrum for 5G and 6G networks has also been picked up for specific radio bands.
Joint EU debt
Costa's plan also cuts repayments of NextGenerationEU debt for 2028-2034 by €10bn in current prices. That is a significant reduction given the recent spike in interest rates, which has pushed up repayment costs.
Repayment of the post-pandemic joint debt would still run from 2028 to 2058, but its "profile" has changed, an EU official told reporters, without detailing what that means for rolling over existing debt with new debt.
"We slightly change the way the capital is paid," the EU official said. "It will start being paid as of 2028. Not in the same amount, but it will start being paid as of 2028."

noticias.titulo: Strait of Hormuz: Athlete swims through war zone to expose war's environmental toll
noticias.resumen: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh completed a 15-kilometre swim through the Strait of Hormuz over three days in November 2026, braving explosions and burning tankers nearby. His three-day challenge aimed to expose the environmental damage caused by the war with Iran.
noticias.texto:
Wearing nothing but swimming trunks, goggles and a UN-branded cap, 56-year-old ocean campaigner Lewis Pugh entered the waters off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, where he found himself swimming within sight of burning ships and towering plumes of smoke. Just 20 minutes into his first swim, two explosions rocked the area and an oil tanker caught fire around four kilometres away, forcing him to abandon the attempt temporarily. The following day, he witnessed another vessel engulfed in flames as he continued his swim through the strategic waterway.
A United Nations Patron of the Oceans, Pugh warned that pollution from damaged tankers could devastate coral reefs, mangroves and coastal ecosystems for decades. Yet sightings of dolphins, turtles and ospreys reminded him of the extraordinary wildlife at risk. Having previously swum in the Arctic, Antarctic and Red Sea to raise awareness of ocean conservation, he delivered a stark appeal: “We’ve got to stop the war. We’ve got to open the strait, and we’ve got to clean up this mess.”
