noticias.titulo: Hagia Sophia's hidden tunnels uncovered as 420 metres of underground network cleaned
noticias.resumen: During cleaning and excavation works carried out at the site, significant remains were uncovered and carefully documented by archaeologists.
noticias.texto:
During cleaning and excavation works carried out at the site, significant remains were uncovered and carefully documented by archaeologists.
The architectural complex around and beneath Hagia Sophia never ceases to amaze.
Six underground spaces, nine tunnels and almost 3,000 tonnes of soil are revealing unknown facets of the monument's history.
An underground world, unknown until now, is gradually being uncovered beneath Hagia Sophia. Galleries, ancient water networks and architectural remains, which may date back to a period earlier than the construction of the present-day basilica in the 6th century, are coming to light during restoration work on the historic monument. So far, 420 metres of underground tunnels have been cleaned, while the Turkish authorities are considering opening some of them to visitors, offering a new perspective on the history of Byzantine Constantinople.
The scale and importance of the work was presented by the Turkish Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, who went down into Hagia Sophia's underground installations, accompanied by scientists involved in the restoration programme. The Turkish television network CNN Türk has for the first time shown images of the underground galleries and the work taking place in areas that for centuries remained covered by earth and other materials.
According to the data released by the Turkish minister, almost 3,000 tonnes of backfill materials have been removed from two areas of the monument, the Vizier's Garden and the western garden, while investigations have identified six underground spaces and nine tunnels. The works form part of the extensive programme of maintenance and restoration of Hagia Sophia, which the Turkish authorities describe as the largest of the period of the Republic of Turkey.
Traces of an earlier era
One of the most important finds has been identified in an underground burial structure, known as a rock-cut burial space or underground burial monument (hypogeum), in the area of the Vizier's Garden.
There, cleaning and excavation work has revealed architectural layers at a greater depth than the previously known level of the floor. Scientists are examining whether they belong to a period earlier than the current building of Hagia Sophia.
As Mehmet Nuri Ersoy explained, the works went 1.5 metres below the floor level that was covered with mud, revealing traces of an earlier building phase.
This finding is of particular historical interest, as the present-day church of Hagia Sophia was built under Emperor Justinian, between 532 and 537, on the site of older Christian churches.
For the moment, however, no secure dating of the newly uncovered remains has been announced. The assessment that they predate the current church remains a matter for scientific investigation.
An underground network with nine tunnels
In the western garden of Hagia Sophia, six different underground spaces have been identified, which are connected by nine tunnels.
According to the Turkish minister, three of these spaces were most likely underground parts of the old atrium, the courtyard that was linked to the church complex.
Investigations are continuing in other areas, some of which take the form of elongated corridors, between four and 4.8 metres wide.
Of the nine tunnels, seven have already been cleared of backfill, while in the remaining two work is under way to record and document them.
The total length of the cleaned sections reaches 420 metres.
The longest tunnel is 180 metres long and is of particular archaeological interest, as scientists are examining whether it might be connected with the so-called Roman Road of Constantinople.
This gallery runs parallel to the facade of Hagia Sophia, from the area in front of the Fatih Madrasa towards the visitors' entrance, with a gradient of about 3%.
Its possible link with the historic road network of the Byzantine capital is another field of research, and for now the exact original function of the tunnel has not been confirmed.
The hidden water network of Constantinople
According to scientists' assessments, the underground tunnels of Hagia Sophia formed part of a broader system for managing the waters of historic Constantinople.
Some sections appear to have served in the distribution of water and the removal of rainwater, functions that were essential for the protection and daily use of such a large architectural complex.
Their discovery makes it possible to study more closely the technical infrastructure developed around Hagia Sophia during the different periods of its history.
At the same time, the works are not limited to cleaning the tunnels. They include repairs to the vaults, stabilisation of the masonry and reinforcement of sections that have suffered damage.
In one of the underground spaces, 56 metres long, structural damage has already been repaired along an 18 metre section. Other tunnels are being reinforced with stainless steel elements, to ensure their structural stability.
The underground galleries open to visitors
Beyond the archaeological and historical significance of the works, the Turkish government is now also examining how some of the underground spaces could be used as accessible areas of Hagia Sophia.
Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced that a special plan is being prepared for presenting the underground structures, with the protection of the monument and the safety of visitors as key conditions.
It has not yet been determined which sections might open to the public, nor has a timetable been announced.
Another issue under consideration by specialists is whether the underground network could be used to improve the ventilation of the monument.
According to the technical assessments presented by the minister, the existing underground opening can currently cover only 3.6% of Hagia Sophia's ventilation needs. Future studies will examine whether some of the historic galleries could contribute to a modern system supplying fresh air, without altering their architectural character.
The history beneath the history
Hagia Sophia, which has dominated the historic core of Constantinople for almost fifteen centuries, continues to be the subject of archaeological and architectural research.
The new investigations are now turning attention to the less familiar parts of the monument, below ground level, where the different building phases and the infrastructure of old Constantinople largely remain out of sight.

noticias.titulo: ‘Brexit is done’: Theresa May tells Burnham to move on
noticias.resumen: The former British prime minister spent three years trying to negotiate a Brexit deal with the EU.
noticias.texto: Former U.K. Prime Minister Theresa May has said she is “aghast” that Andy Burnham might be considering rejoining the EU after her Labour successor opened a debate about Britain’s future relationship with the bloc. “People voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” May said in a BBC interview broadcast Sunday. Her intervention follows Friday’s Brussels summit , where Burnham and EU leaders announced agreements on food trade, emissions trading and youth mobility. Burnham has said he wants Britain to rejoin the EU in his lifetime but has not committed his government to pursuing membership. On Friday, he proposed an “informal brainstorming process” to explore the future relationship, without explicitly putting rejoining on the agenda. His European relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told POLITICO on Friday that the government would take its time setting out those options, given the divisive nature of the debate. May said she was “slightly aghast” at the prospect of further negotiations over EU membership, warning that such talks would consume time across government, from the prime minister to officials. She also accused Burnham of patronizing voters who backed leaving in the 2016 referendum. “He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come out with the right answer,” she added. May campaigned to remain in the EU but became prime minister after the referendum, promising to carry out the result. She resigned in 2019 after repeatedly failing to get her Brexit deal through Parliament.

noticias.titulo: Brussels, Charleroi airports to cancel most flights Monday amid Belgian strike
noticias.resumen: Air traffic controllers will join a nationwide protest against government spending cuts, prompting anger from airport operators over the last-minute disruption.
noticias.texto: Most flights at Brussels and Charleroi airports will be canceled Monday as air traffic controllers join a nationwide strike against the Belgian government’s austerity measures. Belgian air traffic control provider Skeyes said it would be unable to provide normal services between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. local time, effectively grounding commercial flights at the country’s main airports for most of the day. Brussels Airport confirmed Saturday that most arriving and departing flights would be canceled, while Brussels South Charleroi Airport said no aircraft would be able to take off or land during the 14-hour shutdown. Charleroi’s management criticized Skeyes for the short notice of the action, saying the company had informed it of the disruption less than 36 hours in advance, despite the airport having prepared to operate normally. In a statement Saturday, Charleroi accused air traffic controllers of showing a “completely cavalier attitude” toward airlines, passengers and airport staff. It said thousands of travelers and some 3,400 people working at Charleroi would be affected, and called on Belgian authorities to develop a coordinated plan to prevent recurring disruptions. Skeyes has been approached for comment. Monday’s protest is organized by Belgium’s main trade unions against spending cuts and economic reforms pursued by Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s government . Public transport across Brussels is also expected to be disrupted. Passengers have been advised to check with their airlines before heading to either airport. Tommaso Lecca contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: 14 missing after Russian strike as Zelenskyy presses US over Patriot missiles
noticias.resumen: Following the attack near Kyiv, Ukraine's president issued a plea to Washington to authorize air defense missiles financed by allies.
noticias.texto: A Russian drone strike partially destroyed a five-story apartment building near Kyiv, leaving 14 people unaccounted for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday. Rescuers were searching the rubble in Dymer, north of Kyiv, where part of the building collapsed and a fire broke out. Nine people had been evacuated, Zelenskyy added, warning that others could remain trapped. The attack prompted the Ukrainian president to renew pressure on Washington to approve deliveries of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles financed by Ukraine’s allies, amid mounting Russian aerial attacks. “It is particularly difficult to understand the delays in supplying anti-ballistic interceptors to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said on X . He urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles already paid for by Ukraine’s partners through NATO’s PURL program , which allows allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said earlier this month that deliveries under the program, including Patriots, were continuing. Russia launched 186 drones overnight, including 72 jet-powered models, Ukraine’s air force said. Ukrainian defenses shot down or disabled 161, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations. Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked 20 Ukrainian regions over the past week, launching around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles. Many were ballistic missiles, including North Korean-made weapons, he said, accusing Moscow of helping Pyongyang improve their accuracy.

noticias.titulo: Europeans dare to believe Trump could deliver security for Ukraine
noticias.resumen: After months of anxiety, some of Kyiv's allies now think the U.S will help them negotiate an acceptable peace.
noticias.texto: BERLIN — The proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump’s negotiating team to give Ukraine a NATO-style collective defense guarantee has triggered an unusual new mindset among some of Kyiv’s allies in Europe: optimism. European officials close to the peace negotiations are cautiously hopeful that the offer could signal a shift in America’s position in Ukraine’s favor — even though they remain wary that the price Trump will demand for such a sweeping commitment could be too high. After two weeks of shuttle diplomacy, Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner proposed the security guarantee at last week’s press conference in Berlin, claiming the U.S. president is “open” to such a “big deal” and the Russians are now “comfortable” with it too. Neither is yet certain, and one Russian official dismissed the idea. But Russian President Vladimir Putin himself has not yet publicly rejected Kushner’s plan, and European negotiators are taking it seriously, even if they want more information about how it would work. A security guarantee for Ukraine based on NATO’s Article 5 collective defense clause, which states that an attack on one member shall be treated as an attack on all, would change the game when it comes to deterring Russia from invading Ukraine again after this war ends. That is particularly true if, as implied, America, with its mighty military, is bound into such a guarantee. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, back, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner leave a Coalition of the Willing media call in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool photo by Hannah McKay/Getty Images While few details are known about the proposal, it would, if backed up by robust legal, military and political commitments, mean that a new attack on Ukraine would risk a direct conflict with the U.S. An aide in French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the U.S. is heading in “the right direction” but called on the White House to go a step further and give Ukraine full NATO membership. An Article 5 guarantee “is obviously the best guarantee of solidarity among allies,” said the aide, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “So, if we say we’re giving Ukraine Article 5-type guarantees, we shouldn’t overcomplicate things: It means that Ukraine is joining NATO. The alliance’s credibility rests above all on Article 5. Article 5 is an article of faith.” Shifting the mood One reason why some Europeans believe Kushner’s offer is a genuine one is that he was not speaking off the cuff. In private, U.S. officials have been floating the idea for months. There has even been discussion behind the scenes of the French proposal for full NATO membership. Although Ukraine joining NATO is seen as a red line issue Russia would never agree to, Kushner and co. clearly believe their efforts to discuss an Article 5-like option with the Russians have found support in Moscow. And the mood in some parts of Europe has shifted as a result. Families shelter overnight at a Kyiv metro station following warnings of possible Russian air attacks late on Nov. 19, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Roman Pilipey/AFP via Getty Images Diplomats and officials who have spent much of the past two years of Trump’s second term despairing about his repeated torchings of the Western alliance — and worrying that he will sell out Ukraine — now sound relaxed about the U.S. “Clear progress has been made on security guarantees,” said one European official close to the negotiations. “On peace talks there is alignment with the U.S., no maximalist demands and no discussion on European security without the Europeans.” The aim now is that more progress will be possible toward targeted ceasefires in the energy sector and the Black Sea the next time the U.S. convenes peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, not least because Europeans will have their places at the negotiating table. That meeting is yet to be scheduled but officials expect it to take place in Abu Dhabi sometime after the American Thanksgiving holiday on Nov. 26. Details matter Not everyone is convinced. Speaking after Kushner’s announcement, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “not sure” everyone had the same understanding of what an Article 5-like guarantee would mean. “What does it mean, Article 5? That there are some forces of partners on your land. So, my question is: What about American soldiers?” He said Ukraine “would be happy” if the U.S. put military bases in the country “like in the Middle East.” Other Europeans agreed that there was still a lack of detail about exactly what Kushner’s plan would involve. People walk across a bridge during a blackout in Kyiv caused by attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities on Nov. 20, 2026. | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images The most skeptical Europeans are to be found in countries that share borders and a history with Russia, such as Poland and the Nordic and Baltic states, which are often the most hawkish toward Moscow. Poland will be part of the official European negotiating team, which is expected to join the next round of direct negotiations between Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine. One risk Europeans are alive to is that the cost of such a security guarantee could prove to be too high. Americans asked Ukraine recently whether it would give Russia the whole of Donbas in exchange for full NATO membership. That would mean handing over land to Putin that he has not managed to win by fighting. Keeping Russia happy Ukraine’s territory is not the only issue on the table in these negotiations. Kushner has been equally insistent that revising the entire security framework that had governed Europe before the war is essential, including NATO’s relations with Russia. His broad argument is that if Europe’s security framework had been working properly, the war would never have happened. Among Ukraine’s more than 35 allies who gathered in Berlin for the Coalition of the Willing meeting last week, some see Kushner’s point. That’s why the EU’s institutions are happy to offer Putin the chance to discuss European security in a “parallel” track with a peace deal for Ukraine. To other more hawkish officials, Kushner’s argument about overhauling the continent’s defense framework still sounds dangerously like Putin speaking. They comfort themselves with the thought that no decisions will be taken without Europe “at the table” — but being present doesn’t necessarily equate to being in control. “The danger is that an Article 5-style guarantee could somehow become a Trojan Horse in the case of a wider bargain with Moscow, in which Ukraine would surrender the Donbas and ⁠NATO would accept restrictions on its military presence in Eastern Europe,” said Grégoire Roos, of London’s Chatham House think tank. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, China’s President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump meet in Shenzen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool picture by Andres Martinez Casares/Getty Images “Let’s face it: That would basically give Russia a de facto veto over European security. So, yes, we could potentially end up offering Ukraine the vague promise of collective defence while sapping the basic conditions that would actually make it credible.” Roos said he did not believe the Europeans would fall for such a trap. In Poland, for example, officials are watchful for traps and remain steadfast in backing Ukraine, he said. Trump’s friends Timing is also a factor that could be decisive. A European official said Trump wants a deal within weeks — even by the time he hosts G20 leaders in Florida in mid-December, though that won’t happen. Zelenskyy told reporters on Saturday that Americans “really wanted to get all this done before Christmas.” Another key deadline could be Jan. 3, when the new Democratic-controlled Congress starts work. Some leaders who met with Kushner and Witkoff in Berlin last week had feared Washington would be exerting much more pressure for a deal by the end of the year, according to one person present. But in the end leaders were relieved that the U.S. was not strong-arming Ukraine and its allies to rush to an agreement, the person said. Then there is the influence of another key group to keep in mind: Trump’s friends. While EU diplomats voiced relief that the summit in Shenzhen between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping did not deliver a worse outcome for Ukraine and Europe, it still resulted in a joint “peace” declaration in which the trio pledged to reform the United Nations, slapped down the International Criminal Court, and promised to keep talking among themselves about nuclear arms. Trump doubled down on the value of having a close relationship with his “friend” Putin in a press conference on his return to Washington on Friday. “He’d love to end the war,” Trump said of the Russian leader — on the same day that two Russian missiles and a drone hit Poland, and Danish police announced they had thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper. The China summit serves as a reminder to European optimists that whatever they discuss with Kushner and Witkoff in Berlin or Abu Dhabi, ultimately only one person will make the key decisions for the U.S. — and Putin’s line into him just got stronger. “A precedent was created,” said another European official involved in recent diplomacy. “It wasn’t great.” Clea Caulcutt contributed reporting from Paris.

noticias.texto: Listen on Spotify Apple Music Amazon Music Zum ersten Mal in der Menschheitsgeschichte entsteht ein neuer Ozean und mit dem schmelzenden Eis der Arktis entbrennt ein Wettlauf der Großmächte. Es öffnet sich eine neue geopolitische Front. Im Gespräch mit POLITICO-Host Rixa Fürsen analysiert der ehemalige Vizekanzler Robert Habeck die brisante Lage am Nordpol. Der heutige Professor an der Copenhagen Business School und Autor des Buches „Arctic Meltdown“ erklärt, warum Donald Trumps Interesse an Grönland keine bizarre Episode ist und wie China strategische Abhängigkeiten schafft. Die bittere Erkenntnis: Europa findet in der Arktis schlichtweg nicht statt. Habeck ordnet ein, warum die EU aus ihrem geopolitischen Dornröschenschlaf erwachen muss, bevor andere Mächte die neuen Regeln diktieren. Ein ungeschönter Blick auf die Schwächen europäischer Außenpolitik und die harten Realitäten einer schmelzenden Weltordnung. Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig. noticias.titulo: [Interview] Ukraine’s former defence chief predicts new EU security alliance, gives behind-the-scenes look at Russia diplomacy
noticias.resumen: What happens behind the scenes at peace talks with Russia and in negotiations with allies? Oleksii Reznikov, Ukrainian defence minister at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, spoke candidly about his time leading his country's defence efforts. Now lecturing university students about negotiating tactics, he says Europe might soon see a new security alliance.
noticias.texto: First published in Deník N. A new European security alliance consisting of Scandinavian and Baltic countries as well as Poland, Turkey, Romania, and Bulgaria could soon be created, said former Ukrainian defence minister Oleksii Reznikov in an interview. He shared behind-the-scenes insights from negotiations with Moscow near the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion and how he negotiated more military support from Europe. Some say Ukraine might hand over Donbas to Russia in exchange for Nato membership. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said the day before yesterday that Americans had proposed this to him. But is this realistic? This is a move which, based on negotiation theory, I would describe as the Harvard negotiation approach. Incidentally, one of US president Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff studied at Harvard. At its seminars, students learn the term ‘poisoned pill’. It means that during complex negotiations, one side throws it, and when the other side picks it up, discussion about it begins. In reality, however, it is already poisoned. All of a sudden, we start thinking about two things: whether Russia’s demand that Finland leave Nato is actually justified. And whether Ukraine is prepared to concede territory. This so-called concession, coming from the Russian side, conceals a provocation. What do you mean exactly? Either you hand over territory, or you will not be in Nato. Imagine Zelensky says: “No, we will not join Nato.” Ukrainians would say: “But we must join, because our constitution enshrines a strategic course towards full Nato membership.” Zelensky would reply: “We are prepared to give up territory.” Russia is changing lanes, which is dangerous. These are the Kremlin’s usual negotiation tactics: first, take a hardline position, then retreat. US negotiator Steve Witkoff and Russian president Vladimir Putin (Source: kremlin.ru) Are Americans now on Russia’s side? I would not put it that way. But I would recall the events of February 2025, when, a month after Trump’s inauguration, Zelensky visited the White House. I watched that scandalous meeting closely for the entire 50 minutes, because I teach negotiation at university. Trump said during the meeting that he is not one of the parties; he is a mediator who wants to settle this conflict. And I do not think his position has changed. Earlier talks when Americans negotiated separately with the Russians and the Ukrainians is called a “caucus”, when the parties to a conflict sit in separate rooms. And you run back and forth between them as the mediator … Yes. It may appear that the Americans are more on Russia’s side, because they seem to give greater consideration to its arguments. But that is their strategy. They think it is easier to persuade us Ukrainians, that we are in a weaker position. But for the US side, the mere signing of a peace agreement would be a victory. Zelensky was once scolded by his US counterpart in the Oval Office (Source: Zelenskiy official, Telegram) Europe will presumably be involved in negotiations. It may be that an EU delegation is present rather than one individual, as was discussed at the EU summit in Dublin. Does that pose a problem? Europe must be represented at the negotiating table, because its security interests are at stake. And now the question: we are all used to saying Europe, Europe. But what actually is it? Some understand it as the EU, with 27 member states. And the United Kingdom? And Norway? There are other countries that belong to Europe, such as Switzerland. They also have interests. If we say it is, for example, the EU plus two, we can assume that one of the commissioners will be at the talks. The EU has an official foreign minister, Kaja Kallas. It also has a defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius. And there is EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen. All of them have an official mandate to represent the EU’s interests. The negotiators chosen will more than likely be diplomats who know the Russian mentality well. Read more Europe’s mandate on Russia-Ukraine peace talks takes shape, as Putin escalates war Would that include Kallas? Why not? She is from a Baltic country, people who know how to speak with Russians. Ultimately, there will not be 10 people at the table, but two. In December 2019, I was a member of president Zelensky’s delegation. The only meeting with Putin took place at the Élysée Palace then, with French president Emmanuel Macron acting as mediator. Such high-level meetings take place when almost everything is already prepared — when trusted people have worked everything out and approved the proposals. Only when everything is ready do top leaders meet and bless the document, like a priest in a church. A European negotiator is now being sought, and you previously said the appointee should know the Russian mentality. But is it also important that the negotiator is accepted by the Russians? Putin takes notice of only two people in the world: his friend [Chinese president] Xi Jinping in Beijing and Trump. The three of them think they can divide up the world, so they do not care at all who sits at the negotiating table as the [European] negotiator. Not at all. Read more Xi keen to look ‘neutral’ on Ukraine at Shenzhen summit, as China risks spoiling EU relations by helping Putin to wage war Then comes another tier — the other heads of state with whom he negotiates. But Putin does not sit at the negotiating table. [Kremlin aide] Vladimir Medinsky, [sovereign wealth fund CEO] Kirill Dmitriev, or someone else he has designated, who behave entirely professionally and properly. Do Russia-Ukraine negotiations unfold as people expect them to ? The reality is different to what you see on TV. For example, in February 2022, four days after the full-scale invasion, talks were held in Belarus. The first meeting with the Russian delegation! We met on the Pripyat River, at the hunting residence of Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko. The Russian delegation was led by Medinsky [now head of the Russian negotiating delegation and adviser to Putin]. The talks were followed by another round of talks in Belarus, with a fourth round in Istanbul. The Russian delegation behaved entirely in accordance with diplomatic ethics and protocol. And there was no rudeness. They treated us with absolute respect. And not only that: they addressed me by my first name and as Oleksii Yuriyovych. Yet for some reason unknown to me, they addressed the head of our delegation [Davyd Heorhiyovych Arakhamia, chairman of the parliamentary group of the president’s Servant of the People party] as “Davyd”. Yet, they used my full name. How do you expect things to go at new negotiations which will include Europeans? I am convinced that the same happens when Russians meet our Ukrainian representatives. Russian negotiator Dmitriev is a businessman and certainly no thug. Professional negotiators from Europe and Ukraine will not communicate with the Russians in an entirely easy and calm manner. But they will also certainly not behave rudely. Russian president’s special envoy for foreign investment Kirill Dmitriev (right) welcomed US negotiators Witkoff and Kushner at Moscow airport in November (Source: RIA Kremlin ru, Telegram) Will they shake hands? Ah! That is quite a complicated question. I too faced such a challenge [in 2022]. Protocol dictated that we should shake hands, but you simply cannot offer them your hand. It is incredibly difficult – an immensely complicated matter. In Ukraine, there has been much discussion about the ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, shaking hands with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova. It is an unusual situation, but everyone must find their own way. One fundamental thing must be understood: when you are a professional negotiator, you have to leave all your emotions in the next room. After all, you have come here to work in the interest of whoever sent you. It is not about your emotions, but about agreeing a lasting peace in Ukraine’s interest. If you cannot do that, do not travel anywhere. I too had such a dilemma. At a personal meeting, I told the Ukrainian president quite sincerely that I do not feel qualified as a negotiator. He replied: “Oleksii, I understand you, but it is necessary. I feel the same way myself, but we need to resolve the issue of humanitarian corridors, to enable people to leave Mariupol, Berdiansk and occupied Volnovakha. And secondly, we must agree at least on an exchange of prisoners.” Reznikov with Zelensky at the beginning of Russia’s full-scale war. (Source: Oleksii Reznikov via X) So I put all my emotions in my pocket and composed myself and said to myself: “You are a negotiator – you must bring people something positive.” That is why I see no problem in how Europeans, Ukrainians, Russians, and Americans work together. There will be no shouting matches at the table or behind closed doors. After all, such dramatic scenes tend to play out only in front of the cameras as a public relations exercise. Everyone wants to look like they’ve won. And in such complex negotiations, agreements tend to be written in the format of constructive ambiguity . For instance, if you look at the Good Friday peace deal between Ireland and Britain, you will see that it was written in a way that allowed the Irish Republican Army to stand before its own people and say: “We won.” Any agreement that is reached now will be with constructive ambiguity where each side will interpret it as it likes. But I think the most important aspect of peace talks is whether negotiators will have direct contact with their bosses. At Belarus talks, those sitting at the table did not have direct contact. There was one person who had access to the top, but he was not even sitting at the table. [Russian oligarch] Roman Abramovich was busy walking around, observing from a distance and taking coffee breaks. Read more Top Russian oligarch Abramovich loses third EU lawsuit, as Brussels plans tougher blacklist It is said that Ukraine was pushed to reject Russia’s peace terms in 2022 in Istanbul by then-British prime minister Boris Johnson. That suggestion is “durnia” – the Ukrainian word for nonsense. Nobody can influence Zelensky, he makes his own decisions. Johnson’s opinion carried great weight with our president, but not in terms of a dilemma over whether to keep fighting or not. Personally, I think the main reason for the sharp change in the negotiation process with the Russians was not Johnson, but Bucha . When the Russians withdrew from Bucha, Irpin, and Hostomel, they appeared to have shown some goodwill. The very next day, I went there with interior minister Denys Monastyrskyi and general Oleksandr Syrskyi, who was then responsible for the defence of Kyiv. I saw with my own eyes the bodies of the dead with their hands tied behind their backs. It was horrific. That was when we understood that we were fighting an army of rapists, murderers and looters. It was this emotional shock that changed our view on negotiating, not Johnson. Did you always believe you would manage this war? In December 2021, the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations held a closed session. The Pentagon and US intelligence presented a report on the possibility of a Russian invasion of Ukraine. The information then leaked to the press. Everyone kept saying that in the event of an invasion, Kyiv would fall within three days. Ukraine came to resemble someone given a terminal diagnosis. A neighbour brings them flowers and oranges, but will not invest money or anything else in them. After all, they will die tomorrow. That was why they supplied us only with weapons suited to guerrilla warfare and street fighting — their maximum range was two and a half kilometres. Everyone thought Ukrainians would fight as guerrillas. But the Ukrainian people disagreed. Indeed, Ukraine has endured, while Europe does not provide enough aid. As defence minister, what annoyed you most about dealing with Europe? Nothing irritated me, because I was prepared for everything. And I am an optimist. When you go into talks with partners to persuade them to supply you with weapons, you must be optimistic and courteous. I always tried to understand what might deter somebody from helping and look for counterarguments. For instance, we produce our own tanks in Ukraine but we did not have enough ammunition. We therefore needed Western-made tanks, which use a different type of ammunition. I approached Christine Lambrecht, who was Germany’s defence minister at the time, and told her: “I need Leopards [a German tank type].” She replied: “But you have T-72s and T-80s.” I said: “We have tanks, but we will soon run out of ammunition.” She went on: “Oleksii, that is not realistic.” “Why?” I insisted. “Don’t you understand? The Second World War. German tanks cannot fight against Russia; that is a red line that cannot be crossed,” she said. Former German defence minister Christine Lambrecht of the SPD (Source: Henning Schacht, Bundestag) I told her: “All right, Christine, let us approach it differently. Let us at least begin by training Ukrainian tank crews at your training grounds.” She replied: “Oleksii, you are a lawyer, I know you. If I allow you to train, it will mean that I have given you tanks.” So I tried a different approach. I met the Americans and told them: “I need three Abrams tanks. They will protect your embassy in Kyiv. And I will show everyone that I have American tanks, so that the Germans can see that you were first.” Then I turned to the British: “I need three Challengers.” I told them we would place them at a training ground near Lviv. We would be able to say: “Do you see, Germans? We have British tanks.” I also spoke to French president Macron. I told him: “Mr President, we need your tanks.” In the end, we agreed on the delivery of AMX-10 “light tanks”. Then I spoke with Polish defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak. He told me: “Oleksii, what else can we do? We have T-72s, we can give you those.” I replied: “Minister, but you have Leopards.” To the left of Oleksii Reznikov is Mariusz Błaszczak, Poland’s defence minister at the time. (Source: Oleksii Reznikov via X) He replied: “But the Germans will not allow us to give them to you.” I said: “What if you announced that you were prepared to give Leopards to Ukraine if Germany granted you permission?” That is exactly what he did. Polish president Duda announced on television: “We are prepared to give Ukraine 60 Leopards, provided Germany grants us permission.” Then, at Ramstein [the German Allied base], the Polish minister and I organised a so-called tank lunch. Around 15 countries were there, and Boris Pistorius, the newly appointed German defence minister, also arrived. German defence minister Boris Pistorius among Bundeswehr soldiers deployed in Lithuania. (Source: Tom Twardy, Bundeswehr) Everyone asked him: “Boris, how are things on your side?” He replied: “Guys, it is only my second day in office at the ministry.” We asked him whether we could use German training grounds to train Ukrainian soldiers on Western tanks. The Germans would provide instructors, training grounds, fuel and the necessary equipment. He agreed. Ben Wallace [then the British defence minister] winked at me and said: “Boris, since your instructors will be working and the Ukrainian lads will be arriving, how about we start training them on Leopards in the meantime?” “But we are not giving them Leopards yet,” Boris objected. “But it is only training,” I told him. And in the end, he agreed. I went out before the journalists and announced: “I have a small piece of news for you: tank crew training will begin in Germany.” They asked: “On which tanks?” And I said: “Abrams, Challenger, AMX-10, and Leopard too.” A photograph with Boris Pistorius from 2023, when the “first” demonstration Leopard 2 tank arrived in Kyiv. (Source: Oleksii Reznikov via X) Olaf Scholz, then Germany’s chancellor, later declared that we had reached an agreement. Germany would officially supply Leopard tanks to Ukraine. And that is how diplomacy works. Why, from Ukraine’s perspective, is European and US support insufficient? Nobody believes Ukraine can win because nobody believes Russia can lose. In fact, you are afraid of Russia losing. Risks are present in the minds of all kinds of experts. Above all, there is the fear of collapse and chaos across the territory of an empire where nuclear weapons are scattered. The same as what the whole world feared during the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991? Exactly. The second risk is a wave of migrants who could flee an outbreak of civil war. Millions of people would head to Europe, which frightens everyone to death. The uncontrolled fluctuations in the prices of gas, oil, and other energy commodities pose another risk as is the strengthening of Chinese influence. And, the rise of Islamic radicalism in the Caucasus. Russia’s Burevestnik nuclear missile has been successfully launched in test mode only once. However, there have been many tests. (Source: Russian Ministry of Defence) But I still see it more positively. Whereas people said that Ukraine could not win this war, a few months later US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in one of his speeches: “Nobody can win this war.” That is, neither Ukraine nor Russia. Elections will be held across Europe next year. Do you envisage a scenario in which the political leadership in France changes and the new government becomes less helpful to Ukraine? It is not so important for all of Europe to agree on supporting Ukraine. What matters is that there is a group of countries that understand Russia poses a threat. I expect a new security alliance to emerge in Europe. It will be based on Ukraine, with its wartime experience, and the United Kingdom. The Scandinavian countries and the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia as well as Poland will join. I think Turkey will join, too. And Romania and Bulgaria will also consider their involvement.

noticias.titulo: Soft questions, hard Empire: Kusturica’s “Our Baptism” and Putin’s spiritual sales pitch
noticias.resumen: Emir Kusturica’s latest project, Our Baptism, has produced the interview the Kremlin clearly wanted: a ...
noticias.texto: Emir Kusturica’s latest project, Our Baptism, has produced the interview the Kremlin clearly wanted: a Sarajevo-born Serbian director, long sympathetic to Putin and already in company with Steven Seagal and Gérard Depardieu, serves up soft questions so the Russian president can present himself as the guardian of Christian civilization. Sarajevo-born Emir Kusturica, raised in a secular Muslim family, was baptized into the Serbian Orthodox Church in 2005 (taking the name Nemanja at the Savina Monastery) and has since presented the step as a return to the Orthodox faith of his ancestors rather than a conversion. The transcript is less an exchange than a catechism. Kusturica feeds lines about Russia as “a blessing for the entire humanity” and an “ark” that can save “all those who believe in Christ.” Putin accepts both without hesitation. The framing is familiar. Russia is a miracle and a mystery that “requires faith and prayer from its leader.” Moscow is the Third Rome. Russian civilization is unique because it “never took over others” and merely created conditions for other peoples to flourish. The Russian Orthodox Church is the essential spiritual pillar of the state. Communism, in its early form, was “similar to Christianity” in its sense of brotherhood. KGB officers who monitored the Church as “the only legally recognised opposition” somehow ended up baptized. And the war in Ukraine is the latest episode of “divide and rule” by external forces, so Ukrainian soldiers should simply “come over to our side.” Each claim collapses under ordinary scrutiny. The “ark” metaphor is pure messianism. Putin recycles the old Third Rome idea he himself invokes: Christianity moved from Rome to Byzantium to Moscow, and a fourth there shall not be. He presents today’s Russia as the place that can still preserve traditional Christian values against a West that has supposedly abandoned them. That is ideological framing, not evidence. The sharper and more immediate contradiction lies elsewhere. Putin states that the distinctive feature of Russian civilisation is that it “never took over others.” It merely “provided enabling conditions for the development of other peoples and ethnicities” inside the empire, allowing them their languages, traditions and religions. He presents this as a unique, non-imposing character. A state that abducts children and turns them into pro-Putin Russians is doing the opposite of what Putin claims Russian civilisation has never done. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 precisely for the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territories. Children have been systematically removed from their families and communities, relocated into Russia, placed in Russian institutions or with Russian families, and subjected to a programme of identity replacement – Russian language, Russian schooling, Russian patriotic education. That is not enabling someone else’s development. It is taking over persons and remaking them. The warrant does not primarily undercut the religious “ark” rhetoric; it undercuts the assertion that Russia does not impose itself on others. The claim of non-imposition is falsified by the practice the Court has treated as a war crime. Putin’s insistence that Russian civilization “never took over others” is equally ahistorical. The expansion into Siberia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, the partitions of Poland, the absorption of the Baltics, and the successive conquests and reconquests of Ukrainian lands were not acts of gentle hospitality. The Soviet period added its own methods. The current war is the latest chapter, not an aberration. Claiming uniqueness on the grounds of non-conquest while conducting a war of territorial seizure and demographic engineering is not subtle. The KGB officer as spiritual authority Putin’s personal history adds a layer of irony. He began his career in the KGB. The Soviet security apparatus treated the Church as an ideological enemy for decades. Putin’s anecdote that KGB officers assigned to “domestic opposition” units involving the Church “got baptised” and brought Easter eggs to colleagues is presented as evidence of mutual influence. It is more plausibly read as the classic pattern of infiltration and surveillance. The secret police did not become the faithful; the faithful were watched by the secret police. Elevating a former KGB officer to the status of quasi-spiritual leader of “true” Christianity requires an audience willing to overlook the institutional record. The personal baptism story – secretly christened by the future Patriarch’s father at the Transfiguration Cathedral – functions the same way. It is an unverifiable family anecdote turned into destiny. Whether true or embellished, its narrative purpose is clear: to bind the president personally to the Church hierarchy and to the foundational myth of the Russian state. Communism was “similar to Christianity” The most revealing exchange is the brief discussion of the Soviet past. Kusturica contrasts a working “symphony” in Russia with failing liberal systems in the West. Putin responds that the socialist idea itself was “very good, it’s similar to Christianity, with the same sense of brotherhood.” He acknowledges that it later “degenerated into repressions, the suppression of dissenting opinions, concentration camps,” but insists the early stage was a kind of symphony that even explained the success of Soviet intelligence. This is the core ideological move. The Soviet project claimed universal brotherhood and historical inevitability while building an empire on atheist grounds and mass repression. The current project claims to defend traditional Christian values and the continuation of the human race while building (or restoring) an empire on religious-national grounds. The continuity is not accidental. Both versions offer a messianic role for the Russian state, both treat dissent as external subversion, and both subordinate institutions – including the Church – to state power. The early Bolsheviks closed churches and shot priests; the present leadership funds them, restores them, and uses them for legitimacy. The instrument has changed; the purpose of centralized control has not. Ukraine and the call to switch sides On Ukraine, Putin restates the “one people” thesis and attributes the conflict to external “divide and rule.” He cites Soviet-era population figures and industrial capacity, then blames post-independence “nationalists” for decline. Ukrainian soldiers are invited to join “our shared side – the right side of history.” The framing erases Ukrainian agency, language, and political choice, and it erases the decision to launch a full-scale invasion in 2022. Kusturica’s questions rarely press. He notes the growth of Orthodoxy in North America, praises the Church’s unchanged canons, and asks whether people pray for the president. The tone is that of a collaborator in a film project, certainly not a journalist testing claims. The result is useful for domestic and sympathetic foreign audiences: a former KGB officer, head of a state at war, is presented as the defender of eternal values against a decadent West. The larger project The interview fits a broader pattern. Celebrity endorsements, religious soft power, and selective history are used to rebrand imperial restoration. An empire once justified by scientific socialism and proletarian internationalism is now justified by Orthodoxy, traditional values, and the claim to be the last ark of authentic Christianity. The content has been updated; the structure – messianic role for the Russian state, denial of aggressive expansion, and the subordination of spiritual institutions to political ends – remains recognisable. Kusturica’s participation does not create these contradictions. It simply stages them. Russia as miracle, Russia as ark, Russia as the civilization that never conquers, Russia whose former security officer is its spiritual patron: these are assertions for the film. The arrest warrant, the historical record of expansion, the documented treatment of Ukrainian children, and the Soviet legacy of Church repression are the context in which the assertions are made. The gap between the two is the real story. Caption: Vladimir Putin’s interview with film director Emir Kusturica for his project Our Baptism, 20 November 2026 [Kremlin website]

noticias.titulo: Zelenskyy: Americans want trilateral talks before Christmas
noticias.resumen: American partners are proposing a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States before ...
noticias.texto: American partners are proposing a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States before Christmas, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said while speaking with journalists, EUalive’s partner European Pravda reports. Technical meetings between the sides are expected in the near term to prepare the substance and desired outcomes of the talks. Only after that will the location and exact timing of a leaders-level trilateral meeting be settled. The U.S. side has indicated it wants the meeting held before Christmas. “Our security advisors will have a series of contacts – possibly online, possibly in person – to prepare the agenda, meaning the content of the meeting, and the result: how to bring all of us closer to ending the war. The American side said it wants to do this before Christmas. I agreed. The sooner there is a result, the better,” Zelenskyy stated. On Ukraine’s possible Ukrainian participation in the G20 summit, Zelenskyy said no invitation has yet been received from the United States. He nevertheless views the gathering as a suitable venue for a trilateral meeting. The 2026 G20 Leaders’ Summit is set for 14–15 December at Trump National Doral Miami in Doral, Florida, and while Trump has invited Putin, the Russian president has not yet confirmed whether he will attend. “Many leaders have urged the American side to officially invite Ukraine to the G20. We have not received an invitation so far; if we do, we will of course attend. Could a trilateral meeting take place on the sidelines of the G20? I am confident it could. We have heard that some members of Congress take a negative view of Trump having invited Putin. But if Trump invites Ukraine, that is a different story, because a trilateral meeting would then be supported by everyone,” Zelenskyy said. The comments come against the backdrop of a major shift in U.S. domestic politics. In the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats secured full control of Congress, winning a 56–44 majority in the Senate (a net gain of nine seats, including historic flips in states such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina) and a substantial majority in the House of Representatives (projected in the range of 257–173). The results represent a clear rebuke of President Trump and the Republican Party and usher in divided government for the final two years of his term. The new Congress will be sworn in on 3 January, and Democratic control of both chambers is expected to influence U.S. foreign policy priorities, including support for Ukraine and the conduct of any negotiations involving Russia. Zelenskyy has previously indicated, following a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” that Europe will participate in negotiations with Russia aimed at ending the war. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said partners are seeking neutral venues for future talks, with the United Arab Emirates among the locations under consideration. French President Emmanuel Macron has welcomed Russia’s proposal to formalise dialogue with European representatives as a positive step, while insisting that any such contacts must give Europe a full and active role in negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, including in the next round of talks involving the United States and Kyiv. However it remains unclear if Europe would join the Ukraine peace process before trilateral talks involving Moscow, Washington an Kyiv take place. France welcomes Putin’s offer of dialogue but demands a full European role in Ukraine talks This article draws on reporting by EUalive’s partner European Pravda Caption: Photo of President Zelenskyy dated 19 November 2026 [President Zelenskyy on X]

noticias.titulo: Croatians rally in Zagreb demanding justice over psychiatric hospital death
noticias.resumen: Thousands gathered in Croatia’s capital on Saturday evening to protest over the death of 32-year-old ...
noticias.texto: Thousands gathered in Croatia’s capital on Saturday evening to protest over the death of 32-year-old Kristian Josip Peris ​in a psychiatric hospital, demanding accountability for those responsible and ‌better regulation of treatments in hospitals. Peris, a former athlete and coach, died on 21 October after being admitted to the clinic. His death sparked ​public outrage across Croatia after images and video from ​hospital surveillance cameras were published by local media. The footage ⁠showed staff holding a pillow over the restrained patient. “Kristian Josip ​Peris asked for help at the St. Ivan Jankomir clinic and ​during that hospitalization he passed away,” the family lawyer Leon Zrnic said. “In the meantime, a surveillance video was released to the public and it was ​established that they had … hit him, strangled him, that he ​had broken ribs, and as a result of that illegal procedure, he lost ‌his ⁠life.” On Saturday evening people gathered in Ban Jelacic Square carrying candles and white pillows. Media reported that about 1,000 people gathered in the coastal town of Rijeka for the same reason, ​and held a ​protest march. “I watched ⁠the video (the surveillance tape) and I was in shock to see that evil,” Mirna Strugar, who ​attended the protest in Zagreb, said. “I hope this ​will never ⁠be repeated.” Croatian authorities have arrested several hospital employees as part of an investigation. Four medical technicians are under investigation on suspicion of ⁠the ​aggravated murder of a vulnerable person, ​while prosecutors have expanded inquiries to other staff who were present during the incident. With Reuters Caption: Protestors dangle pillows to express anger over video that showed hospital staff holding a pillow over the restrained patient who later died [@DarkoLesinger on X]

noticias.titulo: Elecciones generales emociones
noticias.texto:
Miedo, esperanza, indignación o identidad: las emociones que impactan en las urnas
- Expertos coinciden en que polarización política como la actual potencia aún más el factor emocional al ir a votar
- La campaña influye en el voto del 3,3% de los ciudadanos, según el CIS, y los programas electorales impactan únicamente en el 1,6%
¿Qué pesa más cuando acudimos a votar: la razón o la emoción? Esta es una de las preguntas con más protagonismo sociológico en cada convocatoria electoral. ¿Y cuánto influyen en nuestra decisión factores como el miedo, la esperanza, la identidad o la ira? "Uno no solo vota por cuestiones racionales. Es decir, si votásemos por cuestiones racionales, leeríamos los programas de los candidatos y veríamos cuál es nuestro estilo de vida y a partir de ahí votaríamos al que mejore nuestro estilo de vida. Sin embargo, nadie lee los programas", explica a RTVE Noticias el psicólogo y experto en Intervención Social Sergio García Soriano.
El 29 de noviembre los españoles volvemos a las urnas. Según la última encuesta preelectoral del Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), a la hora de decidir el voto, el 49,1% de personas afirma que, según lo que más le convenza en ese momento, eligen a un partido u otro o no votan, mientras que el 23,5% vota siempre por la misma formación. En cuanto a las razones, el 55,8% se inclina por el partido que mejor representa sus ideas; el 37,4% lo hará por el que está más capacitado para gestionar el país y el 25,3% votará pensando en su situación económica y social personal. Le sigue el intentar evitar que ganen partidos o candidatos de derechas (21,8%), inclinación por el candidato (11,1%); que siempre ha votado por ese partido (10,8 %) y tratar de impedir que ganen partidos o candidatos de izquierdas (7,9%).
Lejos quedan cuestiones como la influencia de la campaña electoral, motivación solo para el 3,3% de los encuestados; o el programa electoral, importante solo para el 1,6%. "Si votásemos al pie de la letra, seríamos racionalistas de nuestra elección, pero en ocasiones votamos por una emoción o por una cuestión interna más relacionada con un esquema de lo que no querríamos ser, con un esquema de lo que estamos en contra. Hay veces que no votamos a favor, sino que votamos para castigar. Y en ese castigo es verdad que hay más emoción que racionalización. Por lo tanto, sí. En ocasiones podemos ser muy permeables frente a la emoción más que frente al argumento", agrega García Soriano, coordinador del grupo de Psicología, Comunicación y Política del Colegio Oficial de la Psicología de Madrid.
El efecto de la polarización
Cada ciclo electoral tiene su letra pequeña, ya sea en cuanto a candidatos, partidos y alianzas, pero, sobre todo, en cuanto al contexto económico y social que vive el país y, por ende, sus ciudadanos.
De cara a las elecciones de este año se atisba un escenario marcado por el alto nivel de polarización política y afectiva. Ahonda en esto Marta Marín, psicóloga clínica de adultos con su propia consulta en Valencia: "Las emociones van a decidir más el voto. Hay más identificación con más fuerzas políticas y más motivaciones del miedo, la ilusión o la rabia. Me parece que son unas elecciones más emocionales, en un momento como más de polarización, de incertidumbre".
"Cuando hay polarización, las emociones tienen más peso que la que la razón. Se deja de percibir la política como una cuestión de propuestas, sino como una cuestión más de identidad. Y, además, hay una cosa que en psicología se llama sesgo de confirmación, que refuerza tus creencias. Y te cuestionas todo aquello que las contradice, entonces es como un pez que se que se muerde la cola", agrega.
Los tipos de votantes según las emociones
Llegados a este punto, ¿podemos clasificarnos atendiendo a factores psicológicos? García Soriano apunta a votantes que se anclan a "diferentes emociones". Entre ellos, uno de los más estudiadas, el miedo. "Es decir, que va a votar siempre condicionado por un temor a que ocurra algo que considere negativo. O bien a que pierde la estabilidad económica, o miedo a una futura inseguridad o que haya un cambio social que de alguna manera le perjudique", afirma el psicólogo.
Juan Antonio Pérez, catedrático de Psicología Social en la Universidad de Valencia, va más allá: "Yo creo que es clave el miedo. Ellos lo saben (los partidos). Tienen equipos muy fuertes analizando. Evidentemente, el miedo es clave para movilizar. O sea, en esta polarización afectiva y en esa competición de bloques, que no es tanto de partidos sino de bloques (...) el miedo moviliza a todos. El hecho de decir ‘que viene la derecha o que viene Vox’ moviliza también a los de Vox".
Convencido de que "no hay decisión sin emoción", remarca que los ciudadanos primero deciden a quién votan y luego justifican o racionalizan el porqué lo hacen. "Entonces, para nosotros la emoción va antes que la razón. O sea, me identifico con mi grupo, o el partidismo negativo: odio al otro bloque, al otro grupo. Entonces, primero eso y después viene la razón, el análisis", opina.
Por otro lado, García Soriano hace referencia a los votantes que se inclinan más por la ilusión o la esperanza, agarrados a una promesa de transformación, una expectativa de mejora, que busca un cambio. Pero también se puede hablar de un votante que está más anclado a la "indignación o al enfado", cuyo sufragio va a expresar un descontento o enfadado con el Gobierno, instituciones o político al que quiere castigar electoralmente.
"En esa indignación también se genera algo relacionado con un resentimiento, es decir, que piensan que los demás tienen un trato privilegiado y a partir de ahí se piensa que a ellos les ha perjudicado", expresa. Agrega un cuarto tipo, que mezcla identidad y orgullo, ya sea en parámetros de identidad nacional o por pertenencia a una comunidad o grupo social. Y no descarta un quinto y hasta sexto: un "votante nostálgico" que siempre va a idealizar el pasado y considerar que determinados cambios siempre han empeorado la sociedad y el "votante aspiracional", que va a votar en función de lo que aspira a ser, ya sea una mejora en su posición social al identificar que hay un éxito en los demás que él quiere conseguir.
Las múltiples variables del comportamiento
¿Hasta qué punto influye el entorno en el que vivimos a la hora de elegir un candidato en las urnas? Nos contesta Pérez. "Bastante", dice. Pero advierte: "Es una idiotez decir que el comportamiento lo explicas con una variable. Siempre hay múltiples interacciones y matices. Pero, por ejemplo, si cogemos el caso de los jóvenes, los que van a votar por primera vez ahora. Este primer voto es fundamental. Lo que votan ahora va a ser ya su camino para el resto de votaciones. Somos muy fieles a votar lo mismo".
¿Y cómo van a elegir el voto estos jóvenes? "Evidentemente, hay muchos factores: el familiar es sin duda clave, los estudios lo avalan, lo que se ve, lo que se discute... Los compañeros de trabajo, de clase... también influye", opina.
En estos comicios, el catedrático ve tres grandes situaciones que dan lugar a distintos perfiles de votantes desde el punto de vista psicosocial. El primero, la intensificación de la identificación o lealtad a una formación política, pero esta vez ampliada a un bloque ideológico de partidos, a derecha o izquierda. Una identidad como "supraordinada", como meta: "Que no ganen los otros, me da igual que sea mi partido o uno de mi bloque".
Como segunda arista, identifica la dificultad de los partidos de convertir a votantes, llevarlos a su terreno si anteriormente votaron a otras formaciones, lo que deriva en la necesidad de potenciar la movilización de "los tuyos". "La gente va a ser muy poco sensible a la campaña", recalca Pérez, que cree que esta sí puede influir, pero más en movilizar que en modificar la orientación del voto.
Y en tercer lugar destaca la polarización, no de ideas o ideológica, sino la afectiva. "Es el odio al otro y la defensa de bloque a muerte y el otro como enemigo".
El poder de los indecisos
Volviendo a la encuesta preelectoral del CIS, realizada entre el 7 y 30 de octubre con un total de 45.074 entrevistas y publicada el 12 de noviembre, llama la atención la cantidad de personas que asume no saber aún a qué partido votarán: el 15,8% están indecisas, solo por debajo de los que reconocieron que elegirán al PSOE y al PP.
"Cuando estás indeciso, se deja hasta el último momento, y ahí, claro, pues vamos a decir que un factor muy importante es en el momento de coger la papeleta. Si van allí, ¿qué les viene a la mente? ¿En qué piensan? Piensan en la vivienda, piensan en Ceuta, piensan en el aborto, piensan en la corrupción... y las redes sociales, por ejemplo, cumplen su papel. Entonces, yo creo que ahí es clave qué temas están activados en esas mentes en el momento que tienen que decidir", opina Pérez.
Algo similar considera Marta Marín, ya que, "si ocurre algo que te remueve una emoción intensa, eso puede inclinar la balanza".
"Si pasa cualquier cosa, como pasó con el accidente del tren o incluso igual no algo tan relevante, pero que ves un debate de cualquier cosa que te llama la atención, entonces puede en ese momento inclinar la balanza hacia una cosa u otra", subraya, como puede ser cualquier noticia o declaraciones de última hora que te despierten más miedo, más esperanza, más confianza o más rechazo. "No es que sean más influenciables, pero sí que son personas que, como tienen aún la decisión tomada, es más fácil que en el último momento puedan inclinarse hacia un lado o hacia otro. Son más flexibles, están más abiertos", concluye.
La firma internacional YouGov publicó el 30 de octubre una encuesta sobre qué piensa la opinión pública de cara a los comicios. La vivienda es el problema que más españoles destacan: más de la mitad, el 53%, la eligen entre sus dos problemas más importantes. El siguiente más mencionado, el nivel de inmigración, lo elige un 35%. La corrupción y el fraude ocupan el tercer lugar, con un 28%.
El informe incluye la consulta a 2.175 españoles sobre qué es lo que más influye en su decisión de votar y a quién votar. Los resultados muestran que el principal factor que impulsa la decisión de voto es frenar un gobierno de derechas (14%), seguido del deseo de un cambio de gobierno (9%) y la corrupción (8%). Entre los votantes del PSOE, el 39% afirma que evitar un gobierno de derechas es lo que más les influye. Asimismo, el 22% de quienes optan por el PP y el 15% de los de Vox mencionan la necesidad de un cambio de gobierno.
"En ocasiones, hay votantes que necesitan las últimas semanas, los últimos acontecimientos para decidirse a votar. El indeciso es un decidido tímido que necesita de otros para interpelarle y para que acuda a las urnas", complementa García Soriano, que pone como ejemplo lo sucedido en las recientes elecciones en Brasil. "Y de cómo, a pesar de las lluvias, hubo ciertos elementos y ciertos estímulos que permitieron el acercarse a las urnas y eso parece que ayudó a un cambio político. Entonces, lo que suceda en las últimas semanas es de alguna manera muy importante para que esos decididos tímidos que saben lo que quieren hacer, pero de alguna forma están en ello o lo están elaborando, pues puedan decidirse", concluye.

noticias.titulo: La Promesa avance semanal
noticias.texto:
Avance semanal de 'La Promesa' del 23 al 27 de noviembre: Curro encierra a Trini en la habitación secreta
- Te contamos qué pasará esta semana en La Promesa
- Descubre las tramas que se resolverán y otras que nacerán en los próximos capítulos
- Disfruta de todos los episodios de la serie en RTVE Play
Adriano y Jacobo han traspasado una línea roja: se han dejado llevar por la rabia y han acabado a puñetazo limpio en medio de una cena familiar. Los Luján se han quedado en absoluto estado de shock. Finalmente, han logrado separar y calmar a los jóvenes. ¿Conseguirán arreglar sus diferencias de una vez por todas? ¿Saldrá a la luz la verdadera razón de su discusión?
Manuel y Curro, por su parte, avanzan en su investigación: han traído a Trini hasta el palacio y se ha reencontrado con Leocadia. ¡Ambas se han reconocido! Ahora, la dependienta de la Joyería Llop es consciente del peligro que corre. ¿Lograrán mantener a salvo a la muchacha?Si quieres saber lo que va a pasar del 23 al 27 de noviembre aquí te dejamos el avance de los próximos capítulos de La Promesa.
Avance del capítulo 952 del lunes 23 de noviembre
Candela no sabe si la habrán cogido como cocinera jefa, había más candidatas. Simona la insta a llamar e interesarse. Leocadia, todavía sorprendida por la visita de Trini, pregunta a Curro por su relación con la Joyería Llop. Ángela sabe que algo raro ocurre... ¿Descubrirá de qué se trata? La señora de Figueroa informa a Lorenzo de que unos encapuchados han cometido un robo en casa de un noble. Éste le resta importancia, pero cuando se queda solo, llama para comprobar si es cierto: los ladrones actuaron con pericia militar. El capitán de la Mata se preocupa: ¡la logia parece verdaderamente peligrosa! Ciro pregunta con esperanza a Lorenzo si eso significa que se va a echar atrás… Manuel empieza a mover hilos para que abran la causa contra Leocadia. Lo primero que hace es ir a consultar el caso con un amigo abogado. Pero los hermanos son conscientes de que Trini corre peligro y de que su testimonio es esencial: ¡hay que protegerla! Por ello, Curro decide encerrar a la muchacha en la habitación secreta en contra de su voluntad.
Avance del capítulo 953 del martes 24 de noviembre
Curro, que ha encerrado a Trini en la habitación secreta, llama a la joyería haciéndose pasar por médico para avisar de que la joven ha sido ingresada de urgencia. Pía y Julieta, por su parte, se presentan en la habitación para hacer compañía a la muchacha, que se mantiene inquieta, ¡sabe que corre peligro!Lorenzo confirma a Ciro que ha aceptado trabajar para la logia: tiene que asumir su destino. Adriano lamenta ante Martina que su plan de casarse con Jacobo siga en pie a pesar de su no embarazo. Parece imposible que los chicos se reconcilien... Candela asegura que le parece bien quedarse en La Promesa si, finalmente, no la escogen para el trabajo. Tomasa ve con rabia cómo vuelve la sintonía de las cocineras. Manuel vuelve de hacer la consulta sobre el caso contra Leocadia. ¿Qué noticias trae? Samuel confiesa a Petra que la boda de Carlo y María es irregular: no avisó al Obispado y, por tanto, ¡la boda podría declararse nula!
Avance del capítulo 954 del miércoles 25 de noviembre
Petra urge a Samuel a que solucione el matrimonio irregular de María y Carlo, pero él lo ve imposible a estas alturas… ¿Conseguirá arreglarlo? Las cocineras se reconcilian: serán más sinceras para evitar malentendidos. Y es que ya se da por hecho que no han cogido a Candela en el otro trabajo… Manuel informa: deberán acudir ante un juez.Trini se muestra dispuesta, pero cada vez está más intranquila. Martina abronca a Jacobo y Adriano por discutir ante el marqués y amenaza con soluciones drásticas. Los chicos terminan haciendo las paces: dejarán de lado sus rencillas por ella, que escucha emocionada desde el otro lado de la puerta. ¿Será la reconciliación definitiva? Lorenzo desvela a Ciro lo que la logia quiere de ellos: los planos de los aviones de Manuel. Ciro trata de rebelarse, ¡es una locura! ¡Lo descubrirán! Ricardo sigue pendiendo de un hilo: o encuentra pruebas del sabotaje o le despedirán. Trini está desquiciada, quiere marcharse ya de ahí, no aguanta más. Manuel acepta, pero primero le contará algo. Si después sigue convencida de marcharse, la dejará ir…
Avance del capítulo 955 del jueves 26 de noviembre
Manuel cuenta a Trini su historia con Jana y su amor por Julieta: debe hacer justicia para poder vivir ahora su amor sin remordimientos. Ella, emocionada, acepta quedarse, pero pide protección para su hermana. Adriano y Jacobo descubren a Martina escuchando y hacen las paces: es curioso cómo funcionan “las parejas de tres”. Lorenzo mete prisa a Ciro con los planos, la logia los espera. Aunque el joven dice que no va a ser fácil, termina abriendo la caja fuerte para coger unos pocos planos… Ricardo no quiere involucrar a nadie del servicio, pero necesita buscar algo contra Julio, y pide cobertura a Teresa para poder salir sin que nadie lo sepa. La relación entre las cocineras mejora, para disgusto de Tomasa. Tendrá que buscar otra víctima de sus manipulaciones… Curro y Manuel cambian a Trini de lugar: se quedará en la posada hasta que el juez los llame a declarar. Así, al menos, verá el sol… pero sigue en peligro. Nadie puede saber que se esconde aquí.
Avance del capítulo 956 del viernes 27 de noviembre
Lorenzo acepta el ritmo de Ciro para entregar los planos: poco a poco. Es importante que nadie los eche en falta. Además, Máximo le advierte que le está vigilando… Curro consigue una habitación para Trini en la posada a la espera de que el juez acepte el caso y la llame a declarar. Pero aquí no podrá recibir visitas, ¿aguantará el encierro? Ángela interroga a Curro por la cena que dijo tener la noche anterior. Él da un relato vago y cuando ella propone pasar un rato juntos, él vuelve a escaquearse: Máximo le ha pedido una reunión. Ángela intuye que le pasa algo que no le cuenta… ¿Descubrirá la verdad? Tomasa inicia un acercamiento a Samuel, le recuerda al padre Tiago, un buen hombre, el cura que tanto le alivió a ella en el pasado. Samuel se ofrece a confesarla, pero de momento, la mujer declina la oferta. Petra advierte a Samuel que tenga cuidado... Martina está de buen humor, parece feliz. ¿Ha cambiado algo de su situación? ¿Ha tomado alguna decisión? Adriano y ella se besan cuando alguien les interrumpe. ¿Les habrán pillado?

noticias.titulo: Sánchez desembarca en Murcia para medir fuerzas en su último domingo de campaña
noticias.texto:
En directo: Sánchez desembarca en Murcia para medir fuerzas en su último domingo de campaña
- El mitin del PSOE coincide con el de Feijóo, que se celebra en la misma ciudad con media hora de diferencia
El presidente del Gobierno y candidato del PSOE a la reelección, Pedro Sánchez, desembarca en Murcia en su último domingo de campaña para tratar de atraer el voto en una comunidad donde está en juego hasta el último escaño y desafiando su declaración como 'persona non grata' por parte de la cámara autonómica.
El acto tendrá lugar en el Pabellón Príncipe de Asturias a partir de las 11.30 horas. Sánchez estará precedido por el secretario general del PSOE en la Región de Murcia, Francisco Lucas, y la cabeza de lista al Congreso por esa circunscripción, la secretaria de Estado de Telecomunicaciones e Infraestructuras Digitales, María González Veracruz.
Los pronósticos para la Región de Murcia son dispares. En la última encuesta del CIS, PSOE y PP aparecen igualados con horquillas de entre tres y cuatro escaños, mientras que Vox conseguiría dos o tres diputados y Frente Amplio podría obtener uno. Sin embargo, otros sondeos hablan de una posible subida de Vox hasta segunda fuerza por delante de los socialistas. Por ello, los de Pedro Sánchez tratarán de llamar a la participación este domingo y movilizar el voto en su favor para hacerse con el último escaño.
Sánchez y Feijóo miden fuerzas en la misma ciudad
Por otro lado, tras el tenso debate cara a cara con el líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ambos candidatos vuelven a medir fuerzas para el 29-N, esta vez con actos de campaña paralelos. A pocos kilómetros del de Sánchez, en la plaza del Cardenal Belluga de Murcia, el PP ha organizado un mitin de su candidato, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. Ambos coinciden no solo en la ubicación, sino también en la hora, ya que empezarán con media hora de diferencia.
Para promocionar el acto de Sánchez, la federación socialista de Murcia ha compartido en redes carteles con lemas como "¡Persona non grata acercándose a Murcia!" o "Ya llega, que viene el perro", en un guiño a la moción de la Asamblea de la Región de Murcia para declarar a Sánchez "persona non grata", aprobada con los votos del PP y Vox y de los dos diputados del Grupo Mixto el pasado 3 de noviembre.

noticias.titulo: Feijoo da un mitin en Murcia tras el baño de multitudes de Valencia donde pidió "no confiarse"
noticias.texto:
Directo | Feijoo da un mitin en Murcia tras el baño de multitudes de Valencia donde pidió "no confiarse"
- Llega al último domingo de campaña después del acto en la Plaza de Toros de Valencia
- En el PP apelan a la movilización e insisten en que "no hay nada ganado"
El candidato del PP a la Presidencia del Gobierno, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, participa este domingo en un mitin en Murcia, junto al presidente de la Región de Murcia, Fernando López Miras; la candidata número uno al Congreso por esta región, Miriam Guardiola, y la alcaldesa de la ciudad, Rebeca Pérez.
Feijóo ha llegado a la plaza del Cardenal Belluga con una canción nueva que habla de "cambio, cambio". Se trata del último domingo de campaña electoral después del gran acto multitudinario que celebró el PP este sábado en la plaza de Toros de Valencia, donde reunió a 12.000 personas, entre militantes y simpatizantes llegados de todos los puntos de la Comunidad Valencina, y donde advirtió de que en el PSOE eran "capaces de todo".
Se da la circunstancia de que este domingo el candidato socialista, Pedro Sánchez, también se encuentra en la ciudad de Murcia, participando en un acto electoral del PSOE en el pabellón Príncipe de Asturias de la misma ciudad.
Tras este acto de Murcia, Feijóo iniciará este lunes la última semana de campaña, que estará cargada de entrevistas y en la que participará en mitines en ciudades como Alicante y Murcia, y en el debate a cuatro el próximo jueves. El viernes será el cierre de campaña en una ciudad que todavía está por determinar y que dependerá, según afirman fuentes 'populares', de cómo vayan las encuestas internas del partido.
Desde Génova, llaman a la movilización en la recta final y advierten a los suyos de que no hay que confiarse, aunque las encuestas les sean positivas, porque no hay "nada ganado" aún. De hecho, estas mismas fuentes hablan de que hay "unos 20 escaños que bailan", en concreto, el "último escada de cada provincia". Además, creen que hay "35 lugares" en los podría cogerlo el PP. También consideran que han logrado "taponar la fuga" de votos a Vox.
(NOTICIA EN ELABORACIÓN...)

noticias.titulo: Del caso Nvidia a la red de inteligencia china: ¿cómo opera Pekín para ganar la carrera tecnológica?
noticias.texto:
Del caso Nvidia a la red de inteligencia china: ¿cómo opera Pekín para ganar la carrera tecnológica?
- La caída del cofundador de Nvidia destapa una maquinaria que rastrea tecnología en EE. UU. e influencia política en Europa
- Del robo en laboratorios universitarios a la ofensiva industrial, los expertos urgen a construir una cultura de seguridad europea
Durante décadas, millones de usuarios han convivido con el nombre de Nvidia en una pequeña pegatina junto al teclado de su portátil. El fabricante de tarjetas gráficas es hoy el principal proveedor de los chips que alimentan la inteligencia artificial y una empresa decisiva en el pulso tecnológico entre Estados Unidos y China.
Pero el gigante tecnológico acaba de sufrir el mayor seísmo de su historia: en pocas semanas ha perdido cerca de 1,5 billones de dólares, según el Financial Times, tras el escándalo que ha afectado a uno de sus fundadores, Jensen Huang, quien mantuvo una relación extramatrominial con una cliente y empresaria china, Alice Huang, sospechosa de desviar microchips avanzados hacia Pekín y bajo escrutinio estadounidense desde 2024.
